You describe a piece of work as a Task — answer a question, fix a bug and open a pull request, review every pull request in a repository — and Orka runs it in your cluster, keeps a durable record of what happened, and returns the result through a REST API, a CLI, a web dashboard, or the chat and editor tools your team already uses. Model API keys and Git credentials stay in the cluster. People, CI jobs, and agents get scoped client credentials — Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens, OIDC tokens, or transaction tokens — instead, and the platform team decides which models, tools, and repositories are allowed. See it before you install it The dashboard demo runs the real Orka dashboard in your browser on sample data for a fictional company, with a guided tour. Nothing is sent to a cluster or a model. The demo videos show the same features on a live cluster. Experimental Orka is under active development. APIs, custom resources, and behavior may change between releases, and it is not yet recommended for production use.

Three custom resources cover most of what you write: Resource What it is Provider A model backend — Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, or any compatible endpoint — and the Secret that holds its API key. Agent A reusable configuration: model, system prompt, tools, and optionally a coding-agent runtime. A template, not a running process. Task One unit of work. Create a Task to make something happen. A Task points at an Agent, and an Agent points at a Provider. A Task has one of three types, and each type runs somewhere different: Type What runs Where it runs ai Orka's own AI worker, which calls the model in a loop with built-in tools such as web search and code execution A per-Task Kubernetes Job agent A coding-agent CLI — Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, or OpenCode — working on a git repository A warm, controller-owned pool, so later Tasks start in seconds container Any container command. No model involved. A per-Task Kubernetes Job Every Task leaves a record you can come back to: its phase, result, artifacts, logs, and an event timeline. A coding agent never holds a Git credential. When it changes a repository, a separate publisher pushes the change and Orka records a verified delivery receipt for the branch or pull request. Architecture explains the full picture, and the Glossary defines every term.

Ask a model, with built-in tools for web search, code execution, URL fetching, and file access. Getting started Hand a coding task to an agent. Codex, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, or OpenCode works on a clean checkout, and Orka publishes the branch and pull request. Agent runtimes Run build and test steps in any container image. Container tasks Run any Task on a schedule, with missed-run and overlap rules. Scheduled tasks Continue a conversation across Tasks with Sessions. Session continuity

Delegate. A coordinator agent splits work across specialists, within the depth, allowlist, and concurrency limits you set. Multi-agent coordination Work toward a goal. An autonomous coordinator plans, delegates, and re-plans across iterations until the goal is met. Autonomous tasks Remember. Agents propose memories, and people review them before any agent uses them. Memory

Review every pull request as it arrives and post findings back. Repository monitors Turn an issue into a pull request by adding the orka:implement label. Planning, implementation, review, and repair follow. Issue-to-PR automation Find security issues with a threat model, validated findings, and remediation pull requests. Security scanning Measure the cost of delivery as tokens per merged pull request. Usage and PR outcomes

Chat with an orchestrator that creates and runs Tasks for you. Interactive chat Watch and steer work in the web dashboard. Web dashboard Script it with the orka CLI. CLI reference Point Claude Code, Cursor, or Continue at Orka through OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints, so nobody needs a provider key. OpenAI-compatible API · Anthropic-compatible API Reach agents from Microsoft Teams, Telegram, or other agents over A2A. Gateways

Keep credentials away from coding agents. Their model keys sit behind a proxy, and Git credentials go only to the publisher. Security Approve consequential actions before they run. Human approval Give agents your own tools — HTTP APIs and MCP servers — behind outbound access policies. Agents, skills, and tools Let people act as themselves by linking their own GitHub account, with approval on every write. Connectors Trace everything with OpenTelemetry and a durable per-Task event history. Observability · Execution events

Bring your own agent runtime, such as an AgentKit container or a Microsoft Foundry hosted agent. Bring your own agent runtime Run agents in sandboxes that suspend, resume, and checkpoint their files. Execution workspaces

If you are an AI agent or a script learning Orka, these pages are the dense ones: Glossary for the vocabulary, and Architecture for components and lifecycles. Resource reference for every custom resource field. API reference and API authorization for HTTP routes and the permissions each needs. CLI command reference for every command and flag, generated from the binary. Built-in tools for the tools Orka gives agents and their parameters. Two rules prevent most surprises. Create resources in the namespace the controller watches (orka-system by default), because resources anywhere else are silently ignored. And treat a Task as done only when its phase is Succeeded — for a coding agent that changes a repository, status.delivery also records the verified result. To work on the Orka source itself, read AGENTS.md in the repository.

These projects live outside the main repository and are versioned separately: Project What it adds orka-gateway-teams Talk to Orka Agents from Microsoft Teams chats and channels. orka-gateway-telegram Talk to Orka Agents from Telegram private chats. orka-gateway-a2a Call Orka Agents from any A2A client. agentkit Build an agent from YAML into a container image, then run it as an Orka runtime. orka-runtime-foundry Run Microsoft Foundry hosted agents as Orka runtimes. orka-integration-kontxt Issue and exchange transaction tokens with Kontxt. orka-integration-agentgateway Route outbound tool calls through agentgateway. orka-workspace The shared execution workspace API and its provider controllers. sessionkit Move Codex conversations between machines and Orka. Vekil A model gateway that fronts GitHub Copilot, OpenAI, Anthropic, and others for coding agents.
Questions, bug reports, and ideas are welcome in GitHub issues. To contribute code, start with CONTRIBUTING.md and the Development guide. Report vulnerabilities privately as described in SECURITY.md.

An Agent can have its own identity in an external identity provider. Tools that call outside services then authenticate as that Agent, not as the namespace or a shared service account. The first issuer is a Microsoft Entra agent identity. There are two ways to use it: Self: the Agent calls a resource as itself, with the app roles granted to its agent identity. For example, an inventory agent that may read one storage container. Delegated: the Agent calls a resource on behalf of the person who started the Task, with on-behalf-of tokens. Entra limits the call to what the agent identity was granted, and the resource limits it to what that person may do. This guide sets up both end to end. The design is ADR 0039. Delegated mode is read-only today Delegated mode runs only on built-in runtimes (codex, claude, copilot, opencode), because those are the only ones whose network Orka controls. Built-in runtimes cannot ask a person for approval yet (#770), and Orka hides write-class connector tools from runtimes that cannot ask. Until that lands, delegated Tools can only read.

In Entra, an agent identity blueprint stands for this Orka installation. Its federated identity credential trusts the controller's Kubernetes ServiceAccount, so no client secret is stored. Each Agent that needs an identity gets an agent identity under the blueprint, with the app roles it needs. In Kubernetes, an Agent names its agent identity. Claiming an identity needs the bind permission on that exact identity, and running work as an identity-bound Agent needs use on the Agent. An OutboundAccessPolicy in agentIdentity mode says which resource a Tool calls and how. The policy never names an identity: it always comes from the Task's Agent. When a Task calls the Tool, the controller asks Entra for a token and injects it into that one request. Tokens never reach the agent runtime, the Task, or logs, and every call writes an audit record.

A cluster whose ServiceAccount token issuer is reachable by Entra. On AKS, enable the OIDC issuer and read its URL with az aks show -g <group> -n <cluster> --query oidcIssuerProfile.issuerUrl -o tsv. An az session for the tenant, as someone who holds these Entra roles, or an administrator who holds them to run the steps that need them: Agent ID Administrator to create the blueprint and agent identities (steps 1 and 2); Privileged Role Administrator to grant Microsoft Graph app roles (step 2), the least-privileged built-in role for that assignment; for Delegated mode, Cloud Application Administrator or Application Administrator to grant the tenant-wide delegated consent in steps 7 and 8 (admin consent roles). Orka installed with Helm in the namespace team-a, with built-in RuntimePools. A release reconciles only its own namespace, so everything below lives there. A model gateway Orka can reach, and a model it serves for the Agent in step 5: built-in RuntimePools reach models only through it (Connect a model gateway). No privileged or hostPath Pod able to run on the controller's node, since one could read the controller's blueprint credential from it: enforce the baseline Pod Security profile on that namespace (kubectl label ns team-a pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline). Admission checks only new Pods, so first run the label with --dry-run=server; it lists running Pods that break the profile. Delete them before you label the namespace; and enforce it on every other namespace whose Pods can be scheduled onto that node, or run the controller on dedicated nodes with the chart's nodeSelector and tolerations, together with admission control that keeps every other Pod from tolerating their taint or naming them in spec.nodeName. A taint alone keeps no one off (Security). No Pod running as the controller ServiceAccount except the controller Deployment's own; delete any other before you configure Orka, since it keeps the identity. Also delete, or move to another ServiceAccount, any other Deployment or ReplicaSet that runs as it, which the controller ServiceAccount's admission policy then leaves unable to run (Security). For Delegated mode, also: Orka's API reachable over HTTPS by the people who will link accounts; Entra sign-in configured for Orka (step 8); a cluster that enforces NetworkPolicy. The steps call Microsoft Graph with curl. Keep these values in your shell: TENANT=<tenant ID> ISSUER=<cluster OIDC issuer URL> # The controller ServiceAccount, whose name the chart derives from the release ORKA_SA=system:serviceaccount:team-a:$(kubectl -n team-a get deploy \ -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName}') SPONSOR=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) # the person responsible for the identities TOKEN=$(az account get-access-token --tenant "$TENANT" \ --scope https://graph.microsoft.com/.default --query accessToken -o tsv) graph() { curl -s -X "$1" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "OData-Version: 4.0" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https://graph.microsoft.com/$2" ${3:+-d "$3"}; } An az token worked for these Agent ID calls when the steps were tested. Microsoft documents that Agent ID APIs can refuse tokens that carry Directory.AccessAsUser.All, which az tokens do; if step 1 answers 403 for a signed-in user who holds the roles above, take TOKEN from an app granted the Agent ID Graph permissions instead (Agent ID setup).

Create the blueprint and its service principal, then let it trust the controller's ServiceAccount. SPONSOR is the object ID of the person responsible for it: you, as set above, or another user's object ID. graph POST v1.0/applications '{ "@odata.type": "Microsoft.Graph.AgentIdentityBlueprint", "displayName": "orka-<cluster>", "sponsors@odata.bind": ["https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/'"$SPONSOR"'"], "owners@odata.bind": ["https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/'"$SPONSOR"'"] }' BLUEPRINT=<appId from the response> BLUEPRINT_OBJ=<id from the response> graph POST v1.0/serviceprincipals/microsoft.graph.agentIdentityBlueprintPrincipal \ '{"appId": "'"$BLUEPRINT"'"}' graph POST "v1.0/applications/$BLUEPRINT_OBJ/federatedIdentityCredentials" '{ "name": "orka-controller", "issuer": "'"$ISSUER"'", "subject": "'"$ORKA_SA"'", "audiences": ["api://AzureADTokenExchange"] }' The subject must match the controller's ServiceAccount exactly, including its namespace.

graph POST beta/serviceprincipals/Microsoft.Graph.AgentIdentity '{ "displayName": "inventory-agent", "agentIdentityBlueprintId": "'"$BLUEPRINT"'", "sponsors@odata.bind": ["https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/'"$SPONSOR"'"] }' IDENTITY=<id from the response> An agent identity's object ID and its client ID (appId) are the same value, so $IDENTITY serves both as the service principal in Graph URLs and as the agentIdentityID and RBAC resource name below. Grant it the app roles its Tools need, as for any service principal. For example, Microsoft Graph's User.ReadBasic.All: read GRAPH_SP ROLE < <(graph GET "v1.0/servicePrincipals?\$filter=appId%20eq%20'00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000'&\$select=id,appRoles" | python3 -c "import json,sys;s=json.load(sys.stdin)['value'][0];print(s['id'],[a['id'] for a in s['appRoles'] if a['value']=='User.ReadBasic.All'][0])") graph POST "v1.0/servicePrincipals/$IDENTITY/appRoleAssignments" \ '{"principalId": "'"$IDENTITY"'", "resourceId": "'"$GRAPH_SP"'", "appRoleId": "'"$ROLE"'"}' For Azure resources, assign Azure RBAC roles to the agent identity instead. Only grant what the Agent's Tools need: these permissions are the upper bound of anything the Agent can do as itself.
documents.s: 2. Create an agent identity and grant it app roles

documents.t: Set the tenant and blueprint, and turn on the use check, which identity-bound Agents require: controller: agentUseAuthorization: enabled: true agentIdentity: entra: tenantID: <tenant ID> blueprintClientID: <blueprint appId> # authority: https://login.microsoftonline.us # sovereign clouds only With tenantID set, the chart mounts a projected ServiceAccount token audienced to api://AzureADTokenExchange into the controller, and the controller uses it as the blueprint's credential. use applies to every Agent With agentUseAuthorization.enabled, creating a Task, RepositoryScan, RepositoryMonitor, or GatewayBinding needs use on the Agents it names, for all Agents, not only identity-bound ones. Grant it before you turn it on.

Claiming the identity (bind) and running work as the Agent (use) are separate grants, in separate Roles, so whoever only starts Tasks cannot also claim the identity for an Agent they can edit: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: namespace: team-a name: inventory-agent-bind rules: - apiGroups: [core.orka.ai] resources: [agentidentities/entra] verbs: [bind] resourceNames: ["<agent identity appId>"] # who may claim this identity --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: namespace: team-a name: inventory-agent-use rules: - apiGroups: [core.orka.ai] resources: [agents] verbs: [use] resourceNames: [inventory-agent] # who may run work as the Agent Bind inventory-agent-bind only to whoever edits the Agent, and inventory-agent-use to whoever starts its Tasks. A cluster administrator already holds both. Everyone else needs a binding, including the ServiceAccount whose token orka uses: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: namespace: team-a name: inventory-agent-use subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount # a ServiceAccount that starts Tasks namespace: team-a name: orka-client - kind: User # a person signed in through Entra (step 9) apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io name: "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant ID>/v2.0#<subject>" roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: inventory-agent-use A person signed in through Entra is checked as the User <issuer>#<sub> from their sign-in token, not their email address: orka auth whoami -o json shows their issuer and subject.
documents.s: 4. Let a namespace claim the identity and use the Agent

documents.t: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: namespace: team-a name: inventory-agent spec: model: name: <model> identity: entra: agentIdentityID: "<agent identity appId>" runtime: type: codex defaultAllowedTools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch, graph-users] ceiling: allowedTools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch, graph-users] An Agent with an identity must set runtime.ceiling.allowedTools, so every Tool that can carry identity-backed data is one the Agent owner listed. List the runtime's built-in tools as well as your own, in both lists. The codex runtime enforces two built-in tool sets: all eight shown above, or exactly Read, Glob, and Grep for Tasks whose workspace intent is read (the default for a Task that names no workspace). An Agent that only reads should use the smaller set, which leaves out shell, file writes, and web access; brokered tools and Tools such as graph-users are listed on top of either. OpenCode's are Read, Write, Edit, apply_patch, Bash, Glob, Grep, and it also needs model.contextWindow and model.maxTokens. One identity belongs to one Agent. The first Agent to claim it holds it in status.identityClaim; another Agent naming it reports Ready=False. Check it: kubectl -n team-a get agent inventory-agent \ -o jsonpath='{.status.identityClaim}{"\n"}{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.message}{"\n"}{end}' IdentityVerified=True means the controller obtained a token for the identity from Entra. The controller keeps that answer for an hour, or until the Agent is edited, so an identity disabled in Entra turns it False and the Agent Ready=False within the hour, not at once. Token requests are not held to that hour: new tokens are refused as soon as Entra refuses them (see What stops identity-backed calls). A change to the Agent's spec checks again at once; metadata such as an annotation does not.
documents.s: 5. Bind the identity to an Agent

documents.t: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: OutboundAccessPolicy metadata: namespace: team-a name: graph-as-agent spec: agentIdentity: mode: Self entra: resource: https://graph.microsoft.com --- apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Tool metadata: namespace: team-a name: graph-users spec: description: Return the display name of one user in the directory. brokeredToolClass: read parameters: {type: object, properties: {}, additionalProperties: false} http: url: "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users?$top=1&$select=displayName" method: GET outboundAccessPolicyRef: name: graph-as-agent Point orka at this release in team-a, as in Connect to the API and Use the CLI but with this namespace. Forward the API in one terminal. The chart names the API Service from the release and any name override, so look it up by its api port: SVC=$(kubectl -n team-a get svc -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=<release> \ -o jsonpath='{.items[?(@.spec.ports[0].name=="api")].metadata.name}') kubectl -n team-a port-forward "svc/$SVC" 8080:8080 and in another, configure the CLI with a token for the orka-client ServiceAccount that step 4 lets run Tasks on the Agent: orka config set-server http://localhost:8080 orka config set-namespace team-a kubectl -n team-a create token orka-client | orka config set-token --file - Run a Task on the Agent that calls graph-users: orka task create "Call graph-users and tell me the display name it returns." \ --agent inventory-agent --name graph-self -n team-a orka task wait graph-self -n team-a orka task get graph-self -n team-a The controller requests a token for <resource>/.default as the agent identity and injects it as Authorization: Bearer. The Tool URL must be HTTPS, without template placeholders. The token goes wherever the Tool's URL points. Whoever may edit a Tool that the Agent's ceiling lists therefore decides where that Agent's token is sent, so treat edit access to those Tools as you treat the identity itself. Each call writes one audit record to the controller log under the agent-identity-audit logger: kubectl -n team-a logs deploy/orka-controller | grep agent-identity-audit A record names: the policy, the Agent and its UID, the identity, and the Task UID; the Tool and its method, and a digest of the call's arguments; for Delegated calls, a keyed pseudonym of the requester; the outcome (issued or refused) and, for a refusal, its reason: policy, binding, delegation, issuer, or canceled (see Troubleshooting). It never contains a token. issued means a token was handed out, not that the resource accepted the request.
documents.s: 6. Call a resource as the Agent (Self)

documents.t: Delegated mode needs more on both sides. The person who starts the Task must sign in to Orka through Entra, so Orka knows who they are, and must link an Entra account once, so Orka holds a user token it can exchange on their behalf.

The person's linked token must be addressed to the blueprint, so give the blueprint an API with one scope: SCOPE_ID=$(python3 -c "import uuid;print(uuid.uuid4())") graph PATCH "v1.0/applications/$BLUEPRINT_OBJ" '{ "identifierUris": ["api://'"$BLUEPRINT"'"], "api": {"oauth2PermissionScopes": [{ "id": "'"$SCOPE_ID"'", "value": "access_agent", "type": "User", "isEnabled": true, "adminConsentDisplayName": "Access agent", "adminConsentDescription": "Allow the application to access the agent on behalf of the signed-in user." }]} }' Then decide which delegated permissions agent identities under the blueprint may use, and consent to them. For Microsoft Graph's User.Read: BLUEPRINT_SP=<object ID of the blueprint principal from step 1> graph POST v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants '{"clientId": "'"$BLUEPRINT_SP"'", "consentType": "AllPrincipals", "resourceId": "'"$GRAPH_SP"'", "scope": "User.Read"}' graph POST "v1.0/applications/microsoft.graph.agentIdentityBlueprint/$BLUEPRINT_OBJ/inheritablePermissions" '{ "resourceAppId": "00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000", "inheritableScopes": {"@odata.type": "#microsoft.graph.allAllowedScopes", "kind": "allAllowed"}, "inheritableRoles": {"@odata.type": "#microsoft.graph.noRoles", "kind": "none"} }' These permissions are the most any delegated call can do. Each call can only do less: the person's own rights on the resource still apply.
documents.s: 7. Give the blueprint a scope and delegated permissions

documents.t: People sign in to this app, both to link their account and to sign in to Orka. Its redirect URI is Orka's connector callback: graph POST v1.0/applications '{ "displayName": "orka-signin", "signInAudience": "AzureADMyOrg", "isFallbackPublicClient": true, "web": {"redirectUris": ["https://orka.example.com/api/v1/connections/callback"]}, "api": {"requestedAccessTokenVersion": 2, "oauth2PermissionScopes": [{ "id": "'"$(python3 -c "import uuid;print(uuid.uuid4())")"'", "value": "orka.access", "type": "User", "isEnabled": true, "adminConsentDisplayName": "Use Orka", "adminConsentDescription": "Sign in to the Orka API."}]}, "requiredResourceAccess": [{"resourceAppId": "'"$BLUEPRINT"'", "resourceAccess": [{"id": "'"$SCOPE_ID"'", "type": "Scope"}]}] }' FRONTEND=<appId>; FRONTEND_OBJ=<id> graph PATCH "v1.0/applications/$FRONTEND_OBJ" '{"identifierUris": ["api://'"$FRONTEND"'"]}' graph POST v1.0/servicePrincipals '{"appId": "'"$FRONTEND"'"}' FRONTEND_SP=<id from the response> graph POST v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants '{"clientId": "'"$FRONTEND_SP"'", "consentType": "AllPrincipals", "resourceId": "'"$BLUEPRINT_SP"'", "scope": "access_agent"}' graph POST v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants '{"clientId": "'"$FRONTEND_SP"'", "consentType": "AllPrincipals", "resourceId": "'"$FRONTEND_SP"'", "scope": "orka.access"}' Create a client secret for the connector and store it in Kubernetes without printing it: graph POST "v1.0/applications/$FRONTEND_OBJ/addPassword" '{"passwordCredential": {"displayName": "orka-connector"}}' | python3 -c "import json,sys;sys.stdout.write(json.load(sys.stdin)['secretText'])" | kubectl -n team-a create secret generic orka-signin --from-file=client-secret=/dev/stdin

controller: connectors: enabled: true callbackBaseUrl: https://orka.example.com oidc: issuer: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant ID>/v2.0 audience: <front-end appId> allowedSubjects: "<subject>,<subject>" # Entra subjects allowed to use Orka namespace: team-a People sign in with a token for api://<front-end appId>/orka.access. The Task's requester is then their verified Entra identity. Entra gives each person a different subject for each app, so a person's subject for this app is not known until they sign in to it. Have them sign in (step 10 shows how) and run orka -t "$ORKA_TOKEN" auth whoami. Until they are on the list, Orka answers 403 and names the subject to add: your sign-in is valid, but its subject "<subject>" is not allowed to use this Orka installation Add it to allowedSubjects and upgrade the release. A pattern with * matches any run of characters, so "*" admits every account the front-end app accepts; list subjects one by one unless that is what you want. Signed-in users are equal within their namespace Today, every subject on allowedSubjects can use every API route in the OIDC namespace. Kubernetes RBAC is not checked for them, except use and bind. Treat the allow-list as the access list. #1037 tracks authorizing signed-in users with RBAC.
documents.s: 9. Turn on connectors and Entra sign-in

documents.t: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: ConnectorProvider metadata: namespace: team-a name: entra-signin spec: displayName: Microsoft Entra oauth: authorizeURL: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant ID>/oauth2/v2.0/authorize tokenURL: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant ID>/oauth2/v2.0/token clientID: <front-end appId> clientSecretRef: {name: orka-signin, key: client-secret} clientAuthentication: ClientSecretPost scopes: read: ["api://<blueprint appId>/access_agent"] tools: - name: graphme class: read source: HTTP description: Return the signed-in person's own profile. parameters: {type: object, properties: {}, additionalProperties: false} http: url: "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me?$select=displayName,userPrincipalName" method: GET Request only the blueprint's scope. Entra leaves offline_access out of the scopes it reports as granted, so asking for it makes linking fail with scopes_denied (#1030). Without it there is no refresh token, so a link lasts until its access token expires, about an hour, and then the person links again. The provider's tools are the only operations a delegated token is released for. Each must have a Tool of the same name. Provider tool names reject hyphens and Kubernetes Tool names reject underscores, so a name both accept starts with a lowercase letter and uses only lowercase letters and digits, such as graphme (#1031). Each person signs in to Orka with a token for the front-end app, here with the device-code flow that isFallbackPublicClient enables, and then links once: DC=$(curl -s https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT/oauth2/v2.0/devicecode \ -d client_id=$FRONTEND -d scope="api://$FRONTEND/orka.access") echo "$DC" | python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['message'])" # After signing in in the browser: ORKA_TOKEN=$(curl -s https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT/oauth2/v2.0/token \ -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code -d client_id=$FRONTEND \ -d device_code="$(echo "$DC" | python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['device_code'])")" | python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['access_token'])") orka -t "$ORKA_TOKEN" connect entra-signin -n team-a --no-wait The consent page ends on an address that carries #completion=<value>. With no dashboard signed in as that person to finish the link, they copy the value and complete it with the same token, using the Connection name orka connect printed: orka -t "$ORKA_TOKEN" connection complete entra-signin-<digest> -n team-a --completion '<value>' The completion value expires a few minutes after consent, so they complete it right away. They pass the same token with -t to create Tasks. They should sign in with the same Entra account they use for Orka. Orka binds the link to their Orka sign-in, but does not check that the Entra account they link is the same one.
documents.s: 10. Describe the linked account and its tools

documents.t: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: OutboundAccessPolicy metadata: namespace: team-a name: graph-for-requester spec: agentIdentity: mode: Delegated delegated: providerRef: {name: entra-signin} maxDelegationAge: 1h entra: resource: https://graph.microsoft.com --- apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Tool metadata: namespace: team-a name: graphme spec: description: Return the requester's own profile, read through Microsoft Graph on their behalf. brokeredToolClass: read parameters: {type: object, properties: {}, additionalProperties: false} http: url: "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me?$select=displayName,userPrincipalName" method: GET outboundAccessPolicyRef: name: graph-for-requester Add graphme to the Agent's tools and ceiling. Then have a signed-in person create the Task through the API or orka, so it carries their identity. Tasks created with kubectl, by a ServiceAccount, or by a gateway have no verified requester, and delegated calls from them are refused. For each call, the controller: checks that the person's linked token is addressed to the blueprint; exchanges it on behalf of the person for a token for the resource; injects that token.
documents.s: 11. Call a resource for the requester

documents.t: Action Effect Delete the Agent, or remove spec.identity New calls from its Tasks are refused at once. The claim stays until bound Tasks end, so no other Agent can take the identity meanwhile Disable or delete the agent identity in Entra New tokens are refused. Cached tokens last at most five minutes, and the resource may still accept them until then; remove spec.identity from the Agent to stop new calls at once Cancel the Task (orka task cancel, or the dashboard) or delete it Its delegated calls are refused at once Stop a Session's turn (orka session cancel) The turn's Task is cancelled, so its delegated calls are refused. The Session takes the next message A Task above it in the delegation chain is cancelled or deleted Delegated calls from every Task below it are refused. A parent that finished normally does not stop its children maxDelegationAge passes Delegated calls are refused. It runs from the creation of the chain's root Task, whether the requester created it directly or with a Session message; time in the chat before that does not count. Child Tasks do not reset it; a new Session turn, which creates a new root Task, does The person disconnects or their link expires Delegated calls are refused

Symptom Cause Agent Ready=False: identity issuer "entra" is not configured agentIdentity.entra.tenantID and blueprintClientID are not both set Agent Ready=False: requires --agent-use-authorization-enabled Set agentUseAuthorization.enabled Agent Ready=False: must set runtime.ceiling.allowedTools Add a ceiling (step 5) Admission denies the Agent: caller is not authorized to bind the Agent's identity The editor lacks bind on agentidentities/entra for that identity ID IdentityVerified=False with AADSTS7000112 The agent identity is disabled in Entra IdentityVerified=False with AADSTS700016 or AADSTS70021 The blueprint ID is wrong, or its federated credential does not match the cluster issuer and controller ServiceAccount Task creation fails: not authorized to use agent … or caller is not authorized to use the Task's Agent The caller lacks use on the Agent Task fails: codex ACP runtime cannot exactly enforce provider-native tool restrictions A codex Agent must list either all eight built-in tools or, for a Task with workspace intent read, exactly Read, Glob, and Grep, in both defaultAllowedTools and the ceiling orka answers 403: your sign-in is valid, but its subject "…" is not allowed Add that subject to oidc.allowedSubjects (step 9) Linking fails with scopes_denied Remove offline_access from the provider's scopes Linking fails with consent_expired The consent link expires within minutes; run orka connect again and finish promptly Audit reason policy The policy changed since the Tool checked it, its target is not HTTPS, or it sets authSecretRef Audit reason binding The Task's identity no longer holds: the Agent was deleted or its spec.identity removed or changed, the claim is being released, or the Task was created before the identity was granted (create it again) Audit reason delegation A Delegated precondition failed: the Task has no verified requester, the person's link expired, maxDelegationAge passed, or the Task, a Task above it, or its Session was cancelled or deleted Audit reason issuer The token request failed: Entra refused it, or, for a Delegated call, the person's linked token is not addressed to the blueprint (the provider must request api://<blueprint appId>/access_agent). IdentityVerified checks only the identity's own app-only token, so it can stay True while delegated exchanges fail The agent sees only MCP broker call failed The audit record gives the reason category; it records no error text, so arguments and tokens cannot leak into it. Showing a safe reason to the agent is tracked in #742

The Agent, policy, and audit design are issuer-neutral. A second issuer adds a sibling of entra under Agent.spec.identity and in the policy, its own agentidentities/<issuer> permission, and its own controller settings. See ADR 0039 for how Google, AWS, Okta, Keycloak, and SPIFFE map onto it.

A type: agent Task runs a real coding-agent CLI — Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, or OpenCode — against a git repository. This page explains how Orka runs them: warm pools of runtime Pods, private sessions inside them, a strict separation between the agent and your credentials, and a durable record of every attempt. In short: Pools, not Jobs. Orka keeps a controller-owned RuntimePool per runtime profile. Its Pod scales to zero when idle and hosts several private RuntimeSessions when busy, so a Task usually starts in seconds. There is no per-Task Job and no fallback path. The agent edits; Orka publishes. The CLI works on a sanitized checkout with no Git credentials. When it finishes, Orka validates the change, and a separate Workspace/Publisher commits, pushes, and verifies it, optionally opening a pull request. Every attempt is durable. Orka records each prompt attempt, so a controller restart never sends the same prompt twice and an uncertain outcome is reported as uncertain. Models through a proxy. Runtimes reach your model gateway through Orka's authenticated provider proxy; no provider key enters the agent. Orka harness v2 (orka.harness.v2) is the controller-to-supervisor contract, carried over HTTP with NDJSON prompt streams. The supervisor in each runtime Pod drives the agent CLI over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) on stdin/stdout. These are separate protocols with independent versions. Orka owns the durable Task attempt, RuntimeSession identity, queueing, workspace validation, delivery receipt, transcript, and result projection; the runtime Pod owns only the short-lived provider process and ACP session for a fenced RuntimeSession. The built-in set is intentionally closed: codex, claude, copilot, and opencode. Operators can also register and conformance-test an external orka.harness.v2 AgentRuntime. A ready strict-governed registration selected through runtimeRef uses the same durable Task and RuntimeSession state machines, while the operator remains responsible for the external service lifecycle and capacity.

Runtime Agent.spec.runtime.type Packaging status Codex codex Immutable Codex ACP image definition is included. Configure a digest-pinned image. Claude claude Immutable Claude ACP image definition is included. Configure a digest-pinned image. Copilot copilot Immutable Copilot ACP image definition is included. Configure a digest-pinned image. OpenCode opencode Immutable OpenCode ACP image definition is included. Configure a digest-pinned image. Built-in runtimes can mount extra command-line tools from read-only toolbox images declared in Agent.spec.runtime.toolboxes; see Toolboxes. Codex, Claude, and OpenCode can also receive Agent Skills from digest-pinned images declared in Agent.spec.runtime.skills; see Runtime skills. External runtimes register through an AgentRuntime that implements orka.harness.v2. Current-generation conformance proves the exact instance, profile, cancellation, duplicate, and workspace-governance claims. Dispatch revalidates the frozen registration, authentication authority, and observed runtime identity before every mutation. See Bring your own AgentRuntime and the adapter contract.

Task (type: agent) -> durable ACP attempt and queue reservation -> built-in path: central authenticated provider proxy -> Vekil/model backend -> controller-owned RuntimePool for one trust domain/profile -> one exact runtime Pod (0 or 1 replica) -> private RuntimeSession HOME/workspace/UID + provider process -> per-session loopback MCP proxy -> controller prompt broker -> external path: authenticated operator-owned AgentRuntime endpoint -> exact fenced RuntimeSession + non-reconnectable prompt stream -> registered provider, MCP, and workspace-governance profile -> workspace delta validation -> artifact + credential brokers -> separate Workspace/Publisher identity -> clean-room clone, prepare, push, verify, and optional PR reconciliation -> durable execution and delivery status projected onto the Task A shared runtime Pod is a same-trust-domain density optimization, not a tenant isolation boundary. Different namespaces/profile digests are assigned different logical pools.

RuntimePools are controller-owned implementation resources. Do not hand-author them for normal built-in Tasks. The controller derives a pool from the Task namespace, runtime type, model, immutable adapter/image digests, tool and approval policy, workspace intent, proxy credential scope, and resource class. The first-release defaults are: one active Pod per pool; up to 10 resident RuntimeSessions; up to 4 concurrently running prompts; scale from zero on durable demand; admit new sessions only while lifecycle is Serving and admission is Accepting; drain to Quiescent before scale-down or replacement. Pool lifecycle is: Serving is the only lifecycle that admits a new RuntimeSession, and only while status.admissionState is also Accepting. Two more lifecycles are not shown above because the controller can enter them from anywhere: Degraded (something is wrong — rollout failed, scheduling failed, quota denied) and Ambiguous (the controller cannot prove what the pool is doing). Both close admission, so new work waits instead of landing on a pool nobody can vouch for. Capacity reservations live in RuntimePool.status and use Kubernetes resourceVersion compare-and-swap. The dispatcher claims a resident/prompt slot before changing an attempt to Reserved, renews or converts it as work moves through the session lifecycle, and reclaims expired reservations after restart. Inspect pools with: orka runtime-pool list orka runtime-pool get '<pool-name>' -o yaml kubectl get runtimepools

The durable Task execution state is independent from the top-level compatibility phase. It is drawn in full under Task lifecycle. Two states are worth calling out here: SubmittedUnknown records a loss in the submit acknowledgement window — Orka sent the prompt and never learned whether the runtime received it. OutcomeUnknown is terminal for that attempt. Do not treat it as a generic retryable failure; the whole point is that a retry might run your prompt a second time. For built-in runtimes, the RuntimeSession lifecycle is: Reading it: Only an idle session can accept a prompt or be evicted. Everything else is busy holding state that must not be interrupted. The session freezes the validated workspace delta and waits in publication_prepared. The controller and clean-room Publisher prepare the commit, push, and verify the remote, recording progress in a Publication. The controller then asks the supervisor to finalize the session using the terminal publication receipt. poisoned is the escape hatch for uncertainty. A session that cannot prove it cleaned up its processes, that its workspace is intact, or that publication was safe is poisoned and deleted rather than reused. The pool may be recycled with it. Any state above can reach poisoned; the arrows are omitted so the main flow stays readable. Validation, publication, finalization, and the release of the Session lease all complete before the Task shows a terminal status. A Succeeded Task means the work is done and verified, not merely started.

ACP control decisions are Kubernetes-authoritative: ControllerEpoch, PromptAttempt, RuntimeSessionControl, BranchClaim, Publication, and ExternalEffect status transitions use resourceVersion compare-and-swap; coordination Leases serialize controller-epoch mutation and one logical Session mutation at a time; RuntimePool.status owns exact-instance lifecycle, demand, capacity, and reservation state. SQLite is not a second ACP control authority. It persists transcript and SessionTurn payloads, deferred outbox projections, and artifacts behind the Kubernetes fences. Cross-store finalization binds the exact outbox projection before releasing the Session lease.

A fence is a set of identifiers attached to every mutating request. The receiver compares them against what it believes to be true and rejects anything that does not match exactly. The problem it solves: a controller can be network-partitioned, lose leadership, come back, and try to finish work it started — while a new controller is already doing that work. Without a fence, the old controller's late request looks identical to a legitimate one. With a fence, its stale controller epoch does not match and the request is refused. The identifiers nest, from the widest scope to the narrowest: Field Rejects Because controllerEpoch a controller that lost leadership a new controller has taken over runtimePoolUID / runtimePoolGeneration a request for a deleted or reconfigured pool the pool it was written for no longer exists in that shape runtimeInstanceID / supervisorBootID a request aimed at a Pod that has since restarted the process that held the session state is gone runtimeProfileDigest a request assuming a different image or profile the runtime is not the one the request was planned against runtimeSessionUID / runtimeSessionGeneration a request for a session that was recreated the new session is not the old one, even under the same name operationID reuse of an operation ID with a different request digest one operation ID identifies one immutable request requestDigest a request whose body was altered in transit the digest covers the whole request expiresAt a request that sat in a queue too long the world may have moved on Session-scoped fields are omitted for pool-wide operations such as drain, which have no session. Identical retries with the same operationID and requestDigest replay the recorded response without repeating the effect, provided the fences and expiry are still valid. These replays return HTTP 200; reusing the operation ID with a different digest returns digest_conflict with HTTP 409. If an authenticated drain request or status probe fails during rollout or scale-down, the controller marks the RuntimePool as Degraded, closes admission, and preserves the old Pod. Later reconciles recheck the drain, and replacement or scale-down requires authenticated quiescence. Prompt or publication outcomes that cannot be proven may put a Task in OutcomeUnknown; see Task lifecycle.
documents.s: What a fence is, and why every request carries one

documents.t: Provider credentials are separate from Git credentials. Built-in ACP Agents do not set secretRef: the controller scopes each RuntimePool to the central authenticated provider proxy, which injects the upstream Vekil/model credential outside the ACP child process. apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: codex-reviewer spec: runtime: type: codex defaultMaxTurns: 20 defaultAllowBash: true defaultAllowedTools: - Read - Glob - Grep model: name: gpt-6-astra OpenCode model IDs use provider/model form, for example openai/gpt-6-astra. OpenCode selects apply_patch for GPT-family models and edit/write for others; Orka normalizes those aliases into one governed mutation capability, so allowing one exposes the group and disallowing one closes the group. For read-intent workspaces, Orka also disables Bash and OpenCode Grep because Grep cannot carry the secret-file exclusions applied to OpenCode Read; Read and Glob remain available when allowed by policy. The cloned repository is untrusted input, so built-in runtimes do not load agent configuration from it that could run commands or change provider routing outside the Orka tool policy: Claude loads no settings files, neither from the repository's .claude/ directory nor from the session home. Repository hooks, env, and CLAUDE.md are ignored. Orka's runtime skills reach Claude as a read-only plugin instead. Codex does not trust the session workspace, so it ignores the repository's .codex/config.toml, including MCP servers and shell environment settings. It still reads AGENTS.md. Copilot runs only hooks from the image's managed policy. Repository hooks in .github/hooks, .github/copilot/settings.json, and .claude/settings.json, and hooks in the session home, do not run. Copilot CLI 1.0.96 still reads repository instruction files, such as AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md, as prompt context. OpenCode 1.19.0 imports project plugins even when project configuration is disabled. Orka therefore refuses an OpenCode session whose workspace root contains .opencode/, opencode.json, or opencode.jsonc, and fails the Task with RuntimeSessionStartFailed. It does not remove those files, because they may be published. The check runs on every session start, including a resume, and again before Orka restarts an adapter that exited while idle. That restart also checks the session's own OpenCode configuration folder and ~/.opencode, which OpenCode reads as global configuration and which the agent can write. Before that check, Orka stops any running operator access command and refuses new ones until the restarted OpenCode accepts the prompt, because those commands run as the session's identity. If the agent added configuration or plugins to any of these, Orka retires the session instead of restarting OpenCode. The replacement session gets fresh configuration folders but the same workspace, so it starts only if the workspace still passes the check. For built-in RuntimePools, Task-level spec.agentRuntime contains runtime overrides such as maxTurns, allowedTools, disallowedTools, and allowBash. For runtimeRef, the registered external profile owns provider, model, prompt, skill, tool, and runtime defaults. Its capabilities.mcpPolicy stores the exact tool and approval policy represented by the profile digests, and Orka uses that same policy for conformance and dispatch. The Agent must omit spec.model, spec.systemPrompt, spec.skills, enabled spec.tools, defaultMaxTurns, defaultAllowedTools, defaultAllowBash, and defaultReasoningEffort. Disabled Agent tool entries are inert and accepted. Task-level allowedTools must equal the registered allowlist when brokered tools are exposed. Orka rejects maxTurns, disallowedTools, and allowBash because those values are fixed by the registration. Repository configuration belongs at top-level spec.workspace.

The default* fields are only defaults: a Task can replace them with its own allowedTools, allowBash, or maxTurns. To set limits that a Task can narrow but never exceed, add a ceiling: spec: runtime: type: claude defaultAllowedTools: [Read, Grep] defaultAllowBash: false defaultMaxTurns: 20 ceiling: allowedTools: [Read, Grep, Edit] allowBash: false maxTurns: 40 Before a Task is bound, Orka resolves the policy it would run with (the Task's override, otherwise the Agent default) and fails the Task if that policy goes beyond the ceiling: Task asks for Result nothing the Agent defaults: Read, Grep, 20 turns allowedTools: [Read] Read allowedTools: [Read, Write] fails: ceiling does not allow tool "Write" allowBash: true with Bash in allowedTools fails: ceiling forbids Bash maxTurns: 100 fails: ceiling allows at most 40 turns How the check reads a policy: Tools. The check uses the tools the runtime would actually expose, after disallowedTools, the Bash gate, and runtime normalization (such as OpenCode's alias grouping) apply. Tool names ignore case. Brokered and custom tool names count too. For scoped names such as Bash(git status), a bare ceiling entry covers every scope of that tool, but a scoped entry covers only that exact scope, compared case-sensitively. A disallowedTools entry narrows the request only when it matches an allowed name exactly, as at dispatch, so bash does not remove Bash. No explicit list. A Task with no allowlist and an Agent with no defaultAllowedTools resolve to the full native tool set, less anything disallowedTools or allowBash: false removes. That usually exceeds a tool ceiling, so set defaultAllowedTools within the ceiling. An allowlist of only blank entries is judged the same way, so it can never slip past a ceiling. Likewise, allowBash defaults to true and maxTurns to 50 when nothing sets them. Explicit empty list. ceiling.allowedTools: [] permits no tools. Unknown keys. A key ceiling does not define, such as a misspelled allowedTool, is rejected rather than dropped, so a typo cannot remove a limit. Coordination tools. The send_message and check_messages tools that Orka injects into delegated child Tasks are not counted against the ceiling. A Task that lists them in its own allowedTools is judged on them as usual. Gateway replies. Eligible gateway Tasks without an explicit allowlist normally get reply_in_conversation implicitly. Under a ceiling, Orka keeps that grant only when the resulting policy still fits: the ceiling must list reply_in_conversation, and the native tool set must fit it (OpenCode's default list, or another runtime's set narrowed by disallowedTools or allowBash: false). Otherwise, include reply_in_conversation in an explicit allowlist and in the ceiling. runtimeRef Agents. Only allowedTools applies; the registered profile already fixes Bash and the turn budget. The check uses the tools the registered AgentRuntime policy exposes, so a tool the registration lists but also denies does not count against the ceiling. Codex. Every Codex session can run shell commands. Even a read-only session with only Glob, Grep, and Read runs read commands through the shell. A Codex Task therefore always fails a ceiling.allowBash: false, so use another runtime when the ceiling must exclude the shell. A Task is checked against the Agent generation it binds to. Changing a ceiling does not affect Tasks that are already bound. When an Agent's own explicit defaults exceed its ceiling, the Agent reports Ready=False with the reason. A ceiling limits what callers may request through the Task API. It does not stop anyone who can edit the Agent from changing the ceiling, so restrict update on Agents to the people who own them.

Agent Tasks default to intent: read when workspace.intent is omitted, but setting it explicitly makes review intent clear. apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: review-repository spec: type: agent agentRef: name: codex-reviewer prompt: Review the authentication package. Do not modify files. workspace: intent: read gitRepo: https://github.com/example/project.git ref: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567 readCredentialRef: name: project-read subPath: services/auth agentRuntime: maxTurns: 20 allowBash: true timeout: 20m The clean-room workspace boundary resolves project-read for one clone/read operation, verifies the source baseline, removes credentials, and stores a sanitized workspace artifact. The runtime downloads that artifact without SCM credentials or direct SCM publication access. A read Task succeeds only after validation proves the final tree still matches the verified baseline. Unexpected changes are classified ReadOnlyWorkspaceModified and poison the RuntimeSession.

Video demo Watch From chat to a GitHub pull request. Source read, target read, target write, and forge API credentials are distinct roles, even when an operator deliberately backs multiple roles with the same Secret. apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: update-documentation spec: type: agent agentRef: name: codex-reviewer prompt: Update the authentication documentation and run its focused checks. workspace: intent: write gitRepo: https://github.com/example/project.git branch: main readCredentialRef: name: project-read publicationGitRepo: https://github.com/example/project.git publicationReadCredentialRef: name: project-publication-read publicationCredentialRef: name: project-publish forgeCredentialRef: name: project-forge pushBranch: orka/update-auth-docs prBaseBranch: main createPR: true prTitle: "fix: handle empty filters" prBody: "Reject empty filters before querying." agentRuntime: maxTurns: 40 allowBash: true timeout: 40m The ACP child may edit the materialized checkout, but its Git configuration, refs, hooks, filters, remotes, and history are never trusted for publication. After prompt settlement, the supervisor freezes the session process tree and produces a bounded, content-addressed workspace delta. The separate Workspace/Publisher then: creates a clean clone at the persisted baseline with the source-read credential; applies the validated delta; prepares a deterministic Orka-owned commit; records the exact tree, commit, and artifact digests; compare-and-swap publishes the exact commit with the target-write credential; independently verifies the remote ref with the target-read credential; reconciles a pull request with the forge-only credential when createPR: true. At reservation, Orka freezes the selected Secret UID/resourceVersion and key for each role. The credential broker releases a value only to the Workspace/Publisher for the exact active operation. No Git or forge credential enters the runtime Pod. Branch push is the minimum durable delivery; pull-request reconciliation is opt-in. Workspace deltas and prepared publication artifacts cross the controller API through short-lived artifact capabilities bound to the operation, method, path, digest, size, media type, identity, and expiry. The Publisher does not hold the artifact signing key. Every spec.workspace field, with defaults, is in the Resource reference.

Pull-request text comes from the frozen Task spec and prompt, never from files or output produced by the agent. Orka rejects secret-like titles and bodies at runtime before publication, including prompt-derived titles. Orka reserves comments beginning with <!-- orka.publisher.pr- for reconciliation. Remove these comments when copying an existing PR body into prBody. The publisher keeps the original title and body when reconciling an existing pull request. A continuation does not overwrite a person's edits. prTitle and prBody apply only when createPR: true. Supplying presentation text alone does not request a pull request; it can remain configured on branch-only Tasks. Explicit prTitle or prBody overrides require a publisher that advertises pull-request-presentation.v1. During a rolling update, Tasks with overrides wait before prompt admission. Tasks without overrides can finish with an older publisher's generic PR text. Do not embed credentials, query strings, or fragments in repository URLs.

status.delivery is the authoritative non-secret receipt. Intermediate states include Validating, Preparing, Prepared, Publishing, and Verifying. Terminal outcomes include: ReadValidated — read-only tree matches the verified baseline; NoChange — a write Task produced no validated change; VerifiedExact — the remote branch equals the prepared commit; DeliveredSuperseded — the prepared commit is present and a verified descendant now leads the branch; ReadOnlyWorkspaceModified — a read Task changed the workspace; CredentialBlocked — a required credential could not be resolved or used; DeliveryConflict — branch ownership or exact-ref reconciliation failed; PublicationOutcomeUnknown — the remote could not be observed after bounded reconciliation; CancelledBeforePublish — cancellation won before publication. Use orka task status <name> or inspect the Task YAML to see execution, RuntimePool, and delivery data.

Use spec.sessionRef for canonical transcript continuity and serialized mutation of one logical session: spec: sessionRef: name: repository-review-session workspace: intent: read gitRepo: https://github.com/example/project.git A RuntimeSession is ephemeral. If its Pod is replaced, Orka creates a fresh provider process from the verified workspace baseline. Codex runtimes advertising native Session support can restore a private SessionKit checkpoint into an isolated home, then load its original UUID with current credentials and policy. Other sessions use the canonical transcript. Neither path replays an accepted prompt. See Codex session migration for the supported format and import/export commands.

A built-in runtime Pod uses a digest-pinned image, a read-only root filesystem, and no service-account token. It holds no Git credential and has no route to source control. Its model traffic goes only to the central provider proxy, and each RuntimeSession reaches Orka tools only through a credential-protected loopback MCP proxy that the controller rechecks on every call. A call to a tool outside the frozen policy, such as one the model names on its own, is refused there as a failed tool call and the prompt continues. The Workspace/Publisher, which does hold the Git credentials, has no access to models or tools. Security describes each boundary.

ACP is active when the controller runs in harness-v2 mode; there is no separate ACP enablement flag. At minimum, set the controller mode and configure immutable images: --controller-mode=harness-v2 --acp-runtime-namespace=orka-runtimes --acp-provider-proxy-namespace=orka-system --acp-provider-proxy-base-url=http://provider-auth-proxy.orka-system.svc.cluster.local:8080 --acp-codex-runtime-image=<repository>@sha256:<digest> --acp-claude-runtime-image=<repository>@sha256:<digest> --acp-copilot-runtime-image=<repository>@sha256:<digest> --acp-opencode-runtime-image=<repository>@sha256:<digest> The provider-proxy flags must match the proxy Pods --acp-provider-proxy-base-url is the address runtime Pods call. Its host must end in .<namespace>.svc or .<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, where the namespace is --acp-provider-proxy-namespace, as in <service>.<namespace>.svc. Otherwise the controller rejects the configuration and RuntimePools report Degraded. Pools without an execution workspace show the error in their status message; execution-workspace pools show runtime configuration is not admitted. The namespace flag is unset by default. With providerProxy.enabled=true, the Helm chart sets it to the release namespace, where the chart deploys provider-auth-proxy. The generated NetworkPolicy allows TCP to Pods matching --acp-provider-proxy-pod-labels in that namespace, on the base URL's port. If those labels miss the proxy Pods, or that port differs from the port the proxy Pods listen on, every provider call is dropped by default-deny egress with no useful error. Mutable image tags are rejected for built-in pools. For Kustomize deployment, apply config/acp-production; config/default alone omits the required cross-namespace Vekil ingress boundary.

Task fails before queueing: for a built-in runtime, verify the Agent has runtime.type: codex, claude, copilot, or opencode, ACP is enabled, and the matching digest-pinned image is configured. For runtimeRef, verify the registration is current-generation, ready, strict-governed, and matches the Task workspace intent. OpenCode Task fails with RuntimeSessionStartFailed: "the OpenCode runtime refuses workspaces containing .opencode, opencode.json, or opencode.jsonc": the workspace root contains one of those entries; the runtime log names it. Run the Task with another built-in runtime, or remove those entries from the repository or branch it uses. Task remains queued: inspect the selected RuntimePool lifecycle/admission/capacity and the runtime Pod scheduling conditions. Agent warnings in Task results: Orka advertises ACP session notices, so Codex and Claude Code send their own warnings, such as Codex's missing model metadata, as notices, which Orka keeps out of the result and does not log. Copilot CLI 1.0.96 ignores notices and still writes its Info: lines into the reply. Task reports OutcomeUnknown: do not retry the same attempt automatically. Inspect the recorded attempt, controller epoch, runtime instance, and event timeline. Read Task fails validation: inspect status.delivery for ReadOnlyWorkspaceModified and treat the session as poisoned. Write Task is blocked: verify all required source-read, target-read, target-write, and forge credential references, the publication repository/branch, and the Workspace/Publisher broker configuration. Require a terminal verified delivery receipt before claiming success. runtimeRef Task is rejected: inspect AgentRuntime.status for current-generation conformance, exact profile and instance identity, strict workspace governance, and valid authentication Secret bindings. Remove unsupported Task overrides such as maxTurns, disallowedTools, or allowBash. spec.execution.workspace Task is rejected: enable the workspace provider API and ACP dispatch with the required admission webhooks, then check the selected classRef, live use authorization, provider heartbeat/contracts, and immutable profile binding. Provider-specific Task selectors are removed. An ACP class must require acp.runtime.v2; its allowed reuse and detach actions must match the request. Core also needs read-only access to native worker Pods when applicable. The rejection reason appears in Task.status.executionWorkspace. Repository access uses top-level spec.workspace; see Agent Sandbox and Substrate.

Built-in harness v2 runtimes support an optional Agent.spec.soul source, independent of the role system prompt. The controller resolves and pins its content before dispatch. Codex and Claude use native instruction settings; Copilot and OpenCode use protected per-session instruction files. These files are not repository content and are not published or restored from a repository workspace checkpoint. External runtimeRef registrations do not accept souls.

Orka runs an ACP RuntimeSession in an upstream Agent Sandbox through the separately deployed orka-workspace-sandbox provider. Core owns Task execution, runtime credentials, admission, and settlement. The provider owns Sandbox resources and reports infrastructure identity through the shared workspace.orka.ai API. The external provider is tested against unmodified upstream agent-sandbox v1.0.3. Install and operate that backend separately. For an existing v0.5 installation, complete the upstream storage migration before installing v1. Execution workspaces compares it with Agent Substrate. Video demo Watch Suspend an agent workspace and keep its files.

Install the shared CRDs and ownership admission policies, then the provider's CRDs, RBAC, registration, and Deployment from the external provider repository. Use a digest-pinned provider image. Its two replicas share a provider-specific leader-election Lease and use a ServiceAccount distinct from Orka core. An operator creates a SandboxProviderConfig and a same-namespace SandboxWorkspaceProfile for an ExecutionWorkspaceClass. These kinds belong to sandbox.workspace.orka.ai/v1alpha1. The class references the registered provider and immutable profile. An ACP class explicitly requires acp.runtime.v2; add Suspend to its allowed lifecycle actions only when the profile enables it. Enable Orka's provider API and ACP workspace dispatch with the required provenance and class-use admission webhooks. There is no core Agent Sandbox backend flag. See workspace configuration. A Task selects only a class: spec: type: agent execution: workspace: classRef: name: sandbox-coding reusePolicy: session Session reuse requires spec.sessionRef. Top-level Task.spec.workspace remains the repository contract for verified source access and clean-room publication. Provider, template, pool, and native resource selectors do not belong in a Task.

Core freezes the class binding and public supervisor request in a dedicated single-session RuntimePool. The provider creates an isolated SandboxTemplate, zero-replica SandboxWarmPool, and SandboxClaim from that request. It verifies the realized Pod, request revision, and allocation identity before reporting startup evidence. Core independently verifies the Pod and network policy, completes the sealed bootstrap exchange, and admits the authenticated runtime instance. Provider readiness alone never authorizes a prompt. The provider receives no private attachment credentials. Core releases them only to the attested process and verifies the resulting boot identity. The runtime Pod has no Kubernetes service-account token or Git publication credential. Core-owned NetworkPolicies select its admitted labels; the provider cannot move the Pod or change its execution template and still receive credentials. The provider advertises ACP runtime allocation and data-only suspension. It does not advertise generic exec, files, TLS endpoints, pooled capacity, checkpoint export, or full-memory restore. Unsupported class requirements fail admission.

A suspend-capable SandboxWorkspaceProfile supplies: apiVersion: sandbox.workspace.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: SandboxWorkspaceProfile metadata: name: sandbox-data spec: suspend: mode: DataOnly volume: capacity: 1Gi accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] The class must permit interactive session reuse and suspension, and set idleTimeout or maxLifetime. A suspended-workspace count cap additionally requires maxLifetime. The claim uses a dedicated durable workspace PVC rather than warm capacity. Its StorageClass must support dynamic provisioning and deletion of the backing PV. Suspension verifies the exact claim, Sandbox, PVC, and PV, puts the Sandbox in Suspended operating mode, and observes the exact Pod UID's absence before reporting suspension. Process memory and credentials are not retained. Cold resume creates a new Pod against the retained volume and repeats startup attestation and credential bootstrap. Delete waits for the runtime Pod and exact PVC/PV to disappear. Missing journals, changed storage identities, and uncertain native outcomes fail closed; removing finalizers is not a recovery procedure.

Before installing the pruned RuntimePool CRD or new core binary, drain every legacy in-tree workspace through its original owner, including retained workspaces in Ready, Suspended, Failed, and Deleted states. The new core startup gate rejects these records across all namespaces. It does not adopt or clean them. See Upgrading. The standalone Sandbox proof writes a non-root filesystem marker, suspends and resumes with a new Pod and bootstrap nonce while retaining exact PVC/PV identities, then observes deletion. It proves provider lifecycle and storage behavior. The separate fake-provider core proof proves actual authenticated Orka RuntimeSession and Task execution. The standalone Sandbox proof does not make that core integration claim. Kind's default CNI does not prove NetworkPolicy packet enforcement.

Orka speaks the Anthropic Messages API at /anthropic/v1/messages, so Claude Code and other Anthropic-native clients can point at Orka instead of at a model vendor. Your cluster holds the API keys; the client holds a ServiceAccount token. The optional shared compatibility router selects the team's installation from its validated ServiceAccount token. It accepts x-api-key or Bearer authentication, with Bearer taking precedence when both are present. Clients can omit the namespace parameter. Coordinator mode is enabled by default Orka rewrites your request before sending it upstream: it discards the tools your client sent, injects its own, and prepends its own system prompt. See Coordinator mode for exactly what changes and how to turn it off — the behavior is identical on both compatibility endpoints. See also OpenAI compatibility for the OpenAI-shaped equivalent. Video demos From chat to a GitHub pull request Two teams, one AI endpoint

Method Path Description POST /anthropic/v1/messages Create a message (streaming & non-streaming) GET /anthropic/v1/models List available models from configured providers PR-blocking live CI exercises this API directly against a live Claude-family backend by checking /anthropic/v1/models and both non-streaming and streaming /anthropic/v1/messages requests. Those live checks keep the default Orka tool-loop behavior enabled unless a client explicitly sets X-Orka-Tools: disabled.

Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens, and OIDC JWTs when OIDC is configured, can use either header: x-api-key: <orka-token> — Anthropic convention (recommended for Anthropic clients) Authorization: Bearer <orka-token> — Standard Bearer token Transaction-token authentication uses Txn-Token: <token> by default. To accept TxTokens as Bearer tokens, the operator must explicitly include Authorization:Bearer in --context-token-headers, for example --context-token-headers=Txn-Token,Authorization:Bearer. Using x-api-key for TxTokens also requires explicit context-token header configuration. See Authentication.

The model field supports two formats: provider/model — e.g., anthropic/claude-opus-5. The part before / matches a Provider CRD name, and the part after is the model name sent to that provider. model — e.g., claude-opus-5. Uses the default provider (from --chat-provider flag or a Provider CRD named default).

Provider CRD configured in the cluster: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Provider metadata: name: anthropic namespace: orka-system spec: type: anthropic secretRef: name: anthropic-secret key: api-key defaultModel: claude-opus-5 Secret with the API key: apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: anthropic-secret namespace: orka-system type: Opaque stringData: api-key: sk-ant-... ServiceAccount token and RBAC for authentication and coordinator tools: Follow the API-client setup to configure orka-client and its Task permissions. Coordinator Task creation requires tasks/create. Agent creation currently does not check a ServiceAccount caller's agents/create permission; see the API authorization limitation. Then create a token: export ORKA_TOKEN="$(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)"

Configure Claude Code to route all API calls through Orka: export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://orka.example.com/anthropic export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client) # Claude Code will now route all API calls through Orka

curl -X POST https://orka.example.com/anthropic/v1/messages \ -H "x-api-key: $ORKA_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \ -d '{ "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 1024, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}] }'

curl -X POST https://orka.example.com/anthropic/v1/messages \ -H "x-api-key: $ORKA_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \ -d '{ "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 1024, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "stream": true }'
curl https://orka.example.com/anthropic/v1/models \ -H "x-api-key: $ORKA_TOKEN"

A client that sets budget_tokens gets an ordinary response and no error telling it why. If you need extended thinking, call the provider directly.

By default this endpoint runs the tool loop itself. When the model returns tool_use blocks, Orka executes the tools, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model produces text. Your client never executes a tool. Coordinator mode describes the full rewrite — which tools are injected, what happens to yours, and the X-Orka-Tools: disabled header that turns all of it off. It applies identically here; the rest of this page covers what is specific to the Anthropic shape.

You POST /anthropic/v1/messages. Orka rewrites the request (coordinator mode) and calls the model. If the response contains tool_use blocks, Orka executes each one, appends the results to the conversation, and calls the model again. Step 3 repeats until the model returns text only. That final response goes back to you. The loop advertises and executes the registered built-in and coordinator tools. Custom Kubernetes Tool resources are not advertised or executed, including those with a built-in name. With X-Orka-Tools: disabled, your client's tool definitions pass through unchanged and your client handles tool execution.

With stream: true in coordinator mode, Orka uses one Anthropic SSE message for the whole tool loop. Each provider turn is buffered and validated before Orka sends its text. message_start opens the message once. content_block_start/delta/stop carries model text and sanitized progress messages, such as [Tool file_read completed]. message_delta and message_stop close the message once. Coordinator mode keeps tool_use blocks and raw tool results inside the server-side conversation. With X-Orka-Tools: disabled, Orka sends provider text and tool_use events to the client without running tools.

Setting Flag Default What it caps Max iterations --chat-max-iterations 50 Tool-loop iterations Max duration --chat-max-duration 30m Wall-clock time for the whole request Tool timeout --chat-tool-timeout 60s One tool execution Max session size --chat-max-session-size 512,000 bytes Conversation size before truncation These are the shared chat settings and apply to streaming and non-streaming requests alike. See Configuration. When a non-streaming request reaches the iteration limit, Orka makes one additional model call without tools to produce a closing summary. A streaming request closes its response at the limit without that additional call.

If the LLM calls the same tool with identical arguments 3 or more times, the proxy injects a warning message asking it to try a different approach. This prevents infinite loops where the LLM repeatedly calls a failing tool.

Tool execution errors: Wrapped as JSON results ({"success": false, "error": "..."}) and fed back to the LLM, which can decide how to recover LLM errors: If the LLM returns a context-too-long error, the proxy truncates the conversation to ~50% and retries once. Other LLM errors terminate the loop and return an Anthropic error response Timeout: If the overall request timeout is reached, the proxy returns whatever progress has been made

Server-side tool execution is enabled by default — no special header needed: curl -X POST https://orka.example.com/anthropic/v1/messages \ -H "x-api-key: $ORKA_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \ -d '{ "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 4096, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Search the web for Kubernetes 1.32 release highlights and summarize them."}], "stream": true }' To let your client manage tools, add X-Orka-Tools: disabled. This disables Orka's coordinator rewrite and tool loop. Requests and responses still pass through Orka's format conversion. Fields including top_p, top_k, tool_choice, and thinking are accepted but not forwarded to the provider.
