# Create a task curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/tasks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "my-task", "type": "ai", "agentRef": {"name": "assistant"}, "prompt": "Explain microservices architecture" }' # Get task result curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/tasks/my-task/result \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)" # List task artifacts curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/tasks/my-task/artifacts \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)" # Download an artifact curl -L http://localhost:8080/api/v1/tasks/my-task/artifacts/output.json \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)" \ -o output.json # Chat with SSE streaming curl -N http://localhost:8080/api/v1/chat \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "message": "Create an AI task that summarizes Kubernetes best practices", "sessionId": "my-session" }'
The tools Orka gives agents, and their parameters, are documented in Built-in tools.

Orka is one controller that turns Task resources into work. Container and native AI Tasks run as per-Task Kubernetes Jobs. Coding-agent Tasks run as private sessions in controller-owned RuntimePools. Everything an agent produces flows back through the controller, which keeps a durable record and, for code changes, hands the work to a separate publisher. If you are new to Orka, read What is Orka? first. For the source tree and storage internals, see Controller internals.

Select the diagram to view it at full size. Requests arrive from the REST API, the CLI, the dashboard, chat, the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints, gateways, and GitHub webhooks. The controller authenticates them, creates or updates Tasks, and dispatches each Task to where it runs: Task type Runs in Reaches models through container A per-Task Job from the general worker or your image — ai A per-Task Job running Orka's AI worker The Agent's Provider and its API key Secret agent A private RuntimeSession inside a RuntimePool Pod The authenticated provider proxy and your model gateway Coding-agent runtimes and the Workspace/Publisher use separate network and credential identities. A runtime Pod can reach only cluster DNS, the provider proxy, and the controller API that serves its prompt-scoped tool broker; it has no Git credentials and no route to your source control. The Publisher has the Git credentials it needs for one operation at a time, and no access to models or tools. Security explains the boundaries.

The controller runs as a single-replica Deployment. It contains: API server. The REST API, chat, the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints, the gateway ingress, signed GitHub webhooks, internal worker APIs, and, when enabled, the web dashboard. Task reconciler and priority queue. Routes container and AI Tasks to worker Jobs, in priority order (0–1000), and coding-agent Tasks to the ACP dispatcher. ACP dispatcher and RuntimePool controller. Reserve pool capacity, run fenced prompt attempts, validate workspace changes, and manage digest-pinned, scale-to-zero runtime Deployments. Agent runtimes covers them in depth. Brokers. The credential and artifact brokers give the Publisher short-lived access for one operation. The prompt MCP broker rechecks every tool call a coding agent makes. Workflow reconcilers. Drive repository monitors, security scans, and gateways, each with durable run history. Stores. Sessions, results, artifacts, plans, memory, scans, monitors, gateway ledgers, and usage live in an embedded SQLite database on a persistent volume. Control decisions for coding agents live in Kubernetes resources instead; see Where state lives.

Image Description General Worker (workers/general/) Runs arbitrary container commands in a per-Task Job. AI Worker (workers/ai/) Runs native LLM/coordination Tasks in a per-Task Job. ACP Runtime (cmd/orka-acp-runtime, workers/acp/) Hosts multiple private Codex, Claude, Copilot, or OpenCode RuntimeSessions through orka.harness.v2; its per-session loopback proxy enforces provider routes and model selection. Provider Auth Proxy (cmd/orka-provider-auth-proxy) Authenticates traffic using the shared proxy credential and forwards it to Vekil. Workspace Publisher (cmd/orka-workspace-publisher, workers/publisher/) Uses a separate identity for clean-room clone, commit preparation, exact-ref publication, independent verification, and PR reconciliation.

Orka installs 29 custom resources. You write a few of them; the controller creates and owns the rest to keep track of work across restarts and failures. Solid arrows are references you type. Dotted arrows are relationships the controller maintains — you can read them with kubectl get, but you never create or edit those objects yourself.

Resource Purpose Task One unit of work: container, AI, or agent Agent Reusable configuration: model, prompt, tools, skills, and optionally a runtime Provider A model backend and its API key Secret Skill Reusable prompt content injected into an Agent's system prompt Tool A custom tool backed by an HTTP endpoint or an MCP server OutboundAccessPolicy How a Tool reaches an external API. See Outbound access RepositoryScan A repository to scan for security findings RepositoryMonitor A repository whose pull requests and issues agents review, implement, and repair ConnectorProvider An OAuth service people may link. Each person's link is a Connection, which the API creates for them. See Connectors AgentRuntime An external agent runtime registration. See Bring your own agent runtime SubstrateActorPool A pool of Agent Substrate actors GatewayClass, Gateway, GatewayBinding Connect chat apps and other agents (gateway.orka.ai). See Gateways ExecutionWorkspaceClass and related resources Sandboxed execution workspaces (workspace.orka.ai) from separately installed providers. Off by default. See Execution workspaces Every field is in the Resource reference.

Read them when you are debugging. Do not edit them. CRD Purpose RuntimePool Controller-owned logical pool for one trust domain and immutable built-in ACP profile ControllerEpoch Current controller holder/epoch and takeover fence PromptAttempt Durable ACP execution/delivery state for one Task attempt RuntimeSessionControl Logical Session lifecycle, exact runtime identity, and mutation lease state BranchClaim Compare-and-swap ownership/baseline for one publication branch Publication Prepared commit, push, verification, and optional PR reconciliation state ExternalEffect Idempotency and reconciliation ledger for consequential brokered calls

There are two lifecycles, and they are not the same thing. The first is the Task phase — what kubectl get task prints, and what the UI shows. Every Task has one, whatever its type: Native and container Tasks without an execution workspace can complete directly from Running to Succeeded or Failed. Finalizing is used when execution-workspace authority still needs revocation. The second is the attempt state — the fine-grained record of one agent run. Native ai and container Tasks do not have one; they use the worker Job lifecycle instead. Built-in type: agent Tasks record every step in a PromptAttempt: Two details the diagram compresses: Every state before Accepted can also jump straight to Failed or Cancelled. The arrows are left out so the happy path stays readable. SubmittedUnknown means Orka sent the prompt and never learned whether the runtime got it. It can only become OutcomeUnknown — never Succeeded and never a retry. Orka would rather leave you with an honest "I don't know" than run your prompt twice. The selected RuntimePool scales from Stopped through Starting to Serving/Accepting. The dispatcher creates or reuses a private RuntimeSession, starts one non-reconnectable prompt stream, renews its lease, and records bounded events. A prompt that may have been accepted is never automatically replayed. After prompt settlement, the RuntimeSession enters validation. Read Tasks succeed only after the final tree matches the verified baseline. Write Tasks with changes proceed through clean-room preparation, exact-ref publication, independent verification, optional PR reconciliation, and finalization. The controller settles the Kubernetes control records and SQLite transcript/outbox payloads before projecting terminal Task status. The top-level Task phase, status.execution, and status.delivery are safe compatibility/read-model projections. The authoritative ACP transitions live in PromptAttempt, RuntimeSessionControl, BranchClaim, Publication, ExternalEffect, RuntimePool.status, and the associated coordination Leases.

Delegation. A coordinator Agent creates child Tasks with delegate_task and collects them with wait_for_tasks. The controller enforces the allowed Agents, depth, and concurrency, and records progress in the parent's status.childTasks. In autonomous mode, the controller reruns the coordinator in a loop, carrying a saved plan between iterations. See Multi-agent coordination and Autonomous tasks. Sessions. Tasks that share a Session run one at a time and see the earlier conversation. Sessions store user and assistant messages only, so a conversation can move between native AI and coding-agent Tasks. A coding agent's session is rebuilt from that canonical transcript and the verified workspace when its Pod is replaced. Tools. Native AI Tasks get built-in tools and custom Tools. Coding agents use their CLI's tools, plus Orka tools through the per-session broker. Memory. AI workers load a bounded set of reviewed, namespace-scoped memories into the system prompt. Agents can only propose new memories; a person reviews and applies them. See Memory. Repository automation. Repository monitors and security scans run their work as ordinary Tasks and keep runs, findings, reviews, and audit events in SQLite. Status on the resource summarizes them; the API and dashboard show the detail. Gateways. An out-of-tree adapter normalizes each external conversation into an orka.gateway.v1 event. A GatewayBinding maps it to one Agent, and unknown or ambiguous identity fails closed. A durable inbox and outbox decouple acknowledgement from execution, deduplicate events, serialize each Session, and deliver replies with stable idempotency IDs. See Gateways and the Gateway API.

Orka needs no external database. It keeps two kinds of state: Kubernetes resources and Leases are the authority for coding-agent control decisions: which controller is in charge, attempt state, Session ownership, branch claims, publications, and external effects. Updates use resourceVersion compare-and-swap, so a stale writer cannot win. SQLite on the controller's volume holds payloads and records: results, artifacts (up to 10 MB each), sessions and transcripts, plans, memory, scan and monitor history, gateway inbox and outbox, and usage. It is written behind the Kubernetes fences and never acts as a second authority. Back up both together, with the snapshot encryption key. See Upgrading.

Area Decision Rationale Result Storage SQLite (embedded) No size limit, zero external dependencies, pure Go via modernc.org/sqlite. Session Storage SQLite (embedded) Normalized schema with efficient querying and pagination. No size limit. Plan Storage SQLite (embedded) Persists autonomous coordination plan state across iterations. Memory Storage SQLite (embedded) Persists durable memories and reviewable memory proposals for namespace-scoped recall. Artifact Storage SQLite stores artifact metadata and BLOB content, 10MB max per artifact. Keeps worker outputs co-located with task/session state while bounding per-artifact size. ACP Control Authority Kubernetes CRD status + coordination Leases resourceVersion CAS and Leases provide shared/watchable epoch, attempt, Session, branch, publication, and external-effect fencing. ACP Payload/Outbox Storage SQLite behind Kubernetes fences Stores transcript/SessionTurn payloads and deferred outbox projections without becoming a second control authority. Security Scan Storage SQLite stores repository scan runs, threat models, findings, and patch proposals. Provides durable repository-security history without an external database. API Authentication Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens plus optional OIDC JWT and generic context-token validation. Native K8s auth by default; OIDC and transaction-token TxTokens support external/request-scoped API clients. Task Queue Priority queuing (0-1000) Higher priority tasks are scheduled first. Secret Management Reference Kubernetes Secrets by role Native workers receive only required Secrets. ACP source-read, target-read, target-write, forge, provider-proxy, publisher-auth, and capability roles stay separate; Git/forge values are brokered only to the clean-room Publisher. Observability Prometheus metrics, structured logs, optional OpenTelemetry traces and GenAI OTLP metrics. Standard K8s metrics/logging with opt-in distributed tracing and model/tool latency telemetry. AI Tools Built-in + extensible via CRDs Ship with categorized built-in tools and can be extended via Tool CRDs. Failure Policy Configurable retry with backoff spec.retryPolicy with max retries and exponential backoff. Session Execution Serial per session Tasks sharing a session run one-at-a-time to prevent race conditions. Worker Security Hardened pods Non-root, read-only rootfs, all capabilities dropped, seccomp RuntimeDefault.

Autonomous mode runs a native type: ai coordinator across multiple Jobs. The coordinator delegates work, saves a plan, and continues from that plan in the next iteration. ACP type: agent runtimes do not support coordination.autonomous. The autonomous planning example includes a coordinator, planner, reviewer, and Task with complete setup instructions.

When a task's agent has coordination.autonomous: true, the controller runs a loop: Creates a Job for the coordinator agent The agent reads the current plan, delegates sub-tasks, and updates the plan When the Job completes, the controller checks termination conditions If not complete, it creates a new Job (next iteration) with the updated plan Repeats until the goal is marked complete, the iteration limit is reached, or execution fails; suspension pauses the loop

Enable autonomous mode on an Agent's coordination config: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: autonomous-coordinator spec: providerRef: name: my-provider model: name: claude-opus-5 coordination: enabled: true autonomous: true maxIterations: 20 # 0 = unlimited maxDepth: 3 maxConcurrentChildren: 5 allowedAgents: - name: coder - name: reviewer Then create a task: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: build-feature spec: type: ai agentRef: name: autonomous-coordinator prompt: "Implement a REST API with user authentication, CRUD operations, and tests"

The controller manages the autonomous loop at the Kubernetes level: Each iteration runs as a separate Job (resilient to pod crashes) Plan state is persisted in SQLite between iterations The task's status.iteration tracks the current iteration number Termination conditions are checked after each Job completes

The LLM manages its own plan using the update_plan tool: { "summary": "Completed auth module, starting CRUD endpoints", "progress_pct": 35, "goal_complete": false, "plan_document": "# Goal
Build REST API...

# Completed
- [x] Auth module
..." } Plan state includes: summary: Human-readable progress description progress_pct: Estimated completion percentage (0-100) goal_complete: Whether the goal has been achieved plan_document: Freeform markdown plan managed by the LLM

The autonomous loop stops when any of these conditions are met: Goal complete: The LLM calls update_plan with goal_complete: true Max iterations: The configured maxIterations limit is reached Pause: The task's suspend field is set to true; the current iteration completes and the Task waits for resume Timeout: The per-iteration timeout is exceeded (fails the task) Reaching maxIterations also gives the Task a Succeeded phase. The Task status message distinguishes goal complete from reached max iterations. Check the final result's deliverable as well as the phase.
The task status shows the current iteration: status: phase: Running iteration: 5 message: "autonomous iteration 5"

View the current plan state while the Task is running. Completion deletes this working state, so the coordinator must include its deliverable in its final result. Read that result through GET /api/v1/tasks/<task-name>/result after completion. # Via API curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ $CONTROLLER_URL/api/v1/tasks/build-feature/plan Response: { "TaskName": "build-feature", "Namespace": "orka-system", "Iteration": 5, "Summary": "Completed auth and CRUD, working on tests", "ProgressPct": 70, "GoalComplete": false, "PlanDocument": "# Goal\n..." }
Suspend an autonomous task: kubectl -n orka-system patch task build-feature --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}' The current iteration will complete, then the task will stop.

An autonomous agent can run for many iterations without a human in the loop. For the steps that should not happen unattended — deploying, spending money, touching production — Orka supports approval gates: the task parks itself and waits for a person to decide. Two things create an approval: Tool gating. List Custom Tool names in spec.coordination.approvalRequiredTools on the Agent. When the agent calls one of those tools, the task parks before the tool executes. Only Custom Tool CRDs can be gated; built-in tools are rejected by validation. The agent asking. In autonomous mode the request_approval tool is auto-injected, so an agent can park its own task when its instructions tell it to seek sign-off. spec: coordination: enabled: true autonomous: true approvalRequiredTools: - deploy-to-production # a Custom Tool CRD name While parked, the task stays in a waiting state and the loop does not advance. Decide from the CLI: orka task approvals '<task>' # list pending approvals with IDs orka task approve '<task>' '<approvalID>' orka task decline '<task>' '<approvalID>' or from the dashboard: the task detail page has an Approvals tab with Approve and Decline buttons. Approving lets the gated tool call proceed; declining returns the refusal to the agent, which continues the loop and can choose another course. One timing note: approvals are derived from the task's execution event stream, so a decision issued in the same instant the task parks can briefly return approval not found. Re-run the command a moment later.

These environment variables are injected into autonomous worker pods: Variable Description ORKA_AUTONOMOUS_MODE Set to true for autonomous tasks ORKA_AUTONOMOUS_ITERATION Current iteration number (0-based) ORKA_AUTONOMOUS_MAX_ITERATIONS Max iterations limit (if configured)

Available to autonomous coordinators for managing plan state: Parameter Type Required Description summary string Yes Brief progress summary progress_pct integer No Progress percentage (0-100) goal_complete boolean No Whether the goal is complete plan_document string Yes Full markdown plan document

Plan state is stored per-task in SQLite (not shared between tasks) Each iteration starts with a fresh LLM context (only plan state carries over) Code artifacts must be persisted via git (using workspace/pushBranch) Per-iteration timeout applies, not total duration timeout

This path builds and pushes images from your checkout and installs the chart generated from the same source. Use it to develop Orka; to try Orka, follow Install Orka instead. In addition to the installation prerequisites: Go, Bun, and Docker — see Development for versions A container registry you can push to and your cluster can pull from

export ORKA_CONTEXT='<your-kubeconfig-context>' git clone https://github.com/orka-agents/orka.git cd orka Choose a registry prefix you can push to and your cluster can pull from. Replace ghcr.io/your-org/orka below, authenticate Docker to that registry, and run the build, push, and install commands in the same shell. Use a fresh tag when rebuilding with local source changes. export ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX=ghcr.io/your-org/orka export ORKA_IMAGE_TAG="dev-$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)" export IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export AI_WORKER_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/ai-worker:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export GENERAL_WORKER_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/general-worker:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export ACP_CODEX_RUNTIME_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-codex-runtime:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export ACP_CLAUDE_RUNTIME_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-claude-runtime:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export ACP_COPILOT_RUNTIME_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-copilot-runtime:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export ACP_OPENCODE_RUNTIME_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-opencode-runtime:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" export WORKSPACE_PUBLISHER_IMG="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/workspace-publisher:${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" make docker-build-all make docker-push-all The Helm command below uses these repositories and the same tag for both native workers. The controller, publisher, and ACP runtimes require registry digests. After pushing, list their references and replace the corresponding digest placeholders in the Helm command: docker image inspect --format '{{range .RepoDigests}}{{println .}}{{end}}' \ "$IMG" "$WORKSPACE_PUBLISHER_IMG" \ "$ACP_CODEX_RUNTIME_IMG" "$ACP_CLAUDE_RUNTIME_IMG" \ "$ACP_COPILOT_RUNTIME_IMG" "$ACP_OPENCODE_RUNTIME_IMG"

Install the development chart from manifest_staging/charts/orka. It matches the source checkout. The root charts/orka directory holds files prepared for release and may not match your code: helm install orka ./manifest_staging/charts/orka \ --kube-context "${ORKA_CONTEXT}" \ --namespace orka-system --create-namespace \ --set controller.image.repository="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}" \ --set controller.image.digest="sha256:<controller-digest>" \ --set workers.ai.image.repository="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/ai-worker" \ --set-string workers.ai.image.tag="${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" \ --set workers.general.image.repository="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/general-worker" \ --set-string workers.general.image.tag="${ORKA_IMAGE_TAG}" \ --set publisher.image.repository="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/workspace-publisher" \ --set publisher.image.digest="sha256:<publisher-digest>" \ --set controller.acpRuntime.codexImage="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-codex-runtime@sha256:<codex-digest>" \ --set controller.acpRuntime.claudeImage="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-claude-runtime@sha256:<claude-digest>" \ --set controller.acpRuntime.copilotImage="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-copilot-runtime@sha256:<copilot-digest>" \ --set controller.acpRuntime.opencodeImage="${ORKA_IMAGE_PREFIX}/acp-opencode-runtime@sha256:<opencode-digest>" \ --wait --timeout 10m The controller issues its own webhook certificate. To bring your own, see Webhook certificate. The chart defaults to 0.0.0-dev, the latest validated main build, not necessarily your checkout. Keep the overrides above for a feature branch or older commit. The Development Images workflow publishes sha-<full-commit> image tags and a development-images-<full-commit> artifact with images.json and values.json; using that values file pins all nine images to the matching build. Tagged controller, publisher, and native worker images use Always pull policy. Changing a registry tag does not restart existing Pods. Coding-runtime tags are resolved to digests at controller startup. To disable an unused runtime, set its image to an empty string, for example --set-string controller.acpRuntime.codexImage=. If Helm refuses to render, that is deliberate — the chart checks its inputs up front rather than installing something broken. Troubleshooting lists the guards and what each one wants. Kustomize instead of Helm Install the shared CRDs from config/crd through your cluster's designated CRD owner before deploying workloads. The config/acp-production workload overlay excludes CRDs; it adds the network policy that stops model traffic from bypassing the provider proxy. make deploy checks the shared CRD prerequisite and creates the artifact, publisher, and proxy Secrets before applying that overlay. Its controller, publisher, and runtime image variables must use the pushed repository@sha256:... references.

Orka currently supports new installations only. Read Upgrading for support details and CRD requirements. When testing a source upgrade, replace all image references with images from the target checkout. --reuse-values preserves previously supplied images; it does not select images for the new source. Explicitly clear unused runtime image fields so older image references are not retained.
Continue with Connect to the API in Getting started. Those commands use your current kubectl context, so select ORKA_CONTEXT first with kubectl config use-context if it is not already current.

Orka ships tools that agents can call without any extra infrastructure. This page lists all of them, which Tasks receive them, and their parameters. To give agents your own tools, see Agents, skills, and tools.

Native type: ai Tasks run Orka's AI worker, which builds its tool list from three sources: Tools you select. Names listed in the Agent's spec.tools (entries with enabled: false are skipped) and in the Task's spec.ai.tools. A name can be a core tool, an opt-in GitHub tool, or a custom Tool resource. Tools Orka adds automatically. Every native type: ai Task gets the memory tools for this warning release. The next release will require coordination or explicit selection; see migration and release notes. An Agent with coordination.enabled: true gets the coordination tools, the GitHub pull request tools, agent management, and update_plan. With coordination.autonomous: true it also gets request_approval. A delegated child Task gets send_message and check_messages. So does a child that runs on a built-in coding-agent runtime. A Task that came in through a gateway can get reply_in_conversation. Nothing else. The annotation orka.ai/disable-coordination-tool-injection: "true" on a Task turns off the automatic coordination, approval, and child-messaging tools. Memory tools remain available during this warning release, and explicitly selected tools still apply. The next release will also suppress automatic memory tools with this annotation. Coding-agent Tasks (type: agent) use their CLI's own tools, such as Read, Grep, and Bash, controlled by the Agent's runtime.defaultAllowedTools and the Task's agentRuntime overrides. Orka-executed tools reach them through a per-session MCP broker that rechecks the Task's policy on every call. See Agent runtimes. When transaction-token authorization restricts tctx.allowedTools, the grant must cover the automatically added tools as well as the selected ones. See Restricted tool grants.

Select these by name in spec.tools or spec.ai.tools. The OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints also offer the first five to clients. Tool Description Parameters web_search Search the web using a configured search API or DuckDuckGo. A failed search returns a tool error, never placeholder results query (required), limit (default 5) code_exec Execute code in a sandboxed environment language (python/javascript/bash), code, timeout (default 30s, clamped to 60s) file_read Read files from the workspace path, offset, limit (max 1MB) web_fetch Fetch and extract URL content url (required), max_chars (default 50000), raw file_write Write or append files in workspace paths path (required), content (required), mode (write/append), create_dirs request_approval Park the Task until a person approves or declines one exact custom-tool call. Added automatically for autonomous coordinators; see human approval. action, targetTool (a custom Tool name), targetArguments (the exact argument object) (required); riskSummary, severity (warning/critical)

When SEARCH_API_URL is set, web_search sends a GET request to that URL with q and limit query parameters and SEARCH_API_KEY, if set, as a bearer token, and returns the response body as the result. Without it, the tool queries DuckDuckGo's HTML endpoint, which often answers requests from cloud and CI addresses with an HTTP 202 challenge page. The tool then returns an error such as DuckDuckGo returned HTTP 202: a native type: ai Task records it as a ToolCallFailed event and passes it to the model, and the compatible endpoints return {"success": false, "error": ...}. Neither the Helm chart nor the controller sets these variables. For a native type: ai Task, set them in the Task's spec.env, with valueFrom.secretKeyRef for the key. Agent runtime Tasks call a brokered web_search that ignores them and always uses DuckDuckGo.

Every native type: ai Task receives these during the warning release, regardless of its selected tools or coordination settings. Calls relying on this compatibility access emit deprecation warnings. The next release will require explicit Agent/Task selection or coordination with automatic injection enabled; see migration and release notes. remember and propose_memory create proposals for a person to review; they never change durable memory directly. See Memory. Tool Description Parameters recall_memory Recall durable namespace-scoped memories query, tags, task_name, agent_name, source, limit, include_disabled remember Submit a durable memory proposal for review content (required); title, description, tags, agent_name propose_memory Submit a memory-adjacent governance proposal title (required); type, skill_name, description, content, patch, agent_name search_transcript Search prior session transcripts query (required); session_name, exclude_session_name, roles, limit, max_snippet_length

Added for Agents with coordination.enabled: true. They are not returned by GET /api/v1/tools. Multi-agent coordination explains how to use them together. Tool Description Parameters delegate_task Delegate a subtask to another agent agent, prompt (required); taskNamespace, agentNamespace, priority, timeout, workspace, maxTurns, allowBash, prior_task, feedback, auto_retry, max_retries wait_for_tasks Wait for delegated tasks to complete tasks (required), timeout (default 10m) create_container_task Create a child container task image, command/args; workspace, prior_task, namespace, timeout, priority, schedule cancel_task Cancel a running child task task_name (required); namespace, reason send_message Send a message to a sibling task to_task (required, or * to broadcast), content (required) check_messages Check for messages from sibling tasks mark_read (boolean, default true) update_plan Update the autonomous execution plan summary, plan_document (required); progress_pct, goal_complete

Creates a child Task for the named Agent and returns {"taskName": "<name>", "status": "created"}. The child is type: agent when the target Agent has spec.runtime, and type: ai otherwise. Parameter Description agent Name of the Agent to delegate to. Required. prompt The child Task's prompt. Required. taskNamespace Namespace for the child Task. Defaults to the parent's. agentNamespace Namespace of the target Agent. Defaults to taskNamespace. (namespace is the legacy form that sets both.) priority 0–1000. Defaults to the parent's priority. timeout Child Task timeout, such as 20m. workspace Repository settings for a coding-agent child, below. maxTurns, allowBash Per-Task runtime overrides for a coding-agent child. prior_task, feedback Apply a completed Task's diff first and prepend review feedback to the prompt. Native children only. auto_retry, max_retries Report structured failure details for the coordinator to act on; see retrying failed children. max_retries defaults to 2. workspace takes the same fields as a Task workspace, with Secret names as plain strings: Field Description gitRepo Credential-free HTTPS source URL. Required for write intent. branch / ref Source branch, or an exact commit, tag, or refs/heads/... ref. With neither, the repository's default branch is resolved and frozen. intent read (default) or write. Publication fields require write. readCredentialRef Secret for clone and read. publicationGitRepo Credential-free HTTPS repository that receives the branch. publicationReadCredentialRef Secret for target preflight and verification. publicationCredentialRef Secret for the branch push. Required for write intent. forgeCredentialRef Secret for the pull request API. Required when createPR is true. pushBranch Publication branch. prBaseBranch Pull request base branch. Required when createPR is true. prTitle, prBody Pull request text, up to 256 and 32,768 characters. createPR Reconcile a pull request after verified publication. Keep the four credential roles on distinct Secrets. delegate_task and chat's create_agent_task both accept optional workspace.prTitle and workspace.prBody. When requesting a pull request, the agent creating the Task should write descriptive text from the request before execution, not from the executing sandbox's output. Omitting either field or supplying an empty string keeps its fallback. Metadata alone does not enable createPR or write intent. Nonempty whitespace-only titles are invalid. Both fields reject secret-like text, and bodies reject reserved publisher reconciliation comments. Validation also applies when createPR is false. With prior_task, the child copies the prior Task's workspace configuration when none is given, and Orka tracks the loop with two labels: orka.ai/iteration (1, 2, 3, ...) and orka.ai/iteration-group (shared by every iteration of the same logical task). Built-in coding-agent runtimes do not accept prior_task, and external runtimeRef runtimes reject it. For those, have the next agent read the published branch instead; see code, review, and publish loops.

Polls the named children every five seconds until each is Succeeded, Failed, or Cancelled, or until timeout passes, then returns their results. Results are read from the controller, and any diff field is stripped so it does not flood the coordinator's context. { "completed": true, "results": [ {"task": "name", "agent": "agent", "phase": "Succeeded", "result": "..."}, {"task": "name", "agent": "agent", "phase": "Failed", "result": "error: ..."} ] } A child delegated with auto_retry: true that failed carries failureDetails with its message, retryCount, and maxRetries. The tool does not retry it; see retrying failed children.

Asks the controller to cancel a child. The controller checks that the caller is the parent's current worker, that the child carries the protected parent link (so Task provenance admission is required), and that the child is Pending or Running. Children running on a coding-agent runtime are refused. The child then completes as Cancelled through the normal path, which deletes its worker Job and releases any session lock. The tool returns {"taskName": ..., "status": "cancellation requested"}, or the child's phase when it has already finished.

Siblings — children of the same coordinator — can message each other through the controller. to_task: "*" broadcasts to every sibling except the sender. check_messages returns the oldest unread messages addressed to the Task or broadcast to its siblings, up to 500 per call, and marks them read unless mark_read is false. A longer backlog is read over several calls. Messages are deleted with the Tasks that own them.

Coordinator Agents get the pull request tools automatically. The issue tools, list_issues, get_issue, and comment_on_issue, need an explicit spec.tools entry. A person can also let these tools act through their own linked account; see Connectors. Every GitHub tool that accepts repo_url checks it against the current Task's workspace repository or its signed transaction repository context. A mismatch fails before Orka reads a credential or calls GitHub. Tools that accept task_name read the repository and credentials from that Task's workspace: tools that write to GitHub (create_pull_request, post_review_comment, comment_on_issue, merge_pull_request, auto_merge_pull_request) use its forgeCredentialRef and never fall back to another credential, and read tools use its readCredentialRef.

Creates a pull request from a branch that Orka independently verified for a completed agent Task. It calls the GitHub API with the child Task's workspace.forgeCredentialRef, or the requester's linked account, and fails if neither is available; it never falls back to the push or read credential. The forge credential never reaches the coding-agent runtime. Require a terminal verified delivery receipt before calling it: a model saying it pushed is not evidence. Parameter Type Required Description task_name string yes Name of the completed child Task whose workspace and delivery receipt identify the publication repository/branch head_branch string yes Branch containing the changes (the pushBranch from the coder task) base_branch string yes Target branch to merge into (e.g. main) title string yes Pull request title body string no Pull request body in Markdown

Checks GitHub CI status for a pull request without merging it. Parameter Type Required Description pr_number integer yes GitHub pull request number to inspect task_name string no Name of the child task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials repo_url string no GitHub repository URL, scope-checked as above wait_timeout string no Maximum time to wait for pending checks, e.g. 30m. Empty means one immediate check poll_interval string no Delay between checks while waiting, e.g. 30s. Defaults to 30s when waiting { "status": "failed", "pr_number": 42, "head_sha": "abc123", "checks_passed": false, "checks_failed": true, "checks_pending": false, "checks_details": "lint (conclusion=failure)", "wait_timed_out": false, "attempts": 1, "message": "one or more CI checks failed" } status is one of passed, failed, pending, no_checks, closed, merged, or unknown.

Fetches a pull request's unified diff, per-file patches with change statistics, and metadata (title, body, author, branches). Parameter Type Required Description pr_number integer yes GitHub pull request number to review task_name string no Name of the child task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials repo_url string no GitHub repository URL, scope-checked as above { "pr_title": "feat: add auth middleware", "pr_body": "Adds JWT-based authentication...", "pr_author": "dev-bot", "base_branch": "main", "head_branch": "feature/jwt-auth", "diff": "diff --git a/auth.go ...", "files": [ {"filename": "auth.go", "status": "added", "additions": 42, "deletions": 0, "patch": "..."} ], "status": "fetched" }

Posts a review with a verdict and optional line comments. Parameter Type Required Description pr_number integer yes GitHub pull request number body string yes Top-level review body text event string yes Review verdict: APPROVE, REQUEST_CHANGES, or COMMENT comments array no Line-level comments, each with path (relative to the repository root), line (new-file line number), and body task_name string no Name of the child task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials repo_url string no GitHub repository URL, scope-checked as above Returns the review_id, status: "submitted", and the review's html_url.

merge_pull_request checks CI once and merges only when every check passed. Otherwise it returns {"merged": false, "checks_passed": false, "message": "CI checks have not all passed: ..."} without failing. auto_merge_pull_request instead polls checks every 30 seconds until they pass, fail, or the pull request closes, and tolerates transient GitHub errors (429 and 5xx). Parameter Type Required Description task_name string yes Name of the child task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials pr_number integer yes GitHub pull request number to merge merge_method string no merge, squash, or rebase (defaults to squash) commit_title string no Custom merge commit title commit_message string no Custom merge commit message timeout string no auto_merge_pull_request only: maximum wait, e.g. 30m or 1h (defaults to 30m) auto_merge_pull_request reports an outcome: merged, ci_failed (returned at once with checks_details), closed, already_merged, or timeout.

List open pull requests (number, title, author, branches, labels, URL) or open issues (number, title, body truncated to 500 characters, labels, author). list_issues returns only unassigned issues by default. Parameter Type Required Description task_name string no Name of a task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials repo_url string no GitHub repository URL, scope-checked as above per_page integer no Results per page (default 30, max 100) page integer no Page number (default 1) unassigned_only boolean no list_issues only: return issues with no assignee (default true) At least one repository source must be available: task_name, the current Task, or ORKA_GIT_REPO.

get_issue fetches an issue's title, body, labels, assignees, state, and first page of comments. comment_on_issue posts a Markdown comment. Parameter Type Required Description issue_number integer yes GitHub issue number body string comment_on_issue only Comment text task_name string no Name of a task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials repo_url string no GitHub repository URL, scope-checked as above

Checks whether a pull request already has an Orka review marker for its current head, so a scheduled reviewer does not review the same head twice. Parameter Type Required Description pr_number integer yes GitHub pull request number to inspect task_name string no Name of a task whose workspace config has the repo and git credentials repo_url string no GitHub repository URL, scope-checked as above head_sha string no PR head SHA to check. If omitted, the tool fetches the current PR head SHA. The tool returns a hidden marker to include unchanged in the later post_review_comment body. It binds the repository, pull request number, and head SHA: <!-- orka:pr-review repo=owner/repo pr=123 head_sha=abc123 sig=... --> Marker signatures do not depend on the live GitHub token, so they survive token rotation. These variables are read by the worker Task that runs the tool: Environment variable Description ORKA_PR_REVIEW_MARKER_SECRET Optional stable HMAC key for marker signatures. Use a Kubernetes Secret or another secret injection path; never store it in the repository. ORKA_PR_REVIEW_MARKER_PREVIOUS_SECRETS Optional comma-separated previous keys, accepted until reviews signed with them have aged out. ORKA_PR_REVIEW_MARKER_TRUSTED_AUTHOR Optional GitHub login trusted for legacy markers and markers signed before a dedicated secret was configured. When omitted, Orka resolves the authenticated GitHub user for the Task credential.

Creates a scheduled type: ai Task that reviews one repository's pull requests on a cron schedule. It is offered by chat and its management tools rather than to every coordinator. Repository monitors are the durable replacement: they keep per-PR runs, items, review records, and audit events that this tool does not. Parameter Type Required Description name string yes Human-readable monitor name. The created Task receives an Orka-generated name. repo_url string yes Credential-free GitHub repository root URL, such as https://github.com/owner/repo, https://github.com/owner/repo.git, or git@github.com:owner/repo.git. Stored in the created Task's spec.workspace.gitRepo. schedule string yes Cron schedule for the monitor Task. agent_ref string yes AI Agent for the monitor Task. It must have coordination enabled and autonomous coordination disabled. namespace string no Namespace for the monitor Task. Defaults to the current task namespace. provider_ref string no Optional Provider reference for the scheduled AI Task. gitSecretRef string no Secret mapped to the created Task's spec.workspace.readCredentialRef. per_page integer no Maximum open PRs to scan per run. Defaults to 30, maximum 100. review_event string no COMMENT, APPROVE, or REQUEST_CHANGES. Defaults to COMMENT. prompt string no Additional instructions appended to the generated monitor prompt. Pull request, issue, branch/tree, blob/file, commit, query-string, fragment, non-GitHub, HTTP, and embedded-credential URLs are rejected before the Task is created, so a copied browser URL cannot widen the monitor's scope. Without gitSecretRef, Orka looks for git-credentials, github-credentials, copilot-token, github-token, and git-token in the target namespace; the Secret must contain a non-empty token, password, or GITHUB_TOKEN key. The created Task receives only list_pull_requests, check_pr_review_marker, check_pull_request_ci, review_pull_request, and post_review_comment, and its prompt tells it to pass the same repo_url to each. Because those tools are scoped to the Task's repository, the monitor cannot use its credential on another repository by changing an argument.

Chat lets you describe what you want in plain language. An orchestrator model decides which Tasks to create, runs them, checks on them, and reports back, streaming its progress as it goes. You can chat from the dashboard, from the CLI with orka run, or over the API. Video demo Watch From chat to a GitHub pull request.

With the API port-forwarded and a client token in ORKA_TOKEN and at least one Provider created, send one message. The orchestrator decides what to do, creates the Tasks it needs, and streams its progress back: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ORKA_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \ -d '{"message": "Run a container task that prints the date, then tell me what it printed.", "namespace": "orka-system"}' \ http://localhost:8080/api/v1/chat Swap Accept: text/event-stream for Accept: application/json to get one JSON reply instead of a stream. From the CLI, the same conversation is: Without --session, each orka run starts a new conversation. orka run --session incident-123 "Run a container task that prints the date, then tell me what it printed." orka run --session incident-123 "What did that task print?"
POST /api/v1/chat — Send a message (SSE streaming or JSON response) GET /api/v1/chat/config — Get chat configuration and available tools DELETE /api/v1/chat/:sessionId — Cancel a chat session

{ "message": "Create an AI task that summarizes Kubernetes best practices", "sessionId": "my-session", "provider": "anthropic", "model": "claude-opus-5", "namespace": "default", "temperature": 0.7, "maxTokens": 4096, "systemPrompt": "Focus on security topics", "agentRef": "my-agent" } Only message is required. All other fields are optional: sessionId: Existing session for continuity (auto-created if omitted) provider / model: Override the default LLM provider and model agentRef: Use an Agent CRD for provider/model/temperature defaults systemPrompt: Appended to the built-in orchestrator prompt namespace: Namespace for task operations

All SSE events use a structured envelope: id: <monotonic-seq> event: <type> data: {"sessionId":"...","content":"...","toolCall":{...},"error":{...},"usage":{...}} Event types: Event Description status Stream opened — confirms session, provider, model message Text content delta tool_call Tool invocation (name + args) tool_result Tool execution result error Error with code and message done Stream complete with usage stats

Send Accept: application/json for a blocking JSON response: { "sessionId": "chat-session-abc123", "message": "I created an AI task...", "toolCalls": [{"name": "create_ai_task", "args": {...}, "result": {...}}], "usage": {"inputTokens": 4200, "outputTokens": 1800, "llmCalls": 3} }

Tool Description create_ai_task Create an AI/LLM-powered task create_container_task Create a container task for shell commands create_agent_task Create an ACP Task using an existing Agent configured with a built-in runtime or a ready external-v2 runtimeRef. check_task_progress Get task phase/status conditions fetch_task_output Get completed task result (truncated to 2K chars) wait_for_task Wait for task completion (max 60s per call, non-blocking) cancel_task Cancel/delete a task list_agents List Agent CRDs with projected summaries list_tools List Tool CRDs and built-in tools list_tasks List tasks with optional status filter

These are only included when the user's message signals CRUD intent: Tool Description create_agent Create an Agent CRD update_agent Update an Agent CRD delete_agent Delete an Agent CRD create_tool Create a Tool CRD with HTTP endpoint delete_tool Delete a Tool CRD delete_session Delete a session and transcript

The system prompt uses XML-delimited sections for optimal tool-calling accuracy: <identity> You are the Orka orchestrator — an AI assistant that manages Kubernetes-native task execution. </identity> <capabilities>...</capabilities> <task_types>container, ai, agent with usage guidance</task_types> <available_agents>...dynamically injected...</available_agents> <available_tools>...dynamically injected...</available_tools> <rules>Operational invariants</rules> <examples>Complete multi-step tool-calling traces</examples> Dynamic context (agents, tools) is built once at request start and cached for the tool loop duration.
Bounded semaphore (--chat-max-concurrent, default 10) Returns 429 Too Many Requests when full
--chat-max-duration (default 30m): Wall-clock timeout per request --chat-tool-timeout (default 60s): Per-tool execution timeout --chat-max-iterations (default 50): Max tool execution loops
--chat-max-tasks-per-turn (default 5): Max tasks created per chat turn Task names use session-scoped prefix to prevent collisions

Repetition detector: Same tool called with identical args 3 times → warning injected, 5 iterations penalized Progress assertion: Every 5 iterations, LLM must summarize progress Graceful termination: On iteration exhaustion, LLM must provide final summary

Structured error responses help the LLM self-correct: { "success": false, "error": "Agent 'my-agent' not found in namespace 'default'", "errorType": "not_found", "suggestion": "Use list_agents to see available agents" }

Chat sessions use prefix chat-session- and type chat in the session store Sessions store message summaries, not full tool outputs Auto-truncation when session exceeds --chat-max-session-size (default 500KB) First user message is always preserved for context

Default to namespace from ChatRequest or authenticated user's namespace kube-system and kube-public are blocked All orchestrator-created resources get labels: orka.ai/created-by: orchestrator, orka.ai/chat-session: <sessionId>
Chat is on by default (--chat-enabled). --chat-provider and --chat-model set the default Provider and model, and the limits above have their own flags. All of them are listed under Controller flags.

Create a ServiceAccount token (or use --token or --token-file) and open the Orka dashboard in your browser, signed in with it. The token goes only to the browser; other orka commands do not use it, and this command does not use ORKA_TOKEN or the config file's token. The browser opens --server, ORKA_SERVER or the configured server, else http://localhost:8080; unlike other commands, dashboard does not find the server through the kubeconfig. The ServiceAccount is in --namespace, ORKA_NAMESPACE or the configured namespace, else "default". The controller serves the dashboard only when it runs with --dashboard-enabled; every other orka command works without it. Usage: orka dashboard [flags] Flags: -h, --help help for dashboard --no-open Print the dashboard URL without opening a browser --service-account string ServiceAccount name (default "default") --show-token Print the dashboard URL with the token in it instead of <redacted>; use only in a trusted terminal -t, --token string Token to sign the dashboard in with (prefer --token-file, which keeps it out of process arguments; ORKA_TOKEN is not used) Global Flags: --kubeconfig string Path to kubeconfig file -n, --namespace string Kubernetes namespace, or set ORKA_NAMESPACE (default: from config, else the namespace the Orka server watches) -s, --server string Orka server URL, or set ORKA_SERVER (default: the Orka Service reached through kubeconfig, else "http://localhost:8080") --token-file string Path to file containing the bearer token (use - for stdin) --txn-token string Transaction token to send via Txn-Token header --txn-token-file string Path to file containing a Transaction token (use - for stdin)

List the approval requests recorded for a task: the tool each one wants to run, its arguments, and how long a pending request has left. Pass an ID (or a unique prefix of it) to print one request with every argument on its own line. --wide adds the severity, risk summary, and who decided and why. With --watch the command polls until the task has a pending request, prints the list, and exits 0. It exits non-zero if the task finishes first (Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled), because then no request is coming, or when --timeout elapses. Ctrl-C stops the wait. Copy a single regular file between the local machine and the execution workspace of a running or retained ACP Task. Workspace paths are relative to the workspace root (the agent's working directory); a leading "/" names that root. Use "-" as the local path for stdout or stdin. Copying out requires the class opt-in "read" or "exec" and the "get" permission on tasks/files; it does not taint the session. Copying in requires the class opt-in "exec" and the "update" permission on tasks/files, and taints the session: it will never be published, reused, checkpointed, or continued. Usage: orka task cp <task>:<path> <local> | <local> <task>:<path> [flags] Examples: orka task cp my-task:src/main.go ./main.go orka task cp ./fix.patch my-task:/tmp-fix.patch Flags: -h, --help help for cp --max-bytes int Refuse files larger than this when copying out (default 67108864, at most 268435456) -q, --quiet Do not print the session taint notice Global Flags: --kubeconfig string Path to kubeconfig file -n, --namespace string Kubernetes namespace, or set ORKA_NAMESPACE (default: from config, else the namespace the Orka server watches) -s, --server string Orka server URL, or set ORKA_SERVER (default: the Orka Service reached through kubeconfig, else "http://localhost:8080") -t, --token string Bearer token for authentication (prefer --token-file or ORKA_TOKEN, which keep it out of process arguments) --token-file string Path to file containing the bearer token (use - for stdin) --txn-token string Transaction token to send via Txn-Token header --txn-token-file string Path to file containing a Transaction token (use - for stdin)

Run one command inside the execution workspace of a running or retained ACP Task. The command runs as the Task session's own unprivileged child identity, never as the supervisor, and is bounded by --timeout and an output limit. It requires the --operator-workspace-access-enabled controller flag, an ExecutionWorkspaceClass opted in with the acp.workspace.orka.ai/operator-access=exec annotation, and the "create" permission on the tasks/exec subresource. Every exec taints the Task's session: it will never be published, reused, checkpointed for forks, or continued. Every exec is audited. Usage: orka task exec <task> [-i] [-t] -- <command> [args...] [flags] Examples: orka task exec my-task -- git status orka task exec my-task -it -- bash Flags: -h, --help help for exec -q, --quiet Do not print the session taint notice -i, --stdin Pass stdin to the command --timeout duration Maximum command duration (at most 1h0m0s) (default 15m0s) --token string Bearer token for authentication (prefer --token-file or ORKA_TOKEN, which keep it out of process arguments) -t, --tty Allocate a terminal for the command (implies -i) Global Flags: --kubeconfig string Path to kubeconfig file -n, --namespace string Kubernetes namespace, or set ORKA_NAMESPACE (default: from config, else the namespace the Orka server watches) -s, --server string Orka server URL, or set ORKA_SERVER (default: the Orka Service reached through kubeconfig, else "http://localhost:8080") --token-file string Path to file containing the bearer token (use - for stdin) --txn-token string Transaction token to send via Txn-Token header --txn-token-file string Path to file containing a Transaction token (use - for stdin)
