Orka defaults to 8 MiB of encoded bundle data, configurable up to 64 MiB. This is a consumer transport limit, separate from SessionKit's native storage limits. A bundle contains the verified manifest and rollout. Authentication files, native SQLite databases, provider configuration, and process memory are excluded. The controller and runtime must both support native Sessions. Use the pinned Codex 0.160.0 / codex-acp 2.1.1 runtime image. Private checkpoints use the controller's existing execution-snapshot encryption key with separate associated data. Retain that key with the SQLite backup. Deploy this schema on a new installation. Existing Orka databases are not upgraded in place; see Upgrading.

Export cannot merge a returned thread into a populated ~/.codex or replace its older local copy. The original UUID is preserved, so a return can collide with that copy. Existing paginated SQLite state can also shadow a newly copied rollout. SessionKit does not modify those databases or reconcile divergent local and cluster histories. Use a separate fresh CODEX_HOME on return and resume the UUID explicitly. Keep CODEX_SQLITE_HOME unset or set it to an absolute path without surrounding whitespace resolving to that exact private CODEX_HOME. The export CLI rejects relative and whitespace-padded overrides, resolves symlinks, and rejects a different database directory, including a nested directory whose existing database state is not checked by fresh-home validation, before fetching or staging the checkpoint. Your original home remains unchanged and can still be an import source. Safe per-thread replacement in an existing home is not implemented.
documents.s: Returning to an existing Codex home

documents.t: A non-null encrypted_content field anywhere in the selected rollout, including reasoning items or compaction history, rejects the migration. This is provider-issued opaque native context, not Orka's checkpoint encryption at rest. Preserving its bytes has not established a supported reload contract with destination provider settings and credentials. Migration neither decrypts nor strips it to make the thread acceptable. Setting reasoning effort to none before creating and continuing a thread can avoid reasoning items on a model that supports that mode. It does not remove existing encrypted content, and some models do not support none. Supported non-encrypted compaction records remain byte-identical. This is not general migration support for reasoning-enabled Codex sessions.

The default limit is 8 MiB, or 8,388,608 bytes, for the complete encoded bundle. Operators can select a limit from 1 byte through the 64 MiB hard ceiling with --native-session-max-bytes or ORKA_NATIVE_SESSION_MAX_BYTES on the controller. The controller propagates that policy to built-in runtime pools, including workspace-backed pools. Independent runtimes must set the same environment variable; their advertised capability limit is also enforced. Changing the built-in runtime policy uses the existing pool replacement and drain path. The local CLI has a separate matching limit. Use orka session migrate --max-bundle-bytes 16777216 import ... or the same flag with export for a 16 MiB bundle. ORKA_NATIVE_SESSION_MAX_BYTES supplies the CLI default when the flag is omitted. Raising only the local CLI limit cannot raise the cluster limit. New clients request the additive native-size capability with X-Orka-Native-Session-Limits: 1; older clients receive the original capability shape without the new field. An older runtime that does not advertise its limit retains the previous 512 KiB bound and rejects larger native restores before request delivery. Capture requests use the same opt-in header; older callers retain the 512 KiB capture limit and its structured rejection behavior. This is a byte limit, not a model token limit. The JSON bundle base64-encodes both the rollout and manifest, leaving approximately 6 MiB of combined raw bytes under the 8 MiB default, slightly less after JSON overhead. The HTTP envelope adds another encoding layer with its own bounded allowance. Ordinary API, prompt, and ACP message limits are unchanged. The cap applies to import and every runtime checkpoint, including growth after continuation. It counts the full saved rollout, including tool outputs and historical records retained after compaction. Orka does not compress or truncate the bundle. Oversized native data is rejected; an established native-continuity Session does not silently fall back to transcript-only continuation. Lowering the policy preserves stored checkpoints but can block export, restore, or new capture until the limit is raised again. Before lowering the cap, pause new native Tasks, let active turns finish and durably finalize their checkpoints, and verify that retained checkpoints fit the proposed cap. If capture is already blocked, preserve the exact runtime Pod and its capture evidence; force-deleting it can lose uncommitted native history. This is an Orka transport restriction, not SessionKit's native storage limit. Larger limits increase memory, temporary storage, and encrypted database usage; choose them for the expected workload.

Native migration requires --server, ORKA_SERVER or a saved API endpoint. Automatic Kubernetes Service discovery is not used: a familiar name, labels, and Service UID do not establish the application's identity. Select the trusted Orka API endpoint explicitly before sending portable history. Provide an API bearer credential (--token, --token-file, ORKA_TOKEN, or a saved Orka token) or a supported transaction token. The CLI never sends a kubeconfig credential to an endpoint named this way, and Kubernetes exec, auth-provider, and certificate credentials are not API credentials. Name the namespace with --namespace, ORKA_NAMESPACE, or a saved namespace: the journal and the import receipt are bound to it. Missing API authentication or namespace fails before capture or persistence of the migration bundle. Configure the endpoint, authentication, and namespace before running the commands below.

Stop every Codex process using the source home before capture. --source-stopped records that assertion; it does not terminate a local client. Use a new Session name and a journal directory outside the source home: orka session migrate import migrated-review \ --codex-home /absolute/source/codex-home \ --thread 01a10020-1222-76e3-977d-d5165792ae72 \ --journal-dir /absolute/private/import-journal \ --source-stopped Import reserves a fresh non-Gateway Session. It allocates no runtime or Task lease. An existing Session, including an empty one, cannot be overwritten. Submit a normal Codex Task with spec.sessionRef.name: migrated-review and spec.sessionRef.create: true for the first continuation. Use the Task's current workspace and tool policy. During admission, Orka installs the bundle in the child's fresh private CODEX_HOME before starting codex-acp. It uses capability-gated session/resume with the original UUID and current cwd, provider, MCP tools, approvals, and sandbox configuration. The runtime must advertise resume support and prove restoring the exact bundle before Orka sends the new user prompt. Canonical history is not injected again. Missing resume support or a failed resume rejects creation without falling back to session/new. The imported history stays native; the Orka transcript records new Tasks.

After a successful Task, Orka proves the provider and its descendants have exited before capture. The checkpoint and canonical terminal result commit together before the Session lease is released. The runtime home is deleted only after that commit. The next Task cold-starts with the saved checkpoint and fresh credentials. Export uses the last committed checkpoint. It does not force an active Task to stop. The checkpoint must still match the exact Session owner and canonical transcript boundary. orka session migrate export migrated-review \ --codex-home /absolute/fresh/codex-home \ --cwd /absolute/local/workspace \ --journal-dir /absolute/private/export-journal \ --codex-bin /absolute/codex-0.160.0 The destination must be a fresh isolated Codex home with directory mode 0700. The journal must be outside it and private, also with directory mode 0700. Authenticate the destination with current local credentials and configure its provider before resuming the UUID. Migration does not copy source authentication or source policy into authority.

Retain the journal and repeat the same command after an uncertain response. The CLI reuses its saved bundle and operation ID. Export also reuses the same frozen SessionKit install plan and receipt. Changing the target, bundle, or cwd with that journal is rejected. The explicitly selected API endpoint must stay unchanged across retries. Automatic Kubernetes Service discovery and streaming are not available for native migration; use --server or a saved trusted API endpoint and supply API authentication as described above. An uncertain runtime install retains its target and frozen journal and closes pool admission. Exact create retries report that retained outcome without allocating another home or starting a child. Automatic reconciliation of that supervisor creation state is not part of this delivery. A capture failure after proven writer exit can retry from the retained private home under a new fenced operation. Receipt reconciliation never starts a capture. If native capture is unsupported and there is no prior native checkpoint, Orka records one warning execution event with reason native_capture_unsupported. The next turn uses the canonical transcript instead of native continuity. The warning survives controller retries and restarts without duplicates. If a prior native checkpoint exists, unsupported capture still blocks settlement; Orka never silently replaces required native continuity with transcript replay. Failed, cancelled, or lost provider prompts do not publish a new native checkpoint. The runtime that ran them is poisoned and retired, so a Task that appends to a Session with a native checkpoint settles its terminal marker with the existing checkpoint carried forward: the checkpoint's transcript boundary advances past the marker, the lease is released, and the next Task resumes the same native state. That state omits only the prompt that produced no result. A successful prompt can retain its native state after delivery failure once workspace finalization and canonical settlement complete. Poisoned workspace validation failures cannot produce a native checkpoint; for appending Tasks on a Session with a native checkpoint they retain the exact runtime evidence and hold the Session lease until reconciliation. Accepted turns with sessionRef.append: false leave the checkpoint unchanged and retire their runtime before a later Task loads the saved state. Native restore reloads Codex's whole saved conversation, so sessionRef.maxMessages limits only the canonical transcript Orka sends when no checkpoint is used. A Task whose sessionRef.throughMessageId names any message other than the Session's latest fails before it binds the Session, with reason NativeSessionHistoryBoundaryUnsupported, because restore cannot stop at an earlier message. A capture intent that reaches the runtime only after it expired is reconciled against the runtime's own record. When the same runtime incarnation never recorded that capture, it reports native_capture_not_started and the controller begins one fresh capture under a superseding intent instead of reconciling indefinitely. A changed canonical boundary makes an older checkpoint unavailable for restore or export. If a native-continuity Session cannot produce a supported checkpoint, Orka retains the runtime evidence and blocks finalization. It does not silently start a new provider thread. An ordinary Session with no native checkpoint may use canonical continuity after a terminal format or size rejection, but only after the runtime proves process exit. Before a capture intent or native checkpoint exists, canonical recovery also remains available after the exact runtime has been retired or replaced. A surviving native-capable runtime still produces its first checkpoint. Normal pool drain preserves resident native evidence until the controller commits the checkpoint and deletes the runtime. Uncommitted native state uses the runtime Pod's temporary storage; a forced Pod loss can destroy it. Recovery with native continuity or a capture intent then blocks on the missing exact runtime or capture receipt. Native bundles are private Session data, accessible only through the migration endpoint. Export requires get on core.orka.ai/sessions. Import requires create on the Session collection and get on the requested name, plus the corresponding context-token Session scopes when enabled. Session deletion removes the native bundle and its receipts with the existing cleanup flow.

The subprocess regressions use explicit barrier acknowledgements and SIGKILL, not graceful shutdown or returned persistence errors. They cover completed capture before checkpoint commit, committed checkpoint before runtime deletion, and supervisor death after capture admission but before snapshot publication. They use scripted ACP responses, without live inference. The controller test runs the production dispatcher in subprocesses. It keeps the Kubernetes API and runtime fixture outside the killed process and reopens the same SQLite database in a replacement process. It checks the prior checkpoint, canonical boundary, immutable capture receipt, epoch fences, prompt counts, and exact-generation cleanup. By default it uses an isolated envtest API server. To exercise a disposable kind API, run from the VM checkout with a kindctl-scoped kubeconfig: ORKA_NATIVE_CRASH_KUBECONFIG="$(.agents/skills/kindctl/bin/kindctl path --tag native-crash)" \ go test ./internal/controller \ -run '^TestACPDispatcherNativeSessionProcessCrash$' -count=3 -v The supervisor test is Linux-only and requires root plus the production ACP exec helper from the pinned runtime image. Its parent kills the subprocess at an acknowledged in-progress capture and checks the missing success receipt, unchanged committed bundle, private evidence, and replacement-boot fencing. It pins the ACP child with a pidfd and proves child exit after supervisor death before any failure-path test cleanup signals the child: ./supervisor.test -test.run '^TestSupervisorNativeCaptureProcessCrash$' -test.count=3 -test.v Run these checks only in disposable test environments. They do not make uncommitted runtime storage durable or enable automatic recovery of a missing capture receipt after forced runtime loss. That case still fails closed.

Some actions should not happen unattended: creating a work order, deploying, spending money, writing to someone's account. Orka can hold such a call until a person approves or declines it, then run exactly the stored action — never a regenerated one — and return the real result to the agent. Approvals appear in three places: Where What gets approved Set up Native autonomous coordinators (type: ai) Custom Tools listed in coordination.approvalRequiredTools, and requests the agent makes with request_approval. The Task parks until a decision arrives. Autonomous tasks External runtimes, such as AgentKit and Foundry agents Orka-executed tools in the runtime's approvalRequiredTools. The tool call stays open while it waits. This page Linked accounts Every write tool that acts through a person's connector Automatic People decide in the Task's Approvals tab in the dashboard, with orka task approve and orka task decline, or through the API. To alert reviewers instead of having them poll, see Alerting reviewers. The rest of this page covers the external-runtime path.

A Task can send a signed webhook when an approval is requested and when it is approved, declined, expired, or cancelled. Select the events next to the Task's webhookURL: spec: webhookURL: https://hooks.example.com/orka webhookEvents: - task.approval_requested - task.approval_resolved This works for all three approval paths and for parked sign-offs, whose decision can arrive after the parked turn Succeeded. A notice carries the approval ID, the gated tool's name, severity, the deadline when the approval has one, and the resolution. It never carries the proposed arguments, the action text, the reviewer's reason, or who decided. Open the approval in the dashboard or the API to review it. A brokered review that times out is sent as expired a few seconds after its deadline. Approval notices are retried for about three minutes, since review lasts at most ten. Treat the notice as an alert. Decide through the dashboard, the CLI, or the API, which check the approval again. See Approval events for the body, deduplication, ordering, and how to verify the signature.

Orka can let an agent look up inventory automatically and require a person to approve a proposed work order. The controller saves the exact action before showing it for review. The tool has not run at that point. Approval lets Orka execute that stored action and return its real result to the waiting agent. This applies to tools executed by Orka for qualified AgentKit and Foundry orka.harness.v2 runtimes. Runtime-native shell and file permissions are a separate capability. Video demo Watch Human approval before an agent takes action.

An external AgentRuntime declares an explicit, sorted MCP policy and a runtime profile whose policy digests match it: spec: capabilities: mcpPolicy: allowedTools: [create-work-order, read-inventory] disallowedTools: [] allowBash: false approvalRequiredTools: [create-work-order] The registered adapter must advertise supportsBrokeredToolApprovals and pass conformance. Task agentRuntime.allowedTools must exactly match the registered policy. Per-Task settings cannot override that frozen profile. Brokered approval support is off by default. After qualifying the exact adapter and hosted configuration, set the supervisor's ORKA_ACP_BROKERED_TOOL_APPROVAL_PROFILE_DIGEST to its complete runtime-profile digest. A mismatched opt-in fails startup. Requalify after changing that profile. Use the profile renderer and manifests in examples/human-approval-v2 for complete configuration, including immutable adapter and image digests. The example tools run against a disposable HTTP counter. One lookup returns inventory without review. One simulated action increments the counter only after approval. It does not create equipment orders or make purchases.

Open the Task's Approvals tab. It shows the proposed operation, a sanitized input preview, and the review deadline. A call-tool wrapper also names its inner operation when that name is present in the inputs. Sensitive values are redacted and oversized previews are bounded. The original executable inputs remain private; the preview is never used as execution input. The same records and decisions are available through the existing API: GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/approvals?namespace=<ns> POST /api/v1/tasks/:id/approvals/:approvalID/decision?namespace=<ns> Content-Type: application/json {"decision":"approve","reason":"Reviewed the asset and quantity"} The list response names the Task it was filtered against (taskUID), its phase at that same read (taskPhase), and whether it is being deleted (taskDeleting), so a poller such as orka task approvals --watch can tell whether a pending request can still be decided without a second lookup by name. Decisions are refused for finished and deleting Tasks. Use decline to reject the action. Reviewers need update on core.orka.ai/tasks/approvals and patch on the parent Task. Gateway-owned Tasks also enforce their existing operate permission. See the authorization reference. The first terminal decision wins. While the bound Task run remains active, repeating that decision returns its saved state. A competing decision receives a conflict. Once the run settles or its binding becomes stale, even an identical decision retry receives HTTP 409. The panel separates the review decision from execution. An approved action can still fail, become stale before starting, or have an unknown outcome. History records the reviewer and decision, then not_started, running, succeeded, failed, or unknown as execution evidence becomes available. When the tool sent nothing or the remote system refused the request, the outcome is failed and its reason says why, for example the HTTP status and message GitHub refused a missing permission with; nothing changed. An unknown outcome means the action may have run. Check the target system before choosing whether to make a new request. The controller logs the redacted cause of both.

The per-Task list answers one Task. To find every request waiting on a person in a namespace, read the approvals inbox or the wider attention view: GET /api/v1/approvals?namespace=<ns>&status=pending GET /api/v1/attention?namespace=<ns>&since=24h Both are computed on each read and need only list on core.orka.ai/tasks. Every Task then passes the same context-token and Gateway read filters as GET /api/v1/tasks, and only Tasks that report a pending approval (a WaitingForApproval condition, or a parked approval wait that still takes a decision) have their approval history read. The inbox lists brokered, worker and parked approvals that can still be decided, soonest deadline first; expired and already decided requests drop out. The attention view adds Tasks with an unknown outcome, failed Tasks and Tasks whose Pod cannot start inside the since window (default 24 hours, at most 7 days), and blocked RepositoryMonitor work actions when the caller may also list repositorymonitors and monitorworkactions. Each item is a short safe summary: Task identity, the tool name of a brokered approval (recorded by the controller from the resolved tool), a fixed label for parked sign-offs, severity and deadline. It never includes action labels built from call arguments, fields of approvals the AI worker records, the input preview, risk summary, wait reason or decision reasons; open the Task's Approvals tab or the per-Task list for those before deciding. Each approval item carries canApprove and canDecline. They are hints from the same checks the decision endpoint runs, including the rule that only the requester may approve a call on a Task that acts on their behalf. null means the hint could not be settled cheaply, for example past the first 20 Tasks of a page for a ServiceAccount caller. The decision endpoint remains the only enforcement point. Results are ranked and paged with an opaque continue token that also fixes the since window. Scans are bounded; when a bound is hit the response sets incomplete: true and names it in incompleteReasons, and the ranking must not be read as complete. sources.approvals and sources.monitors report whether approval history and monitor items were included, unavailable, or forbidden to the caller. sources.approvals is partial when the caller may list a Task that reports a pending approval but may not read that Task's approvals, for example a context token with orka:tasks:list but not orka:tasks:get. Those approvals are left out without detail, so an empty inbox does not mean nothing is pending. unavailable takes precedence over partial; scan bounds are reported in incompleteReasons instead. See the authorization reference.

Review has a maximum of ten minutes. Approved execution has a maximum of four minutes. Approval-required HTTP Tool timeouts must be shorter than four minutes. The MCP call allows fifteen minutes to cover both phases and transport overhead. The Task deadline can shorten either phase and the runtime must keep renewing its normal prompt lease. Configure a Task timeout that leaves room for initial agent work as well as the review. Decline, expiry, and cancellation prevent an unstarted action from running. Before execution, Orka rechecks the Task identity and active attempt, runtime and controller fences, tool definition, and frozen policy. A late decision cannot revive an ended run. Waiting holds no global execution lock, so other Tasks in separate RuntimeSessions can progress when capacity is available. If the agent receives the cancellation result and finishes before prompt cancellation reaches it, Orka retains that completed result. The approval stays cancelled and the action does not run. Direct AgentKit receives the longer MCP timeout from the supervisor. Hosted AgentKit also needs persistent continuation state with a TTL of 1800 seconds and a pinned Foundry agent version whose idle timeout is at least 1800 seconds. See the adapter contract for exact settings and final error codes.

Orka stores the original request in an immutable Secret owned by the Task. It binds the review to the Task UID, attempt, prompt, tool call and operation, runtime identity, arguments, tool descriptor, and policy. Events expose safe metadata and fingerprints. They do not contain the executable request, downstream credentials, or raw tool results. An interrupted broker connection preserves a pending review. Exact redelivery can resume it only while the original authority remains valid. A new controller epoch or supervisor boot invalidates the old run. Those cases keep their evidence and do not replay the prompt or transfer approval to a new run. A pending review whose runtime has disappeared becomes non-actionable when the Task ends or its review deadline expires. Execution reserves a durable external-effect record before review and claims it once after approval. A committed result can be returned again without calling the tool. After a controller restart, Orka repairs missing approval execution events from those durable records. A committed result restores its outcome; a started action without a committed result becomes unknown. Orka never takes over an expired execution lease to try the action again. Task ownership removes the private request Secret when the Task is deleted; retain the Task and its durable stores while investigating an unknown outcome. Enroll external Kubernetes runtimes with deployment.kubernetesRecovery before submitting Tasks if cleanup must survive supervisor loss. Enrollment binds the exact Deployment, Pod, container, and authentication identity. Use a stable runtime instance ID and a newly generated boot ID at each supervisor start. The supported topology has one AgentKit supervisor, or a Foundry supervisor and broker. Init and ephemeral containers invalidate recovery enrollment. For Foundry recovery, first upgrade the controller and qualify the broker, then set the supervisor's ORKA_ACP_FOUNDRY_RECOVERY_PROFILE_DIGEST to the exact runtime profile digest. Recovery is default-off and independent of approval qualification. It records the broker's durable ledger identity before admission. After supervisor loss, Orka requires proof that the original container terminated and that the same broker permanently sealed and retired every remote session under that boot. Keep its ledger intact through recovery. Missing historical enrollment cannot be recreated after the original compute is gone. Cleanup remains blocked when that evidence is absent. Crash validation checks normal Task deletion after those receipts are recorded, including product finalizer release, private request reclamation, and eventual release of retained boot credentials when the registration is deleted. The example acceptance runner uses the real Task and approval APIs. It checks the counter before approval, after repeated decisions, after decline and cancellation, and after expiry. Run it for both a direct AgentKit registration and an AgentKit agent hosted behind the Foundry bridge. Local deterministic model or hosted-process runs prove those transports; Azure-hosted acceptance also requires the deployed Foundry gateway and the configured hosted version.

Label a GitHub issue orka:implement and Orka takes it from there. It plans the change, implements it with a coding agent, opens a pull request, reviews it, repairs it when review or CI asks for changes, and marks it ready to merge. A RepositoryMonitor runs the whole loop, and every step leaves a durable record you can inspect. Runnable example examples/github-label-triggered-issue-loop configures the Agents, Secrets, and monitor for this workflow.

A maintainer labels an issue orka:implement, or runs orka monitor issue implement <monitor> <number>. Orka checks who asked, then records a durable command event. For a label, it verifies the webhook signature and the sender's current GitHub permission. For the CLI or API, it uses your Orka API authorization (orka:monitors:operate and orka:monitors:write under transaction-token authorization; see Create monitor command). A workflow action is queued, bound to the monitor generation, a snapshot digest of the issue, a dedupe key, and the command ID. Orka reads the issue and computes a content digest that excludes Orka's own labels and comments. With spec.issueWorkflow.implementation.requirePlan: true, the default, Orka queues a read-only planning Task when there is no current ready plan. A ready plan continues the original command automatically. A blocked or needs_human plan stops and records why. Implementation runs in a writable, sanitized workspace on a branch the controller chooses. The agent only edits files; the separate Workspace Publisher validates the change, publishes it, and verifies the remote branch. The controller accepts only a matching VerifiedExact delivery receipt, then creates or reuses the pull request and records each GitHub write in its audit log. Review and bounded repair continue on each exact pull request head until the pull request is merge-ready or clearly blocked. Triage and research are not part of the automatic flow. Request them, or any step on its own, through the API or CLI.

Create the Agents. A planner, an implementer, a reviewer, and a repairer, all built-in coding-agent runtimes. Implementation supports Codex and Claude; see the safety model for what each role accepts. Create four credential Secrets — source read, publication read, publication write, and forge — as described in Repository monitors. Orka refuses to run a write workflow when any role is missing or two roles share a Secret. Create the RepositoryMonitor with issue targets, label triggers, and the Agents: spec: targets: issues: enabled: true triggers: github: labels: enabled: true agents: planner: name: issue-planner implementer: name: issue-implementer reviewer: name: pr-reviewer repairer: name: pr-repairer repair: enabled: true review: exactEventEnabled: true publish: enabled: true The Resource reference lists every field. Connect the GitHub webhook. Store a shared secret in the controller's namespace and point the Helm release at it: umask 077 openssl rand -hex 32 | tr -d '\n' > github-webhook.secret kubectl -n orka-system create secret generic github-webhook \ --from-file=secret=github-webhook.secret helm upgrade orka orka/orka --namespace orka-system --reuse-values \ --set github.webhook.secretName=github-webhook Then add a webhook to the GitHub repository that sends Issues and Pull requests events to https://<orka-api-host>/webhooks/github, paste the contents of github-webhook.secret as its secret, then delete the file. The endpoint must be reachable from GitHub, so expose the Orka API through your ingress. Require the readiness check. With review.publish.enabled: true, Orka publishes the commit status orka/<namespace>/<monitor-name>/ready. Require it in branch protection, alongside your CI and approving-review rules.

When a labeled issue arrives at /webhooks/github, the controller verifies X-Hub-Signature-256, checks that the issue belongs to the monitor's repository, checks the sender's current repository permission (triggers.github.labels.requireActorPermission, default write), and records a durable command before starting any work. Rename the label with spec.triggers.github.labels.issues.implement. Set consumeCommandLabels: true to remove the label once the command is recorded. Replayed GitHub deliveries do not create another command. The webhook response confirms intake, not a finished implementation. There is one command label. There is no agent:* label handler and no generic label-to-Task trigger, and ordinary progress needs no label for each step. Planning, research, decomposition, review, and repair can still be requested through the monitor API or CLI for ad hoc work.

orka:pause (configurable with spec.policy.pauseLabels) is a persistent guard on one issue or pull request. It prevents further workflow actions and keeps merge readiness blocked. A bounded Task that is already running may finish, including its publication; use the Task cancellation API to stop it immediately. Removing the label queues fresh reconciliation, not an approval or a replay of an old command. A stop command cancels queued workflow actions and active monitor Tasks, and prevents stale Task results from mutating anything afterwards. It does not depend on label propagation. spec.suspend pauses background runs for the whole monitor. Queued and manual runs can still finish. A pause label is not an atomic merge lock. To stop a merge that GitHub already considers eligible, turn off GitHub auto-merge on that pull request. GitHub sender permission is checked when the label is added and when it is removed.

Pull request events on each new head trigger an exact-head review when spec.review.exactEventEnabled is set. Automatic repair needs spec.repair.enabled, a repairer Agent, and the publication credentials, and is bounded by maxRepairsPerPR and maxRepairsPerHead. Workflow polling observes CI and completed Tasks without requiring another label. GitHub's per-pull-request auto-merge setting owns the merge decision. Orka never enables auto-merge or calls the merge endpoint. When auto-merge is off, the pull request stays open and ready. Repository monitors describes the readiness status and the token permissions it needs. Before disabling readiness publication, deleting a monitor, or changing its repository or tracked branch, remove or replace its required status in the repository's branch protection. GitHub commit statuses persist after the monitor is removed or repointed, and Orka does not revoke them.

Issue and pull request text is untrusted input. Read-only agents never receive GitHub mutation credentials or direct Git credentials. Claude and OpenCode roles receive only scoped read tools with Bash denied. Codex is supported for pull request review and read-only issue triage, research, and planning; it runs inside the RuntimeSession boundary, where the controller rejects elevation requests and classifies any workspace change as a read violation. The monitor API currently accepts Codex only for the reviewer role. Copilot and external runtimeRef runtimes are rejected for this hardened mode. Implementation agents receive only runtime model access and a pre-cloned writable workspace, never Git push credentials. Codex and Claude are supported; Copilot is rejected because its runtime credential can mutate GitHub. Code-changing Tasks must produce a validated patch before any branch push. Denied paths and secret scanning are always enforced, before allowedPaths is checked. GitHub writes are controller-owned and recorded as mutation records. Repair runs only when spec.repair.enabled is true and stays within its limits. Plans and implementations are bound to the issue's content digest, so a human edit makes downstream artifacts stale. Policy labels follow the repository's current GitHub state. triggers.github.labels.requireActorPermission authorizes command intake; it does not override GitHub permissions for editing policy labels. A rejected pause-label webhook does not queue a run, but later inventory still observes the repository's labels.

spec.issueWorkflow.implementation bounds code-changing work: Field Default What it limits maxActive 2 Active implementation jobs per monitor maxAttemptsPerIssue 2 Implementation attempts for one issue maxChangedFiles 12 Files in one orka.patch.v1 patch allowedPaths none Path globs or prefixes, such as api/** or docs/**, that a patch may touch. Pull request repairs use the same list

orka monitor issue plan orka-main 123 orka monitor issue implement orka-main 123 orka monitor issue implementation get orka-main 123 orka monitor issue patch preview orka-main 123 orka monitor mutations list orka-main --kind issue --number 123 orka monitor pr review orka-main 456 --target-sha '<head-sha>' orka monitor pr fix orka-main 456 --target-sha '<head-sha>' orka monitor pr ready readiness orka-main 456 orka monitor work-actions list orka-main --kind issue --number 123 Start debugging with the workflow timeline: orka monitor work-actions list orka-main --status blocked orka monitor doctor orka-main Blocked records carry a short reason such as stale_command_snapshot, security_sensitive, patch_path_denied, validation_failed, or stopped_by_command. The dashboard's Monitors page shows the same reason next to implementation jobs and GitHub mutation records. Patch previews return safe orka.patch.v1 metadata, also available from GET /api/v1/monitors/implementation-jobs/{id}/patch-preview. Transient failures are classified and attached to monitor events and metrics: github_rate_limited, llm_rate_limited, cluster_capacity_blocked, and retry_scheduled. Use orka monitor events <monitor> --event-type run_failed or the dashboard's audit timeline to see them. A pull request the controller creates starts a targeted inventory run, with bounded retries. If that run fails terminally before recording the pull request, fixing the cause (for example, the credentials) does not restart discovery on its own when no schedule or pull request event queues another run. Start a fresh targeted run without a head SHA: orka monitor run orka-main --namespace orka --target-kind pull_request --target-number 456

Pause-label intake and workflow reconciliation can update the same item concurrently, and a stale write can overwrite the stored label or workflow progress. The workflow does not yet guarantee pause enforcement across this race. With automatic repair enabled and readiness publication disabled, a full workflow poll fetches details for every open pull request before applying maxPerRun. That limit bounds the work started, not GitHub reads. Automatic rediscovery after a credential fix is not implemented; use the targeted run above.

orka task exec and orka task cp let an operator look inside the execution workspace of a running ACP agent Task. You can run a command, open an interactive shell, or copy a single file out of or into the workspace. They are debugging tools for administrators, not an agent feature: They are off by default, and an administrator must enable them at three independent levels. Every call needs a dedicated Kubernetes permission, and every authenticated call is audited. Anything that could change the workspace taints the Task's session. After that, the Task is never published, reused, checkpointed for forks, or continued. Commands run as the session's own unprivileged child identity, the same one the agent runs as. They never run as the supervisor or as root, and they never reach the supervisor's credentials. Traffic always goes through orka-api. The CLI never connects to a runtime Pod directly.

Target Supported Class-backed ACP Task (spec.execution.workspace.classRef) on an Agent Sandbox or other Pod-backed provider, while its RuntimeSession is live Yes The same workspace after the Task finished, while it is still attached to the Task or the Task held its last attachment, until settlement suspends or deletes it. With a Suspend class that happens within seconds of completion, and calls then return 409 execution workspace is not running Yes Substrate native-process workspaces Not yet (501) Suspended or deleted workspaces, built-in pools without an execution workspace, container Tasks, external AgentRuntime registrations No The supervisor refuses access whenever the workspace is frozen for validation or is being published. That covers validation, publication preparation, publishing, verification, finalization, cancellation, and deletion.

Start the controller with: --operator-workspace-access-enabled Without the flag, every operator route answers 403 operator workspace access is disabled. The controller refuses to start with the flag unless Task provenance admission is enabled (--task-provenance-admission-enabled or --task-provenance-admission-external), which protects the operator taint.

Annotate the ExecutionWorkspaceClass the Tasks use: kubectl annotate executionworkspaceclass sandbox-debug -n team-a \ acp.workspace.orka.ai/operator-access=exec Value Allows read orka task cp <task>:<path> <local> (copy out only) exec Copy out, copy in, and orka task exec absent or anything else Nothing A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy only lets callers holding the dedicated operator-access verb on the class set, change, or remove this annotation. cluster-admin has that verb through its wildcard. No built-in Orka role grants it, including the class admin role that the raw installer ships. Class editors and Task authors, who only need use on a class, cannot enable operator access. To grant the verb to a platform team: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole metadata: name: orka-workspace-operator-access-admin rules: - apiGroups: ["workspace.orka.ai"] resources: ["executionworkspaceclasses"] verbs: ["get", "list", "patch", "update", "operator-access"] orka-api reads the annotation live on every call. Removing it revokes access immediately, including for running Tasks.

Each operation is authorized with a SubjectAccessReview on a dedicated tasks subresource. Task create/get alone is never enough, and no built-in aggregate role includes these: Operation Resource Verb orka task exec tasks/exec create orka task cp <task>:<path> <local> tasks/files get orka task cp <local> <task>:<path> tasks/files update Each operation also needs get on the Task. apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: orka-task-debugger namespace: team-a rules: - apiGroups: ["core.orka.ai"] resources: ["tasks"] verbs: ["get"] - apiGroups: ["core.orka.ai"] resources: ["tasks/exec"] verbs: ["create"] - apiGroups: ["core.orka.ai"] resources: ["tasks/files"] verbs: ["get", "update"] Context-token (transaction-token) callers need an explicit scope instead: orka:tasks:exec, orka:tasks:files:read, or orka:tasks:files:write. The token's transaction context must also be bound to the Task's namespace. Task scopes never imply these scopes, and they are enforced in every context-token authorization mode. Identities with no Kubernetes identity to review, such as direct OIDC sign-in, are refused.

# One-off command orka task exec my-task -- git status # Interactive shell (Ctrl-C, resizing, and job control behave like a terminal) orka task exec my-task -it -- bash # Pipe stdin git diff | orka task exec my-task -i -- git apply --check - # Copy a file out (does not taint) orka task cp my-task:src/main.go ./main.go orka task cp my-task:/logs/build.log - | less # Copy a file in (taints) orka task cp ./fix.patch my-task:fix.patch Workspace paths are relative to the workspace root, which is the agent's working directory. A leading / names that root, so my-task:/src/a.go and my-task:src/a.go are the same file. Paths with .., NUL bytes, or control characters are rejected. Symbolic links are never followed, in any path component, and a path the session moves out of the workspace during a copy is refused. Copies require Linux 5.6 or later on the runtime node. Copies transfer exactly one regular file. Copying in replaces the destination atomically, and only after the complete upload arrives. The parent directory must already exist. Copying out over an existing local file keeps that file's permissions; a new local file is readable and writable only by you. -t allocates a terminal. Because -t means --tty on orka task exec, pass a bearer token there with --token, --token-file or ORKA_TOKEN. Without a terminal, the first Ctrl-C is forwarded to the remote command as SIGINT and a second abandons the stream. Closing the stream kills the remote command and every process it started. Each operation carries a unique supplementary group that its processes cannot drop. So even descendants that start a new session or process group, or outlive the command, cannot survive the timeout, a disconnect, or the session's validation freeze. When a prompt settles and the workspace is frozen for validation, or the session is deleted, running operator commands are killed. Limit Default Maximum --timeout (exec) 15 minutes 1 hour Exec output (stdout + stderr) 64 MiB 512 MiB --max-bytes (copy out) 64 MiB 256 MiB Copy-in file size — 256 MiB Stdin buffered ahead of the command 8 MiB — Concurrent operations per runtime 4 — orka task exec exits with the remote command's status. Orka-side outcomes use these exit codes: Exit code Meaning 124 Timeout 125 Output or stdin buffer limit 126 Refused, failed to start, lost its connection, or could not write its output locally 130 Interrupted locally

orka task exec and orka task cp into a workspace can change anything the session's identity can write. Before either one starts, orka-api records the acp.workspace.orka.ai/operator-tainted annotation on the Task and on its ExecutionWorkspace. If that write fails, the operation is refused. Only the Orka controller identity can write either annotation, so a Task author cannot remove it. A tainted session: Is never published. The publication is settled as cancelled before publish, and the credential broker refuses forge write credentials. Is never reused. No other Task attaches the workspace, reuses it warm, or cold-resumes it. A continuation queued behind the tainting Task waits for a fresh workspace, and otherwise fails with execution workspace was tainted by operator access. Is never checkpointed. Settlement and idle retention delete the workspace instead of suspending it, even when the class freezes Suspend. ExecutionWorkspaceCheckpoint exports from it fail routing with SourceOperatorTainted, so forks cannot consume it. Is never continued. Its runtime is not captured as the Session's native continuity. A first turn falls back to the canonical transcript, and a Session that already depends on native continuity fails closed. The taint is never cleared. Copying out does not taint. The taint is recorded before the request reaches the runtime. An exec or copy in that the runtime then refuses, for example because the prompt settled at that moment, still leaves the session tainted.

Each authenticated call produces records for when it started and finished, or when it was denied, under one audit ID. Records go to the orka-api log under audit: operator workspace access. Once orka-api has read the Task, they are also emitted as Kubernetes Events on the Task (OperatorAccessStarted, OperatorAccessFinished, OperatorAccessDenied): kubectl get events -n team-a --field-selector involvedObject.name=my-task Not every refusal reaches both places: A refusal before orka-api reads the Task is recorded as denied in the orka-api log only, because an Event needs the Task UID. That covers a missing tasks/exec, tasks/files, or Task get permission, a refused identity or context-token scope, and a controller without --operator-workspace-access-enabled. A request with missing or invalid credentials fails authentication with 401 and produces no operator audit record. Each record includes what is known at that point: the actor and authentication type the namespace, Task, and Task UID the RuntimeSession UID and generation, and the workspace for exec: the command basename, argument count, and a SHA-256 digest of argv. Raw arguments are never recorded. the copy path and byte count the exit code or outcome, and the start and finish times whether the session was tainted Free-text fields (the command basename, copy path, Task name, and outcome) are redacted with Orka's shared credential rules, and a value that still looks like a credential is recorded as [REDACTED].

Error Cause operator workspace access is disabled The controller lacks --operator-workspace-access-enabled. ExecutionWorkspaceClass ... does not allow operator ... The class lacks the annotation, or is read for exec or a copy in. 403 not authorized Missing tasks/exec or tasks/files permission. requires a Kubernetes identity The caller signed in with OIDC. Use a ServiceAccount or kubeconfig token. context token lacks the explicit ... scope Add the operator scope to the transaction token. task workspace is being validated for publication / runtime session is validating The prompt settled and the workspace is frozen. Wait for publication to finish. execution workspace is attached to another Task A continuation took the workspace. Target the current Task. task runtime instance is no longer active / ... was replaced The runtime Pod or workspace was replaced. The old session is gone. not supported for native-process (Substrate) execution workspaces Not available yet for Substrate. runtime supervisor does not support operator access The runtime image predates this feature. Upgrade it. See ADR 0044 for the design rationale.

An agent often spends minutes or hours waiting: for a person to sign off, for the child tasks it delegated to finish, or for a rate limit to clear. A waiting turn still holds a RuntimePool slot, a resident RuntimeSession, and possibly a workspace. With park_until, the agent ends its turn instead. Orka releases that runtime capacity, waits for the event, and then starts a new turn in the same Session. Parking is data-only. Orka never snapshots or restores process memory. The new turn starts from the Session transcript, with fresh runtime credentials, a fresh execution snapshot, and the same checks as any other Session continuation. Running processes, shells, and unsaved in-memory state from the parked turn are gone, and the agent is told so.

park_until is a brokered built-in tool for the built-in ACP runtimes (codex, claude, copilot, opencode). Like every brokered tool, it is offered only when the Agent or Task allows it: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: release-captain spec: runtime: type: claude defaultAllowedTools: [Read, Grep, Glob, delegate_task, wait_for_tasks, park_until] A Task can park only when all of these hold: Requirement Why spec.sessionRef is set and append is true The continuation resumes from the Session transcript, so this turn must be recorded there. The Task is not a gateway conversation turn (promptIncluded/throughMessageID) The gateway starts the next turn itself. No spec.transaction A continuation cannot inherit a transaction token. Orka fails closed rather than re-issue one. No spec.schedule or spec.priorTaskRef Neither can be inherited safely by a later turn. The Task's Agent is not identity-bound Orka, not the requester, creates the continuation, so it cannot re-prove the identity delegation. A continuation whose Agent gained an identity while the turn waited is refused too. The chain has fewer than 32 continuations Bounds runaway park loops.

{"kind": "approval", "reason": "The release notes are ready. May I publish v2.4.0?"} {"kind": "tasks", "reason": "Waiting for the reviewers", "tasks": ["release-captain-child-x7k2p"]} {"kind": "timer", "reason": "GitHub secondary rate limit", "duration": "15m"} An optional timeout (for example "2h") can shorten the wait. The Task deadline always applies. After the call, the agent should end its turn with a short status message. Kind Resumes when The new turn is told approval A person approves or declines the sign-off request in the Task's Approvals tab, with orka task approve / orka task decline, or through the API. The decision, who made it, and their note. tasks Every named child Task has finished, following a child's own continuation chain if it parked too. Each child's final phase. The agent then calls wait_for_tasks to read results. timer The duration has elapsed. That the backoff ended. A parked approval is a sign-off checkpoint. It does not approve any specific tool call. Tools listed in approvalRequiredTools still need their own approval in the turn that runs them. Those approvals still hold a live tool call for up to ten minutes; see Human approval.

status.wait on the parked Task records the state, and the Waiting condition mirrors it. Requested ──turn succeeded──▶ Waiting ──event──▶ Resuming ──▶ Resumed (continuation Task created) │ │ │ turn failed / retried ├─ cancel-wait annotation or Task deletion ─▶ Cancelled ▼ └─ Task deadline leaves < 1 minute ─────────▶ Expired Abandoned Requested. The turn called park_until. Nothing changes until that exact attempt and prompt end. If the turn fails, is cancelled, or is retried, the wait becomes Abandoned and nothing resumes. Waiting. The turn settled Succeeded, so no prompt, tool call, or publication is still in flight. Its runtime capacity has been released: a read-only Session's resident RuntimeSession is retired, which frees its pool slot; write-intent and task-scoped sessions are retired at the end of every turn anyway; a workspace-backed Session follows its frozen onDetach policy. With onDetach: Suspend, the workspace data is cold-suspended and its pool scales to zero. Resuming → Resumed. Orka reserves a deterministic continuation name in status, then creates one continuation Task. It copies the parked Task's agent, runtime, workspace, requester, and Session. It changes three things: a controller-authored prompt describing the event, sessionRef.create: false, and timeout set to the time remaining before the original deadline. The parked prompt is never sent again. If the controller restarts after creating the continuation, it adopts that Task instead of creating another. That recovery requires Task provenance admission, which reserves the continuation lineage annotations to the controller; without it, Orka abandons the wait rather than trust an annotation that could be forged. When timeout expires but the Task deadline still leaves time, the wait resumes anyway and tells the agent it timed out. An undecided sign-off is marked expired. The parked Task keeps the Succeeded phase of its own turn. Tools and people that need the overall result should follow the chain. wait_for_tasks does this automatically: a child whose turn parked is reported as unfinished until its newest continuation finishes, and the result describes that continuation (continuationTask, waitState). A Task webhook follows the chain too. A parked Task sends no task.succeeded notice for its own turn. While its wait is active, nothing is sent. Once it resumes, the continuation, which inherits spec.webhookURL, sends the notice when it finishes. If the wait ends without a continuation, the parked Task sends one notice: task.cancelled for a cancelled wait, and task.failed for an expired wait or for a wait abandoned after a successful turn.

# Stop waiting but keep the Task and its history: kubectl -n team annotate task release-captain orka.ai/cancel-wait="no longer needed" # Or delete the Task. Its continuation, if one was already created, is deleted too: kubectl -n team delete task release-captain Cancelling a coordinator also cancels the waits of its parked children, and it cancels any continuation those children already started. A cancelled or expired sign-off cannot be decided later. A late decision receives HTTP 409.

Separately from parking, a Task that cannot start because runtime capacity is exhausted reports it with status.execution.reason: WaitingForCapacity and a WaitingForCapacity condition: Condition reason Cause RuntimeCapacityUnavailable The RuntimePool is full or not admitting new sessions, or the runtime rate-limited prompt admission. The condition message names the cause when it is known. WorkspaceCapacityUnavailable The execution-workspace pool or provider has no admission capacity. CapacityAvailable (False) Capacity is no longer the blocking reason. The Task stays Pending, is retried automatically, and is cancelled with TaskTimeout if its deadline passes first. A Substrate actor pool that receives ResourceExhausted reports phase Pending with a WaitingForCapacity reason instead of failing.

Metric Labels orka_task_wait_transitions_total kind, state orka_task_wait_duration_seconds kind, state: time from release to the final state orka_task_wait_runtime_releases_total result: resident RuntimeSessions retired on park orka_waiting_for_capacity_total resource (task, substrate_actor_pool), reason

Parking a pending approvalRequiredTools call. That approval is bound to the exact running call, attempt, and runtime fences, and approved execution must happen under that call's frozen policy, so it still waits live. Waking on pull request reviews or CI results. GitHub webhooks currently deliver only issues and pull_request events, and they go to repository monitors, not to Tasks. Until review and check events are routed to Tasks, park on a timer and check again with check_pull_request_ci. Gateway conversations, transaction-bound Tasks, Tasks of identity-bound Agents, and external runtimeRef agents. The design and its safety boundaries are recorded in ADR 0041.

An Agent Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file (YAML frontmatter plus instructions) and optional supporting files. Codex, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, and OpenCode each discover skills in their own skills folder and load a skill's instructions only when the task calls for it. Codex, Claude, and OpenCode Agents list skills in spec.runtime.skills. Each skill comes from a digest-pinned container image. Orka binds the skill folder read-only into the runtime Pod with the same delivery as toolboxes, checks it, and copies it into every session's native skills folder, owned by that session's own identity. Claude is the exception: its sessions share one read-only copy that no session identity owns. Native Agents (type: ai Tasks) keep using the Skill resource and spec.skills; see Agents, skills, and tools.

Skills are instructions, never code that runs on its own. Nothing from a skill image runs: the copier is Orka's own binary, and the supervisor only reads files. A skill may ship scripts, but the agent can run them only through tools its policy already allows, as the session's unprivileged identity. A skill can't widen the session's policy. Frontmatter may contain only name, description, license, compatibility, and metadata. Keys such as allowed-tools, hooks, model, context, and agent are rejected, and so is the shell preprocessing marker !` that Claude Code would run when the skill loads. SKILL.md is untrusted prompt input. It must be UTF-8 text with frontmatter whose name equals the declared skill name, and it fails the same credential-shape check Orka applies to other prompt inputs if it appears to contain a secret. Only folders and regular files. Symlinks, devices, FIFOs, and sockets fail the skill. Limits: 256 entries, 4 MiB in total, 1 MiB per file, 8 folders deep, and 64 KiB for SKILL.md. One skill per folder. A nested SKILL.md (any letter case) is rejected, because Codex and OpenCode would load it as an extra skill that Orka never checked. So is agents/openai.yaml, which Codex reads for tool dependencies it may install. Images are referenced by digest and must come from a registry the operator allowed. Nothing is fetched over the network inside the runtime Pod. Each session gets its own copy, except on Claude. The read-only source is never writable by a session; the copy belongs to the session's unique UID and GID and is deleted with the session. OpenCode's file-editing tools are denied in the skill folders. A session that may run shell commands can still change its own copy, which no other session sees. Claude sessions share one read-only copy instead; see the table below. Orka reserves room for the copies: for every skill, 5 MiB per resident session the pool allows (maxResidentSessions) is added to the session volume limit and to the runtime Pod's ephemeral-storage request and limit. The feature is off by default. A skill that can't be set up fails the Task with a stable reason; an agent never starts without the skills it was promised.

Runtime Native skills folder in the session What else Orka sets Claude skills/<name>/ in a local plugin named orka, outside every session tree Claude loads no settings files, so it never reads ~/.claude/skills. Orka instead passes one plugin folder through the SDK plugins option, with MCP discovery off. The folder belongs to the runtime's supervisor and every session of the runtime only reads it, because a plugin could also carry hooks. Claude lists the skills as orka:<name>. The SDK skills option lists exactly those names, so Claude Code hides every other skill and its Skill tool rejects them. disableSkillShellExecution is on. With a restricted tool policy, Orka adds Skill to the allowed tools; it only loads skill instructions. Codex $HOME/.agents/skills/<name>/ Nothing: Codex always loads user skills. OpenCode $OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/skills/<name>/ The skill permission allows exactly the Orka skill names and denies everything else, including OpenCode's built-in skills. external_directory stays denied except for each Orka skill folder, so the read tool (when allowed) can open a skill's supporting files. That exception is dropped when the session may edit files with a model OpenCode gives apply_patch (GPT models other than gpt-4 and gpt-oss), because that tool checks only a move's source against the edit rules: the skill tool still returns SKILL.md, but supporting files are unreadable. Copilot — Not supported. Copilot CLI in ACP mode keeps loading repository skills (.github/skills, .agents/skills, .claude/skills) whatever its settings say, so enabling its skill tool would also hand the model untrusted repository skills. Agents are rejected at admission. Codex discovers repository skills (.agents/skills in the workspace) on its own, with or without Orka skills; Orka skills don't change that. External runtimes (runtime.runtimeRef) and execution workspaces (Task.spec.execution.workspace) can't receive skills yet; Agents and Tasks that combine them are rejected at admission and planning.

Skills reuse the toolbox delivery, so enable both and allow the registries that serve skill images: controller: acpRuntime: toolboxes: enabled: true allowedRegistries: - registry.example.com/skills imagePullSecrets: [] nodeSelector: {} mountMethod: copy # copy | imageVolume skills: enabled: true The controller flag is --acp-skills-enabled (ORKA_ACP_SKILLS_ENABLED). It requires --acp-toolboxes-enabled, and skills use the toolbox allowlist, pull secrets, node selector, and mount method. See Toolboxes for those settings and the trade-offs between copy and imageVolume.

apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: reviewer spec: model: name: claude-sonnet-4-5 runtime: type: claude skills: - name: code-review image: registry.example.com/skills/code-review@sha256:<digest> - name: release-notes image: registry.example.com/skills/bundle@sha256:<digest> path: /skills/bundle/release-notes # optional; defaults to /skills/<name> Validation, enforced by the CRD schema, Agent admission, Task planning, and again in the runtime Pod: name uses lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens (at most 64 characters) and must equal the name in the skill's SKILL.md. Names are unique per Agent. image is a fully qualified reference pinned by digest (<registry>/<repository>@sha256:<64 hex>), from an allowed registry. path is a clean folder under /skills inside the image, with no . or .. components. It defaults to /skills/<name>. SKILL.md must sit directly in it. At most 8 skills per Agent. Skills are part of the immutable runtime profile: the profile digest covers each skill's name, image, and effective path, in order. Changing any of them creates a new RuntimePool, and Tasks that are already running keep the skills frozen in their execution snapshot.

FROM scratch COPY code-review/ /skills/code-review/ docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t registry.example.com/skills/code-review:1 --push . crane digest registry.example.com/skills/code-review:1 # pin this digest in the Agent A FROM scratch image works because nothing from the image runs. With the copy mount method, folders must be readable and traversable by everyone (o+rx) and files readable by everyone (o+r), because the copier runs as a fixed non-root identity. One image may carry several skills under different /skills/... folders; declare each one with its own path. A minimal SKILL.md: --- name: code-review description: Review a change for correctness, tests, and risky patterns. Use when asked to review a diff or pull request. --- # Code review 1. Run `make test` and report failures first. 2. ...

Skill failures surface through the same RuntimePool condition as toolbox failures: RolloutReady=False with reason ToolboxUnavailable, and Tasks waiting on the pool fail with the same reason. The message names the skill and carries one stable code. Code Meaning Fix TOOLBOX_IMAGE_PULL, TOOLBOX_SOURCE_OPEN, TOOLBOX_MOUNT_FAILED, … on a skill-copy-<n> container or skill-<n> volume The skill image could not be pulled, or path does not exist as a real folder in it. Check the digest, registry access, imagePullSecrets, and the image layout. SKILL_MISSING_MOUNT The supervisor did not find the skill folder in the runtime Pod. Check the node runtime and the RuntimePool events. SKILL_READ_FAILED The skill folder could not be read, or the supervisor's startup check did not finish within one minute. Check the node's image storage and the RuntimePool events. SKILL_MISSING_SKILL_MD SKILL.md is not directly in the skill folder. Fix path or the image layout. SKILL_INVALID_FRONTMATTER The frontmatter is missing, malformed, has a name that does not match, has no description, or uses a key that is not allowed. Keep only name, description, license, compatibility, and metadata. SKILL_UNSAFE_CONTENT SKILL.md is not UTF-8 text, contains !`, or appears to contain a secret; or the skill has a nested SKILL.md or agents/openai.yaml. Remove the construct, credential, or file. SKILL_UNSUPPORTED_FILE_TYPE The skill contains a symlink, device, FIFO, or socket. Ship only folders and regular files. SKILL_INVALID_FILE_NAME A file name contains a control character or is too long. Rename the file. SKILL_TOO_DEEP, SKILL_TOO_LARGE, SKILL_FILE_TOO_LARGE, SKILL_TOO_MANY_ENTRIES (or the TOOLBOX_ equivalents from the copier) A limit was exceeded. Trim the skill. kubectl describe runtimepool <name> shows the condition; kubectl get task <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.execution.message}' shows the Task-side reason.

Any Orka Task can run on a schedule. Set spec.schedule to a cron expression and the Task stops being a one-shot job: it becomes a template, and the controller creates a fresh child Task from it on every cron tick. Each child runs independently with the full spec — the same agent, workspace, and tools a manual Task would get. If you have used a Kubernetes CronJob, the model will feel familiar; the details below are where scheduled Tasks make their own choices.

apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: nightly-triage spec: type: ai agentRef: name: triage-agent prompt: "Summarize new issues opened in the last 24 hours" schedule: "0 2 * * *" # every day at 02:00 timeZone: "America/New_York" # IANA name; defaults to UTC The parent Task never runs itself. Its status tracks the schedule (status.lastScheduleTime, status.nextScheduleTime), and each tick creates a child named <parent>-<unix-timestamp> — so kubectl get tasks shows the history at a glance.

Field Default What it controls schedule — Standard cron expression; setting it makes the Task scheduled timeZone UTC IANA time zone the cron expression is evaluated in concurrencyPolicy Forbid Forbid skips a tick while the previous child still runs; Allow lets runs overlap startingDeadlineSeconds 100 How late a run may start and still count (see below) successfulRunsHistoryLimit 3 Completed successful children retained before cleanup failedRunsHistoryLimit 1 Failed children retained before cleanup suspend false Pauses new runs without deleting the schedule

A tick can be missed — the controller was restarting, or the schedule was suspended when the tick came due. startingDeadlineSeconds decides what happens next: Missed by less than the deadline: the run starts late, once. Missed by more than the deadline: the run is skipped. Scheduled Tasks never queue a backlog of catch-up runs. When a run is skipped this way, the schedule re-anchors to the present: the next run happens at the next cron tick from now, as if the missed window never existed.
documents.s: Missed runs and the starting deadline

documents.t: Set spec.suspend: true to pause a schedule. Children that are already running finish normally; no new children are created while suspended. Set it back to false to resume. If the suspension outlasted startingDeadlineSeconds (it usually does), the missed ticks are skipped — not replayed — and runs continue from the next cron tick after the resume. Resuming a schedule that was paused for a week does not fire a week of backlogged runs.

History is pruned automatically. Only the most recent successful and failed children (per the history limits) are kept; raise the limits if you audit past runs. A run whose approval notices are still pending is kept until they are delivered or fail, even with a limit of 0. Forbid is the safe default for agent work. An agent run that overlaps itself — two children editing the same repository, for example — rarely does what you want. Use Allow only for idempotent, read-only work. Scheduled Tasks are also the mechanism behind prompt-orchestrated monitors such as create_pr_monitor; see Repository Monitors for the purpose-built monitoring resource that supersedes hand-rolled schedules for that use case.

Set spec.webhookURL on a Task and the controller POSTs a JSON notice when the Task reaches a terminal phase (Succeeded, Failed, or Cancelled). A parked agent turn reports when its work ends instead. Every notice is signed with an Ed25519 key. Delivery is durable across controller restarts, retried with bounded backoff, and limited to destinations that are safe for a controller to call. A Task can also opt into approval notices. apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: nightly-report spec: type: ai prompt: "Summarize yesterday's incidents" webhookURL: https://hooks.example.com/orka

The controller fails closed. A destination must be one of: A public http or https host. The name is resolved when the controller connects, on every connection, and every address it resolves to must be globally routable. Loopback, RFC 1918, CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10), link-local (including 169.254.169.254), IPv6 unique-local and link-local, multicast, broadcast, unspecified (0.0.0.0, ::), IPv4-mapped forms of any of these, and the other IANA special-use ranges are refused. A DNS failure is a failed attempt, never a pass, and because the check runs at connect time a name that is re-pointed after validation (DNS rebinding) cannot reach an internal address. A Service in the Task's own namespace, as http://<name>.<namespace>.svc[.cluster.local][:port]/.... The Service must exist, have a selector and a ClusterIP, and not be ExternalName. The controller connects straight to that ClusterIP without DNS. Services in other namespaces and kubernetes.default are refused. The controller never follows redirects (a 3xx is a failed attempt) and never sends webhooks through an HTTP proxy, even when HTTP_PROXY is set, because a proxy would connect on its behalf and skip these checks. If your controller needs an egress proxy, put a same-namespace Service in front of it. A URL with a non-http(s) scheme, a literal non-public IP, a blocked host name, or another namespace's Service is rejected without any network attempt: the delivery goes straight to Failed.

POST /orka HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: application/json User-Agent: Orka-Controller/1.0 X-Orka-Task: nightly-report X-Orka-Namespace: team-a X-Orka-Event: task.succeeded X-Orka-Delivery-ID: 6f1c3c2e-5b0a-4f7e-9a51-0d3f1f7f6a10 Idempotency-Key: 6f1c3c2e-5b0a-4f7e-9a51-0d3f1f7f6a10 X-Orka-Delivery-Attempt: 1 X-Orka-Signature: eyJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsImtpZCI6Ii4uLiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9... {"deliveryId":"6f1c3c2e-...","eventType":"task.succeeded","occurredAt":"2026-11-06T10:00:00Z", "taskUID":"0b9e0f43-...","taskName":"nightly-report","taskNamespace":"team-a", "phase":"Succeeded","message":"...","startTime":"...","completionTime":"...", "attempts":1,"resultRef":{"available":true}} eventType is one of: Event Sent Body task.succeeded, task.failed, task.cancelled Always, once the Task's outcome is known Terminal body above task.approval_requested When selected in spec.webhookEvents Approval body task.approval_resolved When selected in spec.webhookEvents Approval body task.approval_overflow When any approval event is selected and the queue overflows Approval body Every attempt of one delivery sends a byte-identical body under the same delivery ID; only X-Orka-Delivery-Attempt and the signature change. For a parked agent turn, eventType reports the outcome of the work, which can differ from the Task's own phase; see Parked agent turns. Any 2xx response acknowledges the notice. Respond quickly; one attempt times out after 30 seconds.

X-Orka-Signature is a compact JWS (a JWT) signed with alg: EdDSA (Ed25519). Its header carries the signing key's kid, the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the public key. The public keys are published, without authentication, by the Orka API: GET https://<orka-api>/.well-known/orka/task-webhook-jwks.json {"keys":[{"kty":"OKP","crv":"Ed25519","x":"...","kid":"...","alg":"EdDSA","use":"sig"}]} Fetch the JWKS out of band or over a trusted channel: it is what your receiver trusts. Then, for each request: Read kid from the JWS header and find that key in your cached JWKS. If it is missing, refetch the JWKS once (rate-limit this) and try again; reject if it is still missing. Accept only alg: EdDSA. Verify the Ed25519 signature over the first two dot-separated segments. Check the claims: iss is orka.ai/task-webhook; aud is exactly the webhookURL configured on the Task; exp is in the future and nbf is not, allowing about a minute of clock skew. Tokens live for five minutes and are minted for each attempt; payload_sha256 equals the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the raw request body you received, before any JSON parsing. Use task.uid, task.namespace, task.name, event, and delivery_id from the verified claims rather than from headers or the body. Deduplicate on delivery_id (also sent as X-Orka-Delivery-ID and Idempotency-Key). Delivery is at-least-once: a controller that restarts mid-attempt sends the same delivery again. The claim set looks like: { "iss": "orka.ai/task-webhook", "sub": "0b9e0f43-...", "aud": "https://hooks.example.com/orka", "iat": 1793872800, "nbf": 1793872800, "exp": 1793873100, "jti": "6f1c3c2e-....1", "delivery_id": "6f1c3c2e-...", "attempt": 1, "event": "task.succeeded", "task": {"uid": "0b9e0f43-...", "namespace": "team-a", "name": "nightly-report"}, "payload_sha256": "9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08" } Any standard JOSE library that supports EdDSA can do steps 1–3. In Go, github.com/lestrrat-go/jwx/v3 verifies with jwt.ParseString(token, jwt.WithKeySet(set), jwt.WithIssuer("orka.ai/task-webhook"), jwt.WithAudience(webhookURL)) followed by the payload_sha256 comparison. Orka's own reference implementation is taskwebhook.Verify in internal/taskwebhook.

The delivery is recorded in the Task's status, so it survives controller restarts, upgrades, and leader changes: status: webhookDelivered: true webhookDelivery: deliveryID: 6f1c3c2e-5b0a-4f7e-9a51-0d3f1f7f6a10 eventType: task.succeeded occurredAt: "2026-11-06T10:00:00Z" payloadSHA256: 9f86d0... state: Delivered # Pending, Delivered, or Failed attempts: 1 lastStatusCode: 202 A failed attempt (connection error, timeout, refused address, redirect, or a non-2xx response) is retried after 10s, 20s, 40s, and so on, capped at 15 minutes, for at most 8 attempts. After that the delivery is Failed and is never retried. lastError records a short reason with no URL or credential in it. Each attempt is claimed in Task status before it is sent. A controller that dies mid-attempt leaves a two-minute lease; the next controller waits for it, then retries under the same delivery ID. Attempts are sent by a pool of delivery workers, separate from Task reconciliation, so a slow or unresponsive receiver never delays scheduling or monitoring of any Task. Each Task's notices still go one attempt at a time. The pool sends at most --task-webhook-delivery-workers attempts at once (default 8); beyond that, other notices queue until a worker is free. Only one notice is pending per Task. If the Task's terminal state changes before a pending notice is delivered, the controller supersedes it: the old delivery ID is never sent again, a new one carries the newer state, its attempts start over, and superseded counts the replaced notices. Supersession never shortens an existing backoff. If signing is enabled but no signing key is available yet (for example, the Secret cannot be read or holds a malformed key), nothing is sent and no attempt is consumed; the delivery stays Pending until a key is available. If signing is disabled (--task-webhook-signing-secret=""), nothing is sent and the delivery is marked Failed at once. Enabling signing later does not retry notices that already failed this way.

An agent Task whose turn parked ends with phase Succeeded for its own turn while the work continues in a continuation Task. Its notice is therefore not sent when it reaches that phase. It follows status.wait instead: status.wait.state Notice from the parked Task Requested, Waiting, Resuming None yet. Nothing is recorded in status.webhookDelivery, and the Task's cleanup and history pruning are not held up. Resumed None. The continuation copies spec.webhookURL and sends the notice when it finishes. If it parks too, the rule repeats, so the newest Task of the chain reports the outcome. Cancelled One task.cancelled notice. Expired One task.failed notice, as for a Task that runs past its deadline. Abandoned One notice for the Task's phase if the turn itself failed or was cancelled. If the turn succeeded but its continuation could not be created, one task.failed notice. So a receiver sees exactly one notice per chain, and task.succeeded only when the work finished. In a notice decided by the wait, phase is still the parked Task's own phase (Succeeded) and taskName is the parked Task; read its status.wait for the reason. A wait left over from an earlier attempt that a later, unparked attempt replaced does not change the event. Notices from continuations name the continuation Task, whose UID differs from the Task you created. As with any Task, deleting the parked Task or its continuation drops its pending notice. A notice that an earlier controller version left pending for a parked Task is never sent as task.succeeded: it is superseded when the wait ends without resuming, and marked Failed without being sent when the wait resumed.

List approval events in spec.webhookEvents to be told when the Task asks a person to approve something and how that ended. Terminal notices are always sent and cannot be listed or turned off; leaving webhookEvents empty or absent keeps terminal notices only. A Task with webhookEvents must set webhookURL.
