Continuations of a parked turn copy both fields. spec: webhookURL: https://hooks.example.com/orka webhookEvents: - task.approval_requested - task.approval_resolved The approvals come from the approval gate, request_approval, brokered ACP tool calls, and parked sign-offs. A runtime's own permission prompt, which Orka answers from policy, is not an approval and sends nothing. Approval notices use the same signing, headers, destination rules and leases as terminal notices. The JWS event claim is the approval event. The body is different and versioned: {"schemaVersion":"orka.ai/task-approval-webhook/v1", "deliveryId":"2b7c...","eventType":"task.approval_resolved","occurredAt":"2026-11-16T09:01:30Z", "taskUID":"0b9e0f43-...","taskName":"release","taskNamespace":"team-a","streamSeq":42, "approvalId":"acp-tool-approval-v2:sha256:...","targetTool":"github.create_pr","severity":"warning", "expiresAt":"2026-11-16T09:10:00Z","resolution":"approved","parked":false} Field Meaning schemaVersion orka.ai/task-approval-webhook/v1. Reject versions you do not know. deliveryId Deterministic per approval and transition, so a restarted controller sends the same ID. occurredAt When the transition was recorded: the request, or the decision, expiry or cancellation. streamSeq Position of that transition in the Task's approval history; order notices of one Task by it. approvalId The approval to look up in GET /api/v1/tasks/{task}/approvals. Absent on task.approval_overflow. targetTool, severity The gated tool and severity label, when the approval has them. expiresAt Present only when the approval really expires then: brokered ACP reviews and parked sign-offs. resolution On task.approval_resolved: approved, declined, expired, or cancelled. parked true for a parked turn's sign-off. A notice never carries the argument preview, the action or risk text, the reviewer's reason or identity, or any digest. Fetch details from the approvals API, which checks the caller's access. How approvals reach a receiver: Requested is sent once per approval. Resolved is sent once, for the first decision. A brokered review that passes its expiresAt resolves as expired once the controller records it, a few seconds after the deadline. An approval gate request that is still pending when its Task ends gets no resolved notice, because nothing resolves it. A parked sign-off stays open after its turn Succeeded, so its resolution arrives while the parked Task is finished. Notices of one Task are sent in streamSeq order, each after the previous one settles. A request whose notice failed does not hold back its resolution. An approval notice gets 5 attempts, retried after 10s, 20s, 40s and 60s, so it settles within about three minutes. Review windows are short, and a late alert is of little use. While no signing key is available, an approval notice waits without using an attempt, as a terminal notice does, but only until its signingDeadline, five minutes after it was queued. A notice still waiting then is marked Failed unsent, with lastError "webhook signing key unavailable past the approval notice window", and is never sent or recreated. Later notices then go ahead once a key is back. Terminal notices keep waiting until a key is available. Selecting approval events on a Task whose spec can still change, or selecting them again after removing them all, does not replay earlier approval history. Notices start with the first transition recorded after the controller sees the selection. Removing an event retires its pending notices unsent. Deleting a Task drops its pending approval notices. Scheduled-run history pruning waits for them: a run, or any Task in its continuation chain, with a pending approval notice is kept past successfulRunsHistoryLimit or failedRunsHistoryLimit until the notice is delivered or marked Failed, and is then pruned. A Task with the same name as an earlier one never receives the earlier Task's approvals. Receivers should: Verify the signature exactly as for terminal notices. Deduplicate on deliveryId. Delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once. Order by streamSeq, and tolerate gaps and a resolution without its request. Treat a notice as an alert, never as authority: decide through the approvals API, which revalidates the approval. Status records the queue and its cursor: status: approvalWebhooks: projectedSeq: 42 tracking: true notices: - deliveryID: 2b7c... eventType: task.approval_resolved transition: Resolved approvalID: acp-tool-approval-v2:sha256:... resolution: approved streamSeq: 42 state: Delivered # Pending, Delivered, or Failed attempts: 1 signingDeadline: "2026-11-16T09:06:30Z" The queue holds at most 16 notices. Delivered and failed notices are pruned, oldest first, to make room; a pending notice is never dropped. If 15 notices are pending at once, the controller records one task.approval_overflow notice whose streamSeq is the first transition it did not notify, sets overflowed: true, and notifies no later transition for that Task. omitted counts the transitions it skipped. Read the approvals API after an overflow notice. A signing outage alone overflows the queue only if 15 notices are queued within five minutes of each other. Each notice is marked Failed at its signing deadline, before new transitions are queued, and frees its slot.

The controller signs with the Ed25519 key in the current item of a Secret in a namespace of its own: <release namespace>-task-webhook-signing for the Helm chart (override with controller.taskWebhooks.signingNamespace), or orka-task-webhook-signing for the kustomize install (flag --task-webhook-signing-namespace). The Secret is <fullname>-task-webhook-signing for the Helm chart, where <fullname> is the chart's full name (orka for a release named orka; override the Secret name with controller.taskWebhooks.signingSecretName), or orka-task-webhook-signing for the kustomize install. On first use, the controller creates that Secret and mints current if either is missing. Keys are PEM-encoded PKCS#8, which is what openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 writes. A malformed key is never replaced: delivery pauses until it is fixed. Every replica rereads the Secret at least every 15 seconds, so rotation needs no restart. To rotate: NS=orka-task-webhook-signing # <release namespace>-task-webhook-signing for Helm SECRET=orka-task-webhook-signing # <fullname>-task-webhook-signing for Helm openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out new.pem OLD=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get secret "$SECRET" -o jsonpath='{.data.current}') kubectl -n "$NS" patch secret "$SECRET" --type merge \ -p "{\"data\":{\"previous\":\"$OLD\",\"current\":\"$(base64 -w0 < new.pem)\"}}" shred -u new.pem The new key signs from then on. The JWKS publishes both current and previous, so a token signed by a replica that has not yet reloaded still verifies, and receivers that see the new kid refetch the JWKS. After TokenTTL plus the reload interval (in practice, wait at least ten minutes), drop previous: kubectl -n "$NS" patch secret "$SECRET" --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/data/previous"}]' If a key is compromised, rotate and remove previous at once. Receivers that keep the old JWKS cached keep trusting the old key until they refetch. Setting --task-webhook-signing-secret="" disables signing. Since notices are never sent unsigned, that also stops webhook delivery: notices for Tasks that finish while signing is disabled are marked Failed and are not retried after signing is enabled again.

Anyone who can read or change the signing Secret can forge notices, so it lives alone in its own namespace and only the controller is bound there: get and update on that one Secret, and create on Secrets there. This closes two paths: A Task's or Agent's secretRef mounts a Secret from the Task's namespace. Tasks live in the release namespace, so a secretRef cannot name the key. Worker roles are bound in the release namespace only, so no worker can read or replace the key with its own permissions. The protection also depends on no worker being able to act as the controller. The default AI worker RBAC profile lets the AI worker create Secrets and Jobs in the release namespace (for code_exec and child Task credentials). A ServiceAccount-token Secret or a Job could name the controller's ServiceAccount, and a Job's Pod could carry the controller's labels, which would put it behind the API Service that publishes the JWKS. The <fullname>-ai-worker-identity-protection ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, which both installs ship, blocks all three. The AI worker may only write Opaque Secrets, may only create or delete code_exec's own ServiceAccounts (so it cannot replace a platform account and inherit its RoleBindings), and may only create code_exec Jobs: each runs as its own per-run ServiceAccount with no token mounted, carries only code_exec labels, uses only emptyDir and Secret volumes, gets no host namespaces, privilege or capabilities, and runs under a RuntimeDefault or Localhost seccomp profile. Keep that policy installed (Helm workers.ai.identityProtection defaults to true; turning it off reopens the path to the controller's identity under the default worker profile), and: Do not grant the AI worker other ways to run Pods or request tokens. An OutboundAccessPolicy serviceAccountRef grants the AI worker TokenRequest for that account, so the controller refuses Orka's own ServiceAccounts there: any labeled orka.ai/platform-identity: "true", plus the controller and worker accounts it is configured with, labeled or not. The AI worker's own account is allowed, since a token for itself gives it nothing new. Do not keep ServiceAccount-token Secrets in the release namespace. The default AI worker profile can read every Secret there, so any such Secret hands the worker that account's token. The controller refuses to start with a signing namespace that is the watch, controller Pod, ACP runtime or agent-host namespace. The chart also refuses the client namespace when rendering; the controller cannot see that one, so kustomize and other installs must keep it apart themselves. Keep the signing namespace free of other workloads and of role bindings beyond the controller's and your cluster administrators'.
documents.s: Who can read the signing key

documents.t: Orka's built-in coding agents (Codex, Claude, Copilot, and OpenCode) can only run the programs already inside Orka's runtime image. A toolbox is an ordinary container image that holds extra tools under one folder, such as /opt/yq-jq/bin. An Agent lists its toolboxes, and Orka makes each toolbox folder appear read-only at the same path inside the runtime Pod and puts its pathEntries on the agent's PATH.

Nothing from a toolbox runs as root. The supervisor only checks, with lstat, that the declared folders exist. Agent processes stay non-root with no capabilities and NoNewPrivs set, so setuid bits and file capabilities grant nothing. Toolboxes add tools, nothing else. No credentials, no extra network access, and no extra Kubernetes permissions. A tool that needs those, such as gh or kubectl, is installed but cannot reach anything. Images are referenced by digest and must come from a registry the operator allowed. Tags are rejected. The feature is off by default. A toolbox that cannot be set up fails the Task with a clear ToolboxUnavailable reason. An agent never starts without the tools it was promised, and nothing retries forever. Runtime skills use the same image delivery, registry allowlist, pull secrets, node selector, and mount method.

Enable toolboxes in the chart and name the registries that may serve them: controller: acpRuntime: toolboxes: enabled: true allowedRegistries: - registry.example.com/tools # host plus optional path prefix - ghcr.io/my-org imagePullSecrets: [] # Secret names in the runtime namespace nodeSelector: {} # merged into runtime Pods that bind toolboxes mountMethod: copy # copy | imageVolume The same settings exist as controller flags: --acp-toolboxes-enabled, --acp-toolbox-allowed-registries, --acp-toolbox-image-pull-secrets, --acp-toolbox-node-selector, and --acp-toolbox-mount-method. An allowlist entry matches the exact registry host (and port) and whole repository path segments only. registry.example.com.evil.io never matches registry.example.com, and registry.example.com/tools-evil never matches registry.example.com/tools. Validation makes no network calls.

copy (default) imageVolume Works on Every Kubernetes version Orka supports Kubernetes 1.36+ with containerd 2.2+ or CRI-O 1.33+ on the selected nodes How An init container copies the toolbox folder into a scratch volume and sanitizes it on the way: modes become 0555/0444, setuid/setgid/sticky bits and file capabilities are dropped, symlinks are copied as text and never followed, and FIFOs, sockets, and device files fail the copy Kubernetes mounts the toolbox image directly as a read-only image volume with a subPath; the files arrive as they are, and the Pod's existing protections (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, dropped capabilities, device rules) keep them harmless Start time measured with a 146 MB toolbox 14 s when the image is not on the node yet, 7 s when it is 9 s / 1 s Architecture check Done by the copier Done by the supervisor through an unprivileged child before it reports ready With imageVolume, the controller reads the API server version at startup. On a server older than 1.36 it logs an error and rejects Agents with toolboxes with ToolboxUnavailable: image volumes need Kubernetes 1.36 or newer. It never silently falls back to copying, so you always know which method is running. Orka cannot read the container runtime version from the API, so use nodeSelector to pin toolbox Pods to qualified nodes. Runtime pools scale to zero after a period of idleness, so the start-time difference lands on real users often; prefer imageVolume when your cluster supports it.

apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: release-helper spec: model: name: gpt-5.4 runtime: type: codex toolboxes: - image: registry.example.com/tools/yq-jq@sha256:<digest> mountPath: /opt/yq-jq # the folder the tools live in, inside the toolbox image pathEntries: [bin] # added to PATH as /opt/yq-jq/bin Validation rules, enforced by the CRD schema, Agent admission, Task planning, and again inside the runtime Pod: image is a fully qualified reference pinned by digest (<registry>/<repository>@sha256:<64 hex>), from an allowed registry. mountPath is exactly /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew or /opt/<name>. It must be clean (no .., no //, no trailing /) and <name> must not be one the runtime images already use: codex, codex-acp, claude, claude-agent-acp, copilot, opencode, ripgrep, yarn-v1.22.22, and orka-skills, where Orka binds runtime skills. Two toolboxes may not share, contain, or sit inside each other's mountPath. pathEntries are clean relative paths inside mountPath with no ... No path may contain :, ,, NUL, or control characters. At most 4 toolboxes, 8 pathEntries per toolbox, and 256 bytes per path. Order matters: toolboxes and their pathEntries are appended to PATH in the order you declare them, after the system folders (/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin), so a toolbox never replaces a system command. The supervisor also writes a ~/.profile into each session home that re-adds the toolbox folders, because agents such as Codex run commands through a login shell and Debian's /etc/profile resets PATH for non-root users. Changing any toolbox field creates a new RuntimePool; Tasks that are already running keep the toolboxes frozen in their execution snapshot. Agents with toolboxes get a short Orka-generated note at the start of the first prompt of each runtime session that lists the toolbox folders. It lists folders from the Agent spec, never file names from inside the image, so a toolbox author cannot put text in front of the model.

Every built-in runtime image runs on Debian 13 ("trixie") with glibc 2.41. Toolbox binaries must run with that glibc. Runtime Final base Debian glibc Codex node:22.22.0-trixie-slim 13 (trixie) 2.41 Claude node:22.22.0-trixie-slim 13 (trixie) 2.41 Copilot node:22.22.0-trixie-slim 13 (trixie) 2.41 OpenCode debian:trixie-slim 13 (trixie) 2.41 Static binaries work everywhere. Dynamically linked tools must find their libraries inside the toolbox (for example through an rpath) or in the runtime image itself, which is deliberately small.

The toolbox copier and the supervisor check that the ELF files in each pathEntries folder match the node's CPU architecture, because Kubernetes pulls an arm64-only image onto an amd64 node without complaint. Build for both architectures and verify each download with its own checksum, since the amd64 and arm64 release files differ: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM debian:bookworm-slim AS fetch ARG TARGETARCH RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates RUN set -eu; case "$TARGETARCH" in \ amd64) sha=<sha256 of yq_linux_amd64> ;; \ arm64) sha=<sha256 of yq_linux_arm64> ;; \ *) exit 1 ;; esac; \ mkdir -p /out/opt/yq-jq/bin; \ curl -fsSLo /out/opt/yq-jq/bin/yq "https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/download/v4.54.1/yq_linux_${TARGETARCH}"; \ echo "$sha /out/opt/yq-jq/bin/yq" | sha256sum -c -; \ chmod 0755 /out/opt/yq-jq/bin/yq FROM scratch COPY --from=fetch /out/ / LABEL ai.orka.toolbox='{"version":1,"mountPath":"/opt/yq-jq","pathEntries":["bin"]}' docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t registry.example.com/tools/yq-jq:1 --push . crane digest registry.example.com/tools/yq-jq:1 # pin this digest in the Agent A FROM scratch image works because the copier never runs anything from the toolbox image: Orka hands its own static copier binary into the toolbox container through a scratch volume.

dalec-homebrew builds Homebrew formulae into a container image. Put every formula in one image under /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew and declare pathEntries: [bin]: toolboxes: - image: registry.example.com/tools/brew-curl-jq@sha256:<digest> mountPath: /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew pathEntries: [bin] Homebrew prefixes need glibc 2.38 or newer, which all four runtimes provide. Known blockers: git cannot be built yet (sozercan/dalec-homebrew#32) and Homebrew's own glibc cannot be bundled (sozercan/dalec-homebrew#33).

The label is optional and informational. Version 1 has this shape: {"version": 1, "mountPath": "/opt/yq-jq", "pathEntries": ["bin"]} The Agent spec always wins over the label. Orka never reads image labels when it validates or mounts a toolbox; a future orka toolbox command will use the label to suggest Agent settings and pin digests.

A toolbox failure sets the RuntimePool's RolloutReady condition to ToolboxUnavailable and fails every Task waiting on that pool with the same reason. The message carries one stable code: Reason Meaning Fix TOOLBOX_IMAGE_PULL The toolbox image could not be pulled after five minutes from the first observed pull failure; invalid image names fail immediately. Check the digest, registry access, and imagePullSecrets. TOOLBOX_SOURCE_OPEN copy mode only: mountPath does not exist in the image, or a symlink sits somewhere in its path. Image volumes report a missing mountPath as TOOLBOX_MOUNT_FAILED and leave a symlinked one to the node runtime to resolve. Build the image so the folder exists as a real directory at exactly mountPath. TOOLBOX_MISSING_PATH_ENTRY A pathEntries folder is missing or is not a real directory. Fix the entry or the image layout. TOOLBOX_ARCH_MISMATCH An ELF file in a pathEntries folder is built for another CPU architecture. Publish a multi-architecture image or pin toolbox Pods to matching nodes with nodeSelector. TOOLBOX_UNSUPPORTED_FILE_TYPE The toolbox contains a FIFO, socket, or device file in copy mode, an overlong symlink chain, or a PATH symlink that leaves the toolbox root. Remove special files or rewrite the symlink within the toolbox; only folders, regular files, and PATH symlinks resolved entirely within the toolbox are supported. TOOLBOX_TOO_DEEP, TOOLBOX_TOO_LARGE, TOOLBOX_FILE_TOO_LARGE, TOOLBOX_TOO_MANY_ENTRIES A copy limit was exceeded (48 folders deep, 2 GiB total, 512 MiB per file, 200,000 entries). Trim the image; keep only the tools' folder. TOOLBOX_SOURCE_CHANGED A file changed while it was being copied. Rebuild the image; a toolbox must be immutable. TOOLBOX_MOUNT_FAILED With imageVolume, the subPath does not exist in the image or the node runtime cannot mount image volumes. Check the image layout and the containerd or CRI-O version on the selected nodes. TOOLBOX_MISSING_MOUNT The supervisor did not find the toolbox folder in the runtime Pod. Check the node runtime and the RuntimePool events. TOOLBOX_PERMISSION_DENIED A toolbox folder is not readable and traversable by everyone (o+rx), or a tool in a pathEntries folder is not readable and executable by everyone. Agent processes run as arbitrary UIDs that own nothing in the image. Build the image with world-accessible folders and 0755 tools. This reason comes from image volumes; copy mode sanitizes modes only after reading, and its copier also runs as a fixed non-root UID, so source folders still need o+rx and files o+r or the copy fails with TOOLBOX_SOURCE_OPEN or TOOLBOX_COPY_FAILED. TOOLBOX_COPY_FAILED Another I/O error during the copy. See the init container logs (toolbox-copy-<n>) on the runtime Pod. kubectl describe runtimepool <name> shows the condition; kubectl get task <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.execution.message}' shows the Task-side reason.

Not supported yet, and rejected with a clear message at admission and again at planning: external runtimes (runtime.runtimeRef); Tasks with spec.execution.workspace (execution workspaces, including Agent Sandbox and Substrate). Tools that need credentials or network access, such as gh or kubectl, can be installed but cannot reach anything: runtime Pods have no internet access and no Kubernetes permissions. Credentials and outbound access go through connectors and outbound access; see the design issues linked from the toolboxes epic for approvals and Kubernetes API access.

Install the latest Orka release with Helm, then run a small test task. The whole install is one Helm command. It creates the orka-system namespace for Orka itself and a second namespace, orka-runtimes, for the Pods that run coding agents. These commands use your current Kubernetes context, name the installation orka, and use the namespace orka-system. For development, build from source.

You need these tools on your machine: kubectl connected to your cluster. For a laptop, kind or minikube is fine. Helm 3 or newer. Your cluster needs: Permission to create namespaces, CRDs, and cluster-wide RBAC. A default StorageClass. Orka stores its database on a small persistent volume. HTTPS access to ghcr.io from the nodes and from the controller Pod. The controller looks up image digests at startup. No existing Orka installation or Orka CRDs. If a previous install left CRDs behind, see Upgrading. NetworkPolicy enforcement is recommended for production, because Orka uses NetworkPolicies to keep model credentials away from agent Pods. It is not required for a test install. kind and minikube work without it. You do not need a model API key to install Orka. You add providers and models after the install.

Install the latest chart from Orka's Helm repository. It already includes the matching image tags, generates its own encryption key, and issues its own webhook certificate. helm repo add orka https://orka-agents.github.io/orka/charts helm repo update orka helm install orka orka/orka --namespace orka-system --create-namespace \ --wait --timeout 10m The command returns when Orka is ready, which takes a minute or two on a laptop while the images pull. To bring your own webhook certificate or use cert-manager, see Webhook certificate.

Check that the Deployments are ready and the data volumes show Bound: kubectl -n orka-system get deployments,pvc Then run a container task. This test does not call a model. kubectl -n orka-system apply -f - <<'YAML' apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: release-install-check spec: type: container command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "printf ORKA_INSTALL_OK"] timeout: 3m retryPolicy: maxRetries: 0 YAML kubectl -n orka-system wait \ --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded task/release-install-check --timeout=3m When the command reports condition met, Orka has completed its first task. Back these up The install created two Secrets that the controller filled in on its first start. orka-agent-execution-snapshot is the key that encrypts saved agent execution records; without it, Orka cannot read those records after a restore, so back it up with the data volume. orka-webhook-tls is the self-signed certificate for Orka's admission webhooks, which the controller renews on its own. Never run helm upgrade --force on this release, because it would replace both with the chart's empty versions. To supply your own key or certificate, see Snapshot encryption key and Webhook certificate.

Connect to the API with a port-forward and a client token. Add a provider and run your first AI task with an API key or a model server your cluster can reach. To run coding agents such as Codex or Claude Code, connect a model gateway. This step is optional and can come later.

On a throwaway kind or minikube cluster, deleting the cluster removes everything. Uninstall deletes Orka's data helm uninstall removes the persistent volume claims that hold the task database and workspace data. Unless your StorageClass retains released volumes, that data is gone. A later reinstall starts empty; recovering records means restoring both the volumes and the snapshot key Secret from a backup. Take that backup first if you care about what is stored. On a cluster you keep: helm uninstall orka --namespace orka-system Helm leaves the CRDs, the two generated Secrets, and the orka-system namespace in place. To remove those too: kubectl delete namespace orka-system orka-runtimes kubectl get crd -o name | grep '\.orka\.ai$' | xargs kubectl delete Deleting the CRDs deletes every Orka resource in the cluster. See Upgrading for the details.
This page is for people changing Orka itself. For how the pieces fit together, read Architecture first.

The AI worker uses a pluggable provider interface: type Provider interface { Complete(ctx context.Context, req *CompletionRequest) (*CompletionResponse, error) Stream(ctx context.Context, req *CompletionRequest) (<-chan StreamChunk, error) Name() string } Implementations exist for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI. Provider selection is configured via the Provider CRD, which stores credentials in Kubernetes Secrets.

LLM calls use exponential backoff with jitter: Default: 3 retries Backoff: baseDelay × 2^attempt, capped at 30s, with ±10% random jitter Retryable status codes: 429, 500, 502, 503, 529 Non-retryable: 401, 403 (trigger fallback instead), context canceled/deadline exceeded (never retried) Stream retry: Peeks at the initial stream event to detect errors before consuming the stream

Failed providers are temporarily cooled down to prevent repeated failures: Cooldown formula: 1min × 5^(errorCount-1), capped at 1 hour Rate-limited providers (429) are tracked and skipped in subsequent requests Cooldown is per-provider and resets on successful requests

The OpenAI provider automatically detects which API to use: Tries the Responses API first If the endpoint returns 404/405 or a known unsupported-API error code, switches to Chat Completions API The API mode is stored as an atomic.Int32 for thread-safe switching Once detected, the mode persists for the provider's lifetime Copilot-compatible Responses API 403s are handled as a scoped fallback to Chat Completions. Generic 403s still surface as provider errors instead of being treated as unsupported API signals.

The Anthropic SDK appends v1/messages to the base URL — strip trailing /v1 from custom baseURL to avoid doubled paths system messages in the conversation are sent as user text messages; only tool messages become user tool_result blocks Tool input JSON parsing errors are silently ignored (_ = json.Unmarshal)

SQLite via modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go, no CGO dependency) stores Orka payload/read-model data. ACP control authority is deliberately excluded: controller epochs and Session mutation ownership use Kubernetes Leases, while attempt, Session, branch, publication, and external-effect transitions use CRD status resourceVersion CAS.

Startup creates the complete current layout in one transaction for an empty database. Production startup opens the store through OpenLockedStore, which holds the exclusive controller lock, validates an existing database against the exact current layout, and upgrades an exactly recognized older layout in place after taking a verified backup beside the database. Unknown, partially modified, and newer layouts are refused without changes. Reopening a current layout validates it without rewriting records or changing their IDs and ordering. The lower-level NewDB constructor and in-memory stores validate only and never migrate. The database support policy lists the recognized layouts. Table Primary Key Purpose results (namespace, task_name) Task output data (BLOB) sessions (namespace, name) Session metadata, active_task field for locking, token counters session_messages id (FK → sessions) Individual messages with role, content, tool_calls (JSON) messages id + namespace + parent_task Inter-agent messages, broadcast via to_task='*' plan_states (namespace, task_name) Autonomous loop state: iteration, progress %, goal_complete flag memories id Durable namespace-scoped memories with provenance, tags, disabled/deleted flags, and recall counters memory_proposals id Reviewable memory/skill/policy/workflow proposals with status, reviewer, and review notes artifacts (namespace, task_name, filename) Artifact metadata and BLOB content, 10MB max per artifact session_turns / outbox tables stable IDs ACP transcript/SessionTurn payloads and deferred terminal projections committed behind Kubernetes epoch/Session fences security_scan_runs id Repository scan run lifecycle, mode, commits, timestamps, summary, and errors security_threat_models (namespace, repository_scan, version) Versioned repository threat models generated or edited for scans security_findings id Deduplicated findings with severity, confidence, validation, evidence, and PR linkage security_patch_proposals id Patch proposal tasks, branches, artifacts, status, and PR linkage for findings

WAL mode with single-writer enforcement: SetMaxOpenConns(1), SetMaxIdleConns(1) Per-connection pragmas (set on every new connection, not persistent): busy_timeout=5000 — wait up to 5s for locks synchronous=NORMAL — balance between safety and performance foreign_keys=ON — enforce referential integrity Namespace scoping: All queries filter by namespace — data isolation is enforced at the SQL level

Sessions use optimistic locking via an active_task column. AcquireLock atomically sets active_task only if it's currently empty. Tasks that fail to acquire the lock requeue every 5 seconds. The lock is released on task completion or deletion (via finalizer cleanup). There is no timeout — if the lock holder crashes, the lock persists until the task is deleted.

Inter-agent broadcast messages (to_task='*') are scoped by parent_task: WHERE (to_task = ? OR (to_task = '*' AND parent_task = ?)) This ensures only sibling tasks (same parent coordinator) receive broadcasts. Senders don't receive their own broadcasts.

Workers authenticate these routes with their ServiceAccount token. Endpoint Method Description /internal/v1/results/:namespace/:taskName POST Submit task result /internal/v1/artifacts/:namespace/:taskName/:filename POST Upload task artifact /internal/v1/sessions/:namespace/:name/transcript GET Get session transcript /internal/v1/plans/:namespace/:taskName POST Save plan state /internal/v1/plans/:namespace/:taskName GET Get plan state /internal/v1/messages/:namespace POST Send inter-agent message /internal/v1/messages/:namespace/:taskName GET Get messages for a task

Workers call this to persist autonomous plan state. Endpoint: POST /internal/v1/plans/{namespace}/{taskName} Request Body: { "summary": "Completed phase 1", "progress_pct": 25, "goal_complete": false, "plan_document": "# Plan\n..." } Response: 204 No Content
Workers call this to load the current plan state at startup. Endpoint: GET /internal/v1/plans/{namespace}/{taskName} Response (200): Same as public plan endpoint. Errors: 404 — No plan found

Workers call this to send messages to sibling tasks (same parent coordinator). Endpoint: POST /internal/v1/messages/{namespace} Request Body: { "fromTask": "worker-a", "toTask": "worker-b", "parentTask": "coordinator", "content": "Found a bug in the auth module" } Use "toTask": "*" to broadcast to all siblings. Response: 204 No Content

Workers call this to check for unread messages. It returns the oldest unread messages, ordered by ID, up to 500 per call; a longer backlog is read over several calls. With markRead=true exactly the returned messages are marked read. Endpoint: GET /internal/v1/messages/{namespace}/{taskName}?parentTask={parentTask}&markRead={true|false} Query Parameters: parentTask (required) — Parent coordinator task name (scopes messages to siblings) markRead (optional, default: true) — Whether to mark returned messages as read Response (200): [ { "id": 1, "namespace": "orka-system", "fromTask": "worker-b", "toTask": "worker-a", "parentTask": "coordinator", "content": "Found a bug in the auth module", "read": false, "createdAt": "2026-01-15T10:30:00Z" } ]

Orka can serve a Model Context Protocol endpoint so an agent in your editor can hand work to an Orka Agent, follow it, answer its approval requests, and read its result. The agent in your editor plans; the Orka Agent runs in the cluster with the cluster's credentials, workspaces, and policies. The endpoint is a thin client of the public REST API. Each tool call replays the equivalent REST request inside the API server with your credentials, so it can never do more than you could do with curl. There is no separate MCP permission model to configure.

The endpoint is off by default. Start the controller with: --mcp-server-enabled or set ORKA_MCP_SERVER_ENABLED=true. It is served at POST /mcp on the API port (8080). --mcp-max-concurrent (default 16) bounds concurrent MCP requests per API replica. Long waits (wait_for_task, tasks/result) give up their request slot and use a separate pool of half as many wait slots (at least one), so waits never block approvals, cancellations, or other requests. Excess requests and waits receive HTTP 429 with Retry-After, or a busy error for a wait. A request body may be at most 1 MiB, measured after any Content-Encoding (gzip, deflate, br, or zstd) is removed; a compressed body that expands past the limit is refused with HTTP 413 without being expanded. The endpoint is a stateless Streamable HTTP server. It answers every request with one JSON body, issues no Mcp-Session-Id, and opens no server-sent event stream; GET /mcp returns 405. It supports protocol versions 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, and the sessionless 2026-07-28 revision (server/discover and per-request _meta). It does not accept JSON-RPC batches, so it does not negotiate 2025-03-26, the one revision that requires them; initialize with that version is answered with 2025-11-25. Mirrored headers are validated against the JSON-RPC body and never used for authorization. A 2026-07-28 request must send MCP-Protocol-Version (equal to its _meta version), Mcp-Method, and, for tools/call, Mcp-Name (plain or =?base64?…?=); a missing or mismatched header is 400 with error -32020. A client that declares the Tasks extension must also send Mcp-Name equal to params.taskId on tasks/get, tasks/update, and tasks/cancel. An unsupported version is 400 with -32022 and the supported list, and a method the server does not implement is 404 for a 2026-07-28 request. Any Mcp-Session-Id is ignored. The in-process REST replay forwards only your credential headers (Authorization, x-api-key, configured context-token headers) and request labels (Host, User-Agent, trace context); no other header you send reaches the REST route.

Use the same credentials as the REST API: a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token in Authorization: Bearer <token>; an OIDC token in Authorization: Bearer <token> when OIDC is configured; or a transaction token in Txn-Token: <token> (or the configured context-token header). For a quick start, mint a short-lived token for the orka-client ServiceAccount and port-forward the API: export ORKA_TOKEN="$(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client --duration 8h)" kubectl -n orka-system port-forward svc/orka 8080:8080 The endpoint does not implement MCP OAuth discovery; configure the header in your client. Requests with a browser Origin header must match ORKA_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS when that allow-list is set. With the endpoint enabled, the CORS allow-list also accepts the Mcp-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method, and Mcp-Name request headers.

claude mcp add --transport http orka http://localhost:8080/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $ORKA_TOKEN" Or check a project-scoped .mcp.json into the repository and keep the token in your environment: { "mcpServers": { "orka": { "type": "http", "url": "https://orka.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${ORKA_TOKEN}" } } } }
In ~/.cursor/mcp.json or the project's .cursor/mcp.json: { "mcpServers": { "orka": { "url": "https://orka.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:ORKA_TOKEN}" } } } }

In .vscode/mcp.json. VS Code prompts for the token once and stores it securely: { "inputs": [ { "type": "promptString", "id": "orka-token", "description": "Orka API token", "password": true } ], "servers": { "orka": { "type": "http", "url": "https://orka.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:orka-token}" } } } } To use a transaction token instead, send "Txn-Token": "<token>" in headers and omit Authorization.

Every tool takes an optional namespace. Namespace resolution, --watch-namespace, and --enforce-namespace-isolation behave exactly as for the REST route. Tool What it does REST route it replays list_agents List Agents (name, runtime, model, tools, readiness) GET /api/v1/agents get_agent Describe one Agent GET /api/v1/agents/:name create_task Run a prompt on an Agent, with an optional workspace and session POST /api/v1/tasks; GET /api/v1/agents/:name only when taskType is omitted; GET /api/v1/tasks/:id only when it returns an MCP task get_task Status, pending approvals, plan progress, delivery and pull request GET /api/v1/tasks/:id; GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/approvals while running list_tasks List Tasks, optionally by label selector GET /api/v1/tasks wait_for_task Wait up to 50 seconds for a Task to finish or need a decision GET /api/v1/tasks/:id, GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/approvals cancel_task Ask a Pending or Running Task to stop POST /api/v1/tasks/:id/cancel list_pending_approvals Show a Task's approval requests GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/approvals decide_approval Record a human's approve or decline decision POST /api/v1/tasks/:id/approvals/:approvalID/decision get_task_result Read the result text in chunks GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/result list_task_artifacts List uploaded artifacts GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/artifacts get_task_artifact Read a text artifact in chunks GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/artifacts/:filename create_task builds the same request as POST /api/v1/tasks with type, prompt, agentRef, and the optional timeout, workspace (Task spec.workspace), and session (spec.sessionRef with append: true, which continues an existing Orka Session and records the Task's turns in it). Give taskType (agent for Agents with a CLI runtime, ai for native Agents) to skip the Agent lookup; otherwise the caller also needs get on the Agent. Omit name to generate one starting with mcp-. cancel_task requests cancellation exactly like POST /api/v1/tasks/:id/cancel: the controller then ends the Task as Cancelled, and its result and artifacts are kept. The request returns before that, with the Task's current phase and whether this call recorded the request.

decide_approval records the decision under your identity, exactly like orka task approve. It is annotated as destructive so clients ask before running it, and its description tells the model to call it only after you have decided. Keep tool confirmation on for it in your client. A model that may approve its own delegated actions defeats the purpose of human approval. Clients that support the MCP Tasks extension can instead show the request to you directly; see below.

create_task returns as soon as the Task exists. Use wait_for_task in a loop, or use MCP Tasks if your client supports them. The server advertises both shapes: The io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension. When a request's _meta client capabilities declare the extension, create_task returns a task (resultType: "task"). tasks/get reports its status; once it completes it includes the create_task result. The extension reserves failed for JSON-RPC errors, so a failed Task is completed with an isError: true result, and a cancelled Task carries no result. While a human decision is pending the status is input_required and inputRequests holds one form elicitation per pending approval, keyed by approval ID, asking for decision (approve or decline) and an optional reason. Answer with tasks/update: accept records the chosen decision, decline declines the request, and cancel leaves it pending. Each answer is recorded through the REST decision route under your identity. An update that failed partway can be retried as sent: an answer matching a decision already recorded succeeds, and an update with any answer that contradicts one is refused before anything is recorded. tasks/cancel requests cancellation through POST /api/v1/tasks/:id/cancel. 2025-11-25 task-augmented calls. A tools/call for create_task with params.task returns { "task": { ... } }. tasks/get returns the task, tasks/result waits up to 50 seconds for the result and otherwise asks you to poll again, and tasks/cancel requests cancellation and returns the task with its current status. Answer approvals with decide_approval; the server sends no elicitation requests on this path. Only create_task supports task augmentation: params.task on any other tool is refused with -32601 before the tool runs. A task-augmented create_task that creates no task answers with a JSON-RPC error, not a tool result. params.task is part of the 2025-11-25 revision only; a 2026-07-28 request that carries it is answered as if it did not. In both shapes the task ID is returned only once tasks/get resolves it, so you can poll at once. The server checks by reading the new Task under your identity; a caller who may create Tasks but not read them still gets the ID. If the new Task cannot be read within five seconds, the call returns an error that names the Task instead of an ID (an error result under the extension, a JSON-RPC error for a 2025-11-25 call): read it with get_task rather than creating it again. A result whose REST response is larger than 8 MiB cannot be read through MCP. A finished task still reports the Task, with resultUnavailable naming the REST route to read the result from, and get_task_result returns an error saying the same. Orka Task MCP task status Pending, Scheduled, Running, Finalizing working Running with a pending approval request input_required Succeeded completed Failed failed; completed with an isError result under the extension Cancelled, or being deleted cancelled A task ID names the Task's namespace and name and pins its UID. A later Task created with the same name is a different MCP task, and the old ID reports "task not found". Cancellation is asynchronous: the task reports its current status until the controller ends the Task as Cancelled. Result reads, approval decisions, and cancellation carry the UID to the REST route, so they never read, decide, or cancel a later Task that reuses the name. MCP keeps no state of its own: every tasks/* call re-reads the Task with your credentials, so a controller or API restart changes nothing. A finished task is never reported without its output because a result read failed: tasks/get and tasks/result return an error you can retry instead. tasks/list is not supported; use list_tasks.

Tool results are summaries, not raw API objects. Task summaries omit environment variables, Secret references, transaction metadata, and runtime identifiers. Prompts, status messages, approval details, results, and artifacts pass through the same credential redaction Orka uses for durable memory, which removes bearer and Txn-Token headers, JWTs, well-known API token shapes, credential assignments, and signed URL parameters. Redaction is best-effort pattern matching, not a guarantee. Results and artifacts are returned in chunks of at most 256 KiB (32 KiB by default). The whole text is redacted before it is split, so a credential that crosses a chunk boundary is still removed; offset and nextOffset refer to the redacted text. Binary artifacts are refused; download them through the REST API. list_agents and list_tasks return at most 50 items per page. list_pending_approvals and list_task_artifacts are not paged and return at most 200 entries.

POST /mcp itself only authenticates. Each tool call is authorized by the route it replays: the same SubjectAccessReviews for ServiceAccount callers, the same OIDC subject and namespace policy, the same transaction-token scopes and tctx constraints, the same Gateway and workspace-class checks, and the same refusal before any effect. A denied call returns a tool error with the REST status, for example Orka API returned 403: .... See the authorization reference for the permissions behind each tool. Each replay is also recorded by the API's request logging and metrics under its REST path, so audits see the same routes as for direct API use.

Memory lets agents carry knowledge from one Task to the next: project facts, decisions, conventions, and procedures. In a shared cluster, memory that any model output could change would be a liability, so Orka makes writing a memory a review request. Agents propose; a person reviews and applies; only then do future Tasks see it. Memory is scoped to a namespace and available to native type: ai Tasks. The current model has three related concepts: Concept Purpose Persistence Durable memory Reviewed project facts, decisions, conventions, or reusable context that can help future tasks Stored in SQLite as namespace-scoped memories records Memory proposal A worker- or user-submitted suggestion for memory, policy, workflow, or skill changes Stored in SQLite as memory_proposals for review Transcript search Compact search over prior session messages Stored in SQLite session transcript tables Memory proposal review is non-applying. Reviewing a proposal as accepted or rejected records the decision only. Accepted proposals with type: "memory" or a consolidation type can then be applied explicitly. A memory apply creates (or idempotently returns) durable memory linked back to the proposal; a consolidation apply changes the memories it targets. Both steps record who took them: reviewer on the review and appliedBy on the apply. The server takes these names from the signed-in identity of the request. A client cannot set them: a request body with a non-empty reviewer or appliedBy is rejected with 400 Bad Request, and a request without an identity is refused. Video demo Watch Review and publish an agent's memory.

Memory proposals follow an explicit review/apply lifecycle: New proposals start with status: "pending". Review decisions only apply to pending proposals and record either status: "accepted" or status: "rejected"; review does not create durable memory. Accepted proposals with type: "memory", or one of the consolidation types, require an explicit apply request before they change durable memory. Rejected or archived proposals cannot be applied. Accepted memory proposals can suggest durable memory tags by including a Tags: line in the proposal description. The apply step reads tags from the first Tags: line only, normalizes them, and ignores later Tags: lines. Example: Reusable release procedure discovered during task execution. Tags: release, testing

Over many Tasks, memory collects duplicates, entries that later work contradicted, and stale facts. Three proposal types consolidate existing memories. Like every proposal, each is reviewed and applied by a person; nothing changes until it is applied. Type Targets Applying it memory_merge two or more memories creates one memory from the proposal's content and retires every target into it memory_supersede one memory creates one memory from the proposal's content and retires the target into it memory_retire one or more memories disables every target A consolidation proposal names each memory it changes in targets, with the generation of the memory it read. Every memory has a generation: 1 when it is created, and one more each time its content, tags, provenance, disabled or deleted state changes. A recall does not change it. Any proposal may also cite the Sessions it drew on in sources, each with a sessionName and an optional messageId. A proposal names at most 20 targets and 20 sources. { "namespace": "orka-system", "type": "memory_merge", "title": "One release checklist", "content": "Release PRs run make lint-fix and make test, then the e2e suite.", "targets": [ {"memoryId": "mem-release-1", "generation": 1}, {"memoryId": "mem-release-2", "generation": 3} ], "sources": [{"sessionName": "release-review"}] } Applying a consolidation proposal changes its targets in one transaction, and only while every target is still at the generation the proposal names and is not deleted. If any target changed, the apply returns 409 Conflict and changes nothing: the proposal was written against content nobody reviewed since. It stays accepted, so archive it. Applying one also requires update permission on every target memory, besides the usual permission to apply proposals and create memories; see API authorization. Consolidation proposals are reviewed and applied only through /api/v1: the worker-facing internal routes check only the namespace, so they refuse to review or apply one with 403 Forbidden. A merge or supersede marks each target deleted and disabled, and sets its supersededBy to the new memory, so the replaced record and its provenance stay readable: list with includeDeleted=true&includeDisabled=true, since deleted memories are disabled too. A retire only disables its targets, which you can enable again. The apply response is the memory created, or for a retire the first target.

A consolidation run is a scheduled native type: ai Task that reads the namespace's current memories and its recently changed Sessions, and finds consolidation proposals and new memories worth adding. It never changes memory itself. In DryRun mode, the default, it only reports what it found. In Propose mode it also creates a pending proposal for each finding, for a person to review and apply as usual. Start with DryRun, read a few reports, and switch to Propose once the findings are worth reviewing. apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: memory-consolidation namespace: orka-system spec: type: ai schedule: "0 3 * * *" agentRef: name: memory-curator ai: prompt: Focus on release and testing conventions. memoryConsolidation: mode: DryRun # or Propose minNewSessions: 5 # skip the run when fewer Sessions changed maxOperations: 10 # 1 to 20 lookback: 168h # how far back the first run reads; at most 720h spec.ai.prompt steers what the run focuses on. The run uses a fixed Orka system prompt, no tools, no skills, no soul, and no injected memory, whatever the Agent or Task configure. The field requires an ai Task without sessionRef, and cannot be added, removed or changed after the Task is created.

A run reads the transcripts of everyone's Sessions in the namespace, which no ordinary Task can. Creating a Task with memoryConsolidation, or changing the spec of one, therefore requires list and get on sessions and list on memories in the namespace, since the run sends memories to the model and its report quotes them, and in Propose mode also create on memoryproposals. A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy checks the person making the change, so nobody without those permissions can edit a run's prompt, Agent or provider to steer it or send the transcripts elsewhere. The Orka API, which creates Tasks with its own identity, checks the same permissions for the person calling it, and a transaction token also needs the session-read and memory-read scopes, and in Propose mode the memory-write scope. The scheduled runs the controller creates from a Task are covered by the check on that Task. A run sends transcripts to the model of its Agent or Provider. Whoever can edit that Agent or Provider can change where they go, for every Task that uses it, so restrict who can edit the Agent and Provider a consolidation run uses as you restrict who can read Sessions. Memory and proposals are namespace-wide. Enabling consolidation means what one person's Session taught can reach everyone's prompts, after review.

Each run reads the Sessions that changed since the last completed run of its mode in the namespace, or within lookback for the first one: chat and task Sessions only, never gateway conversations; the 50 most recently changed of them, however long ago they were created, and the newest 40 user and assistant messages of each, found among its newest 200 records and each cut to 2,000 characters. Tool messages are dropped, so memory an agent recalled cannot come back as new evidence; every active memory, up to 200, with its generation and recall counts, each cut to 2,000 characters and at most 10 tags of 40 characters; at most 60,000 characters of memories and, separately, 60,000 characters of transcripts, counted as they are encoded for the model with every field name, ID and timestamp, so memories never crowd out what the run learns from. Within a Session the limit keeps the newest turns, which the model still reads in order. A report whose input reached any limit says inputTruncated: a memory, tag or message cut to its length, these character budgets, 200 memories (a namespace with more has its least recently updated memories left out), 50 changed Sessions, or a Session's 40 messages. Sessions left out are read again only if they change again. A model that still cannot take the input fails the run, which leaves its Sessions for the next one. DryRun and Propose keep separate places, so dry runs never use up the Sessions a proposing run has yet to read. When fewer than minNewSessions Sessions changed, the run is skipped without calling the model. A skipped or failed run does not move its mode's place: the next run reads the same Sessions again, from where the first run started, up to 720 hours back. A mode's first run that fails before it records its window leaves no place, so the next run reads its own lookback. A run's window ends 15.5 minutes before the run begins, the longest a stamped Session write can still take to commit, so a change still being written is read by the next run rather than missed. After a gap longer than 720 hours, such as a suspended schedule, the window starts 720 hours back, and the report's windowCutFrom says where its mode had last stopped. A run records its input when it begins: a retried Pod reads the same input, and its result is checked against exactly what the model saw. The recorded input is deleted when the run finishes, or when its Task fails, is cancelled or is deleted first, and no other copy of it is kept. A run whose Task ended without finishing it is marked abandoned, and the next run in its mode reads its Sessions again. Once a run's Task is deleted, its stored report is cleared too, and Orka keeps only the few finished runs that mark where each mode's next run starts, so a recurring run's history does not grow the store. Only the worker of the run's own active Task can begin or complete it, and once its Job is revoked it can do neither, even before Kubernetes shows the revocation. Only one run at a time reads a namespace's memory. A run that begins while another is running fails with a conflict. A run that read its inputs while another run in its mode completed reads them again from where that run ended, so the two never read the same Sessions. A run that is still running after two hours stops blocking, whether or not its Task is still active; the run that takes over marks it abandoned, so it can neither resume nor create proposals. Orka cannot yet tell which Task wrote a Session, so turns of scheduled Tasks and parked continuations are read like any other.

The model's result is untrusted. A response the model did not finish fails the run at once. A finished response without an operations list is not accepted either: the worker asks once more, and otherwise the run fails. Either way, the run's Sessions are read again. A run that finds nothing to change submits an empty list. Orka then checks every operation against what the run read and drops one that fails, recording why: every target is a memory the run read, at the generation it read, still active at that generation, and no two operations change the same memory; every source is a Session the run read, and an add cites at least one; new memory content is non-empty and at most 1,200 characters; at most maxOperations operations; the run removes at most max(1, ⌊memories read ÷ 4⌋) memories. A merge of k memories removes k−1, a supersede removes none, and a retire of k removes k, so a run can always merge two duplicates. Contradictions the model could not settle are reported as conflicts, not proposed.

A run's report holds its mode and status (completed or skipped), the window it read, how many memories and Sessions it read, each kept operation, each dropped one with its reason, the conflicts, the IDs of the proposals it created, and a short summary. The Task result is only the report's structure, marked structural: each operation's type, targets and sources, each dropped operation's index and reason, the memories each conflict names, the proposal IDs and the counts. It has no titles, content, reasons the model wrote, tags, conflict notes or summary, since anyone who can read the Task can read its result, and that text comes from everyone's Sessions and from memories. The full report is at GET /api/v1/tasks/<run>/memory-consolidation-report, which also requires list and get on sessions and list on memories (for a transaction token, the session-read and memory-read scopes as well as Task read), while the Task exists. A dropped operation's reason never repeats what the model named, only memories the run read. A report that would be larger than 256 KiB is marked abridged, dropping, in order, the dropped operations, the conflicts, the summary and the kept operations' text until it fits. The proposals keep their full text. A run that finds nothing to change is a normal, reported outcome. Proposals a Propose run creates are attributed to the run's Task, so orka memory proposal list --task-name <run> lists them.

When an AI worker can reach the controller internal API, it loads reviewed durable memories before invoking the model. The durable memory section is appended to the system prompt as background project context, separate from the current session transcript. In this warning release, every native type: ai Task receives the memory tools, regardless of Agent spec.tools, Task spec.ai.tools, or coordination.enabled. They cannot yet be disabled per Agent, including with enabled: false or the orka.ai/disable-coordination-tool-injection Task annotation. When a model calls a memory tool that is neither explicitly selected nor covered by coordination, the worker logs a deprecation warning. The next release will stop adding these tools unless the Agent enables coordination or the Agent/Task explicitly selects them. In that release, the disable-injection annotation will also suppress automatic memory tools; explicit selections will remain available. See the migration and release notes and tool parameters. Tool Purpose recall_memory Query durable namespace-scoped memories by text, tags, provenance, and limit remember Submit a durable memory proposal for review propose_memory Submit a memory-adjacent governance proposal such as memory, policy, workflow, or skill content search_transcript Search prior session transcripts and return compact snippets remember and propose_memory intentionally submit proposals instead of mutating durable memory directly. This keeps shared memory reviewable and prevents live model output from silently changing future task context.

Durable memory injection is bounded to keep prompts stable: Setting Default Purpose ORKA_MEMORY_CONTEXT_LIMIT 5 Maximum memories to inject into the worker prompt ORKA_MEMORY_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS 6000 Maximum durable-memory prompt section size The worker also truncates individual memory entries before prompt injection. Memory infrastructure is best-effort: failure to load memory should not prevent task execution.

Each memory records how often agents recalled it: recalledCount and lastRecalledAt. Only a recall counts. When an agent's recall_memory call returns memories, each memory it returned gains one count, and its lastRecalledAt becomes the time of the call. Only a recall by the verified worker of an active Task, or through the controller's tool broker, is counted. Memories loaded into a prompt's durable memory section, and memories an operator lists through the API or CLI, are not counted. Neither is a recall whose result is larger than 1 MiB, the most an agent's tool call receives. Counting a recall does not update the memory: updatedAt, and so the order in which memories are listed and loaded into prompts, stay as they were. Counting is best effort: it runs in the background without blocking the recall's response, so it never delays or fails the recall, and when many counts are already running a new one is dropped. Deleted memories are not counted, and a new memory always starts with none, whatever its create request names.

All public endpoints require a ServiceAccount bearer token and are under /api/v1. Endpoint Method Description /api/v1/memories GET List durable memories /api/v1/memories POST Create durable memory /api/v1/memories/:id GET Get durable memory /api/v1/memories/:id PUT Update durable memory /api/v1/memories/:id DELETE Soft-delete durable memory /api/v1/memories/:id/disable POST Disable memory for normal recall /api/v1/memories/:id/enable POST Re-enable memory for normal recall Supported list query parameters: Parameter Description namespace Namespace to query query or q Text search over memory content and tags sessionName Filter by session provenance agentName Filter by agent provenance taskName Filter by task provenance parentTask Filter by parent task provenance source Filter by source such as task, session, user, system, memory_proposal, or e2e tags Comma-separated tags ids Comma-separated memory IDs includeDisabled Include disabled memories when true includeDeleted Include soft-deleted memories when true limit Maximum rows to return Example: TOKEN=$(kubectl create token orka-client -n orka-system) curl -sS http://localhost:8080/api/v1/memories \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -G \ --data-urlencode namespace=orka-system \ --data-urlencode query="release checklist" Create durable memory: curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/memories \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "namespace": "orka-system", "source": "user", "content": "Release tasks should run make lint-fix and make test before merging.", "tags": ["release", "testing"] }' Only applying a proposal links a memory to it, so a create request with a sourceProposalId is rejected with 400 Bad Request.

Endpoint Method Description /api/v1/memory-proposals GET List memory proposals /api/v1/memory-proposals POST Create a memory proposal /api/v1/memory-proposals/:id GET Get a memory proposal /api/v1/memory-proposals/:id/review POST Record a review decision without applying it /api/v1/memory-proposals/:id/apply POST Apply an accepted memory or consolidation proposal to durable memory /api/v1/memory-proposals/:id/archive POST Archive a proposal without applying it Supported list query parameters: Parameter Description namespace Namespace to query taskName Filter by task provenance agentName Filter by agent provenance type Filter by proposal type, for example memory, memory_merge, memory_supersede, memory_retire, skill, policy, or workflow status Filter by status such as pending, accepted, rejected, applied, or archived query or q Text search over title, description, content, and skill name limit Maximum rows to return Create a proposal: curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/memory-proposals \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "namespace": "orka-system", "taskName": "release-review", "agentName": "release-agent", "type": "memory", "title": "Release validation command", "description": "Reusable release procedure discovered during task execution.\nTags: release, testing", "content": "Run make lint-fix and make test before merging release PRs." }' Review a proposal: curl -sS -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/memory-proposals/mprop-example/review?namespace=orka-system" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "status": "accepted", "reviewNote": "Valid reusable release procedure." }' Review returns the stored review record: id, namespace, status, reviewer, reviewNote, and reviewedAt. reviewer is the identity that made the request. Review records governance state only; it does not apply the proposal as durable memory. Apply an accepted memory proposal: curl -sS -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/memory-proposals/mprop-example/apply?namespace=orka-system" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" Apply returns the durable memory as JSON. The created memory has source: "memory_proposal" and sourceProposalId set to the proposal ID, and the proposal is updated to status: "applied" with appliedMemoryId, appliedBy (the identity that made the request), and appliedAt. Repeating the apply request is idempotent and returns the same durable memory. Only accepted proposals with type: "memory" or a consolidation type can be applied; rejected and archived proposals cannot be applied. A consolidation apply returns the memory a merge or supersede created, or a retire's first target, and returns 409 Conflict when a target changed since the proposal was written; see Consolidation proposals.

Store durable memories only for reusable project facts, decisions, conventions, or procedures. Do not store secrets, credentials, tokens, raw transcripts, one-off task status, or sensitive personal data. Memory and proposal persistence passes content through sensitive-text redaction. Disabled and deleted memories are excluded from normal recall by default. Memory writes are namespace-scoped and authenticated through the same ServiceAccount-token API model as other Orka APIs. Applying accepted memory proposals preserves proposal-to-memory linkage for auditability.

Accepted proposals are not automatically converted to durable memories; they require the explicit apply endpoint. Only accepted proposals with type: "memory" or a consolidation type can be applied to durable memory. Durable memory search currently uses store-level filters and substring matching rather than semantic ranking. Transcript search returns snippets, not model-generated summaries. External memory backends are not part of the default implementation.

A coordinator agent splits a job into pieces and hands each piece to a specialist agent. The model decides what to delegate and how to combine the results. The controller decides what is allowed: which Agents the coordinator may delegate to, how deep delegation may go, and how many children run at once. Every delegation is an ordinary child Task, so you can watch, cancel, and audit it like any other Task. The coordinator is a native type: ai Agent. Its children can be native AI Agents, or coding-agent Agents (Codex, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, OpenCode) that run on RuntimePools. Runnable examples code-review/ runs one code-and-review pass and opens a pull request on approval. self-bootstrapping/ creates the specialists it needs before delegating to them.

Task "refactor-auth" (coordinator Agent) depth 0 ├── delegate_task(agent: "backend-dev", ...) → child Task, depth 1 ├── delegate_task(agent: "coder", ...) → child Task, depth 1 │ └── delegate_task(...) → grandchild Task, depth 2 └── wait_for_tasks([...]) → collected results You create a Task whose Agent has coordination.enabled: true. Its AI worker gives the model the coordination tools. Each delegate_task call creates a child Task owned by the parent. The child is type: agent when its Agent has spec.runtime, and type: ai otherwise. The controller checks the child against the guardrails before it runs, and records every child's progress in the parent's status.childTasks. wait_for_tasks blocks until the children finish and returns their results. The coordinator writes the final answer and the parent Task completes. Deleting the parent deletes its children.

Create the specialists first. One native AI Agent and one coding agent: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: backend-dev namespace: orka-system spec: providerRef: name: anthropic systemPrompt: inline: "You are a backend developer specializing in Go and Kubernetes." tools: - name: code_exec - name: file_read --- apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: coder namespace: orka-system spec: model: name: gpt-6-astra runtime: type: codex Then the coordinator. allowedAgents is the list of Agents it may delegate to: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: project-coordinator namespace: orka-system spec: providerRef: name: anthropic systemPrompt: inline: | You are a project coordinator. Break the request into subtasks, delegate each one to the right specialist with delegate_task, wait for the results with wait_for_tasks, and write a final summary. coordination: enabled: true maxDepth: 2 maxConcurrentChildren: 3 allowedAgents: - name: backend-dev - name: coder Start the work with an ordinary Task: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: refactor-auth namespace: orka-system spec: type: ai agentRef: name: project-coordinator prompt: | Refactor the authentication module for better security and testability. Split the work into API changes and tests. timeout: 30m The coding agent needs the provider proxy, like any coding-agent Task. For a long-running goal that needs several rounds of planning, turn on autonomous mode.

orka task children refactor-auth kubectl -n orka-system get tasks -l orka.ai/parent-task=refactor-auth While it runs, the parent's status lists each child with its Agent, phase, and the first 500 characters of its result: status: phase: Running childTasks: - name: refactor-auth-child-xyz1 agent: backend-dev phase: Running - name: refactor-auth-child-xyz2 agent: coder phase: Succeeded result: "Updated 12 files to use the new auth context..." Children carry the labels orka.ai/parent-task and orka.ai/delegated-agent, so you can select them with kubectl -l.

The controller checks every child against its parent's Agent before the child runs: Field Default What happens allowedAgents [] A child for an Agent not on the list fails. With an empty list, the coordinator can delegate only to Agents it created itself with create_agent. maxDepth 3 A child deeper than this fails. The top-level coordinator is depth 0. maxConcurrentChildren 5 A child beyond this limit waits, and starts when a sibling finishes. It does not fail. The AI worker also bounds each run. A native AI Task gets up to 10 rounds of model calls and tool calls; a coordinator gets 50, and an autonomous coordinator 100 per iteration. The full set of coordination fields is in the Agent reference.

Purpose Tools Delegate and collect delegate_task, wait_for_tasks, create_container_task, cancel_task Talk between siblings send_message, check_messages Remember recall_memory, remember, propose_memory, search_transcript Work with GitHub create_pull_request, review_pull_request, post_review_comment, check_pull_request_ci, merge_pull_request, and more Create specialists create_agent, delete_agent Plan (autonomous mode) update_plan Parameters and return values for each are in Built-in tools.

Children of the same coordinator can coordinate directly with send_message and check_messages, for example to share a finding or avoid duplicated work. Messages go through the controller, never Pod to Pod, and only siblings can read them. Send to "*" to broadcast to every sibling. Messages are deleted with the Tasks that own them.
documents.s: Let children talk to each other

documents.t: wait_for_tasks never retries anything. Delegating with auto_retry: true only adds structured failure details, so the coordinator can decide: { "agent": "coder", "prompt": "Implement the feature", "auto_retry": true, "max_retries": 3 } A failed child then reports: { "task": "parent-task-child-abc", "phase": "Failed", "failureDetails": { "message": "out of memory", "retryCount": 0, "maxRetries": 3 } } To retry, the coordinator calls delegate_task again, changing the prompt if it wants to, and tracks its own attempt budget. max_retries defaults to 2 and is information for that decision, not a limit Orka enforces.

When the coordinator's Task carries transaction metadata, its children inherit the same transaction identity, so parent and child work can be audited by one transaction ID. If the worker can exchange tokens, delegate_task and create_container_task also request a narrower child token before creating the child. The worker needs: ORKA_CONTEXT_TOKEN_TTS_ENDPOINT=https://transaction-token-tts.transaction-token-system.svc/oauth/token ORKA_CONTEXT_TOKEN_SUBJECT_TOKEN_FILE=/var/run/orka/transaction-token/token ORKA_CONTEXT_TOKEN_CHILD_SCOPE=orka:agents:run The child scope must already be in the parent's scopes; asking for more fails before the child exists. The child token is stored in a short-lived Secret owned by the child Task and mounted into the child's worker.

A common pattern is a loop between a coding agent and a reviewer until the change is approved, then a pull request. Coding agents never hold Git credentials: the coder edits a clean checkout, and Orka's publisher pushes the validated change to pushBranch and records the result in the child's status.delivery. The reviewer reads that published branch. The pull request tools then act with the coder Task's forgeCredentialRef, or with the requester's linked account; the push credential is never used for the GitHub API. A delegated child can create a branch but cannot update one that already exists: updating a branch needs workspace.expectedRemoteSHA, which delegate_task does not expose. So each revision publishes to a new branch, starting from the previous revision's branch, and the coordinator stops once the pull request exists. Repairs to an open pull request belong to a repository monitor or to a direct repair Task that sets expectedRemoteSHA; the github-cicd example shows both. A coordinator prompt for this loop: You are a coordinator agent. Follow this protocol: 1. DELEGATE implementation to the coder agent with workspace.intent = write, gitRepo, publicationGitRepo, a new pushBranch (for example feature-x-1), and four distinct Secrets: readCredentialRef (clone), publicationReadCredentialRef (verify), publicationCredentialRef (push), and forgeCredentialRef (pull request API). Tell the coder to edit only. 2. WAIT for the coder's result and require a verified delivery receipt. 3. DELEGATE review to the reviewer agent with workspace.intent = read on the PUBLISHED branch: publicationGitRepo (or gitRepo for same-repository publication) at branch = that revision's pushBranch. 4. WAIT for the reviewer's verdict. 5. IF verdict == "CHANGES_NEEDED" AND revision < 3: DELEGATE the fix to the coder agent again (workspace.intent = write) with branch = the previous pushBranch, a NEW pushBranch (feature-x-2, ...), and the reviewer feedback in the prompt. Go to step 2. 6. IF verdict == "APPROVED": Call create_pull_request with the last coder task's name and pushBranch, then call check_pull_request_ci. 7. Report the PR URL, the review result, and the CI status, and stop. Do not delegate further writes to the PR branch. Require a terminal verified delivery receipt before creating a pull request. A model saying it changed or pushed files is not evidence. Write and publication Tasks describe the receipt. For a pull request flow that runs without a coordinator — on every PR, or from an issue label — use repository monitors and issue-to-PR automation instead.

Orka emits OpenTelemetry traces and metrics for controller, chat, tool, native AI worker, Orka harness v2 controller/supervisor, ACP runtime GenAI, and Agent Substrate client paths when telemetry is enabled. ACP runtime internals remain observable primarily through durable Task execution/delivery status, RuntimePool status, bounded events, and structured logs. The GenAI signals are backend instrumentation: they are exported over OTLP to your collector/backend and are separate from the Orka React UI. Telemetry is disabled by default. Disabled mode keeps the hot path on the global OpenTelemetry no-op providers and does not configure OTLP exporters. For retained team usage and tokens per merged PR in the dashboard, see Usage and PR outcomes. That report records counts independently of telemetry and includes measurement gaps.

Start the controller with telemetry enabled and point it at an OTLP endpoint. gRPC is the default exporter protocol: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector.otel.svc:4317 \ orka-controller --enable-telemetry --enable-tracing is kept as a compatible alias and enables the same traces and metrics. Existing Prometheus metrics on --metrics-bind-address continue to work independently. For an existing Kubernetes Deployment, set both the controller flag and the collector environment. Setting OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT alone does not enable telemetry: These commands assume a Helm install named orka That makes the Deployment orka-controller. If you installed with kubectl apply -f .../deploy/orka.yaml it is orka-controller-manager instead. See Troubleshooting. kubectl patch deployment orka-controller -n orka-system --type=json -p='[ {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--enable-telemetry"}, {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-","value":{"name":"OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT","value":"http://otel-collector.otel.svc:4317"}}, {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-","value":{"name":"OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_INSECURE","value":"true"}} ]' Use OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf (or signal-specific OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_PROTOCOL / OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_PROTOCOL) for HTTP/protobuf collectors. Signal-specific endpoints are also supported: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT.
