When controller telemetry is enabled and a worker-reachable OTLP endpoint is configured, AI worker Jobs receive: ORKA_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=true OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT and related standard non-secret OTLP environment variables ORKA_TRACEPARENT when a Task was created from an already-traced API/chat/tool request The controller copies only worker-safe OTLP settings into AI worker Pods: Copied when set Not copied OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT / OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS / OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_HEADERS OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL and signal-specific protocol vars OTLP certificate and client-key env vars OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_INSECURE and signal-specific insecure vars OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT and signal-specific timeout vars ORKA_BAGGAGE OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_COMPRESSION and signal-specific compression vars Worker endpoint values must be reachable from the worker Pod. Empty, loopback, and unspecified hosts such as localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, and :: are not copied into worker Jobs. If a signal-specific endpoint is unreachable, its signal-specific overrides are dropped instead of sending a broken per-signal configuration to the worker. Telemetry environment for AI workers is controller-owned: task-supplied ORKA_ENABLE_TELEMETRY, ORKA_TRACEPARENT, ORKA_TRACESTATE, and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP* values in spec.env are ignored. Generic container Tasks preserve user-supplied telemetry env, because Orka does not instrument arbitrary container processes. Managed ACP RuntimePools are not per-Task Jobs and do not inherit Task.spec.env. The controller emits acp.prompt, acp.session.create, acp.session.continue, and acp.publication.reconcile spans from the Task's trace annotations. It also exports RuntimePool desired/ready replica, resident-session, active-prompt, queued-Task, admission-state, and completed scale-to-zero metrics on the Prometheus metrics endpoint. With controller telemetry enabled and a worker-reachable trace endpoint, managed supervisors receive ORKA_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=true and non-secret OTLP endpoint, protocol, insecure and compression settings for traces and for ACP GenAI metrics. Generic and signal-specific endpoints retain their normal SDK semantics; signal-specific settings take precedence. A missing or invalid trace endpoint disables supervisor export. Metrics-only configuration enables neither supervisor tracing nor supervisor metrics. A metrics-specific endpoint that is not worker-reachable drops supervisor metrics rather than falling back to the generic collector; so does a metrics setting the supervisor would reject. Substrate native runtimes accept 32 environment entries per container and Orka's own settings use most of them, leaving three for supervisor telemetry. Orka therefore passes the fewest settings that keep each signal's SDK meaning: One generic endpoint when it resolves to both signals' URLs, otherwise one signal-specific endpoint per exported signal. A generic OTLP/HTTP base URL becomes the signal URL the SDK would derive from it (/v1/traces or /v1/metrics appended). A protocol, insecure or compression value that both signals share, once, under its generic name. An explicit grpc protocol is the supervisor's default and is not passed. When traces and metrics together would need more than three entries, for example separate OTLP/HTTP collectors per signal, supervisor metrics are dropped and traces are kept. A dropped signal never falls back to a generic endpoint. On a native runtime the three-entry budget does not apply: Orka fits telemetry last, from every configured signal, into the entries its other settings leave. A runtime whose workspace can suspend uses two more, and empty model limits are omitted. When traces and metrics do not fit, metrics are dropped; when traces alone do not fit, supervisor telemetry is left out rather than publishing a workload the provider would reject. With --runtime-telemetry-collector-egress, the gateway allowlist admits only the collectors the fitted runtime exports to. The RuntimePool's TelemetryReady condition is True with reason TelemetryProjected when every signal fits, and False with reason NativeEnvironmentLimit and the entry counts when a signal was left out. Headers, certificate paths, resource attributes and content-capture settings are never copied. Adding metrics settings changes the supervisor Pod template, so existing RuntimePools roll through their normal drained replacement the first time a controller with these settings runs. The v2 mutation client sends W3C traceparent/tracestate HTTP headers outside canonical request bodies and operation capabilities. Authenticated supervisor operations emit acp.supervisor.* spans under the current controller operation, with Task UID/attempt, prompt/operation IDs and runtime pool/session identity. Context is request-local, including for reused sessions. Missing or invalid context starts a separate trace; disabled telemetry does not affect execution. Provider CLI children receive no tracing environment variables or instrumentation. Supervisor spans never capture prompts, completions, raw tool arguments or error text, even if a content-capture environment variable is set. Collector routing is an operator prerequisite. Managed RuntimePool network policies permit DNS, controller API and provider proxy traffic; enabling telemetry does not add collector egress. Under an enforcing CNI, configure a separate, narrowly selected collector route/policy before expecting exports. Pod-level collector access also permits provider children to reach that collector, because they share the Pod network. Choose a collector and authorization boundary accordingly. This feature does not install a collector or alter managed policies. Agent Substrate runtimes have no Pod network policy to extend; they can opt in to an explicit collector egress rule. External supervisors can opt in with the same environment settings. Supervisor exporters require http:// or https:// endpoint URLs and the scalar settings listed above. Unsupported ambient SDK settings (including OTLP headers, certificate paths and resource attributes) disable supervisor telemetry before SDK initialization, so malformed values cannot enter SDK diagnostics. The content-capture flag is ignored. Use an authorized local collector. Export is asynchronous and bounded. Initialization/export failure does not fail a Task, and supervisor shutdown spends at most two additional seconds flushing traces. Unavailable collectors can result in dropped spans. Use these sources of truth for runtime state: Task.status.execution for fenced attempt, RuntimePool, RuntimeSession, prompt, and terminal outcome; Task.status.delivery for workspace validation/publication state and non-secret receipts; RuntimePool.status for lifecycle, admission, exact Pod/boot identity, capacity, and pressure; Task execution events and controller/runtime/publisher structured logs. Do not add credential-bearing OTLP headers to runtime images or provider child environments. The provider child-environment allowlist remains unchanged. Credential-bearing OTLP header environment variables are not copied from the controller into task workloads. Use an in-cluster collector endpoint or a worker-scoped credential mechanism if your collector requires authentication. Kubernetes task workloads require ORKA_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=true; OTLP endpoint variables alone do not enable telemetry. Standard SDK sampling is available through OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG (for example always_off, always_on, or parentbased_traceidratio).

The Prometheus endpoint on --metrics-bind-address exports orka_approval_decision_duration_seconds, independently of OpenTelemetry enablement. It measures seconds between the stored approval request timestamp and the first committed terminal decision timestamp. Buckets cover one second through one day, with longer waits included in the +Inf bucket. The only labels are: Label Values outcome approved, denied, cancelled, expired path acp for broker-owned approvals with a call binding; worker for built-in AI worker approvals Human approvals and declines record approved and denied. ACP wait/deadline expiry records expired; Task cancellation or loss of the original tool/prompt authority records cancelled. Recovery records a sample when it commits a missing terminal decision from a verified execution receipt. Revocation after a human decision preserves that original decision and adds no second sample. Polling, receipt replay, rejected decisions and rolled-back writes add no samples. Worker approvals currently have human decisions only: passive timeout metadata, Task termination and cancellation do not create worker terminal approval events. This metric does not introduce worker expiry or agent parking. A pending approval whose expiry is derived for display is counted only when a terminal event commits. Missing or backwards timestamps are omitted. Labels contain no Task names, approval IDs, users or request text. Histograms are in memory and reset on process restart. Existing terminal events are not replayed into the histogram. A crash between committing a decision and observing it, or between scrapes, can lose a sample; use durable approval events for audits. Pending requests retained across a restart still use their original request timestamps when a new decision commits.

A delegated Task should appear as one distributed trace: task.run └─ agent.step / chat.tool_loop.iteration ├─ chat {model} ├─ execute_tool {tool.name} └─ execute_tool delegate_task └─ child task.run └─ child agent.step / chat.tool_loop.iteration ├─ chat {model} └─ execute_tool {tool.name} An Orka harness v2 Task continues the same Task-carried trace across controller and supervisor: <Task-carried parent span> ├─ acp.session.create / acp.session.continue │ └─ acp.supervisor.session.create # when a runtime session is created ├─ acp.prompt │ ├─ substrate.router POST # Substrate-routed runtimes only │ ├─ acp.supervisor.prompt │ │ └─ invoke_agent {runtime} │ │ ├─ chat {model} # one per model call through the provider proxy │ │ └─ execute_tool {tool} # one per ACP tool call │ └─ acp.publication.reconcile # live write-workspace delivery └─ acp.publication.reconcile # recovery after the prompt span is gone For Substrate-routed runtimes, substrate.router carries the Task trace into atenet-router, so Substrate's routing spans, including a resume the router triggers for a suspended Actor, join the Task trace when Substrate exports traces. See Agent Substrate. Model client spans measure provider-call latency only. Tool spans are siblings of the model client span under the same agent/chat step, not children of the model client span. Task creation stamps the current W3C trace context into Task annotations. The controller extracts that context for task.reconcile and controller-side ACP spans. Supported native worker Tasks also receive ORKA_TRACEPARENT in their Jobs. Orka harness v2 runtime requests carry traceparent and tracestate headers to authenticated supervisor operations; provider CLI children remain outside this instrumentation. Delegation stamps the active execute_tool delegate_task span context onto the child Task so child controller, supervisor and native-worker spans remain linked. Outbound HTTP and MCP Tool CRD requests receive W3C traceparent headers. If a Tool config supplies its own traceparent header, the active Orka trace context wins.

Tracer Span Attributes orka.api HTTP/API middleware spans HTTP request/route/status metadata orka.chat chat.request, chat.tool_loop.iteration session metadata; chat.iteration, orka.tenant, requested model, tool-call count orka.worker task.run orka.task.id, namespace, and agent name when known orka.acp acp.prompt, acp.session.create, acp.session.continue, acp.publication.reconcile orka.task.id, namespace, attempt/prompt identity, RuntimePool/RuntimeSession identity, prompt/session outcome, publication identity, and agent name when known orka.acp.supervisor acp.supervisor.* authenticated runtime operations Task UID/attempt, prompt/operation IDs and runtime pool/session identity; no request content orka.gen_ai (ACP supervisor) invoke_agent {runtime}, chat {model}, execute_tool {tool} gen_ai.* agent/provider/model/usage/tool metadata, orka.task.uid, orka.acp.prompt.id; see GenAI telemetry for ACP runtimes orka.substrate substrate.router {method} Router method, authority and response status only go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/.../otelgrpc substrate.ateapi.v1.Control/{Method} client spans gRPC method and status; no metadata or message events orka.agent agent.step iteration, requested model/provider, tool-call count, Orka task metadata orka.gen_ai chat {model} gen_ai.* provider/model/token metadata and error.type orka.gen_ai execute_tool {tool.name} gen_ai.tool.*, orka.tool.name, orka.tool.kind, orka.tool.result.size_bytes, parent/child task fields for delegation orka.controller task.reconcile task name, namespace, type, and propagated trace context Use orka.task.id to find a Task trace, orka.tool.name to find specific tool executions, and orka.parent_task.id / orka.child_task.id to follow delegated children. Tool spans do not include raw arguments, result bodies or error messages.

OpenTelemetry traces are exported to your collector/backend and are queried in that backend. Orka's Task trace API (GET /api/v1/tasks/:id/trace) and CLI (orka task trace) are different: they build an execution read model from stored Orka events for UI/CLI troubleshooting. The two systems share task and tool terminology, but the Task trace API does not read from the OTel backend.
documents.s: OpenTelemetry traces vs Task trace read model

documents.t: Orka emits low-cardinality, content-safe attributes alongside GenAI attributes: Attribute Meaning orka.task.id Task name orka.task.namespace Kubernetes namespace orka.tenant Tenant; currently the namespace fallback orka.agent.name Agent name/runtime when known orka.parent_task.id Parent Task name on delegation spans orka.child_task.id Child Task name after creation orka.tool.name Tool name orka.tool.kind builtin, delegate, or http orka.tool.result.size_bytes Tool result size only; never the body Useful backend queries: Find a Task trace: filter spans by orka.task.id = "<task-name>". Find tool calls: filter by orka.tool.name = "delegate_task" or another tool name. Locate child work: filter by orka.parent_task.id or orka.child_task.id. Split built-in vs external tools: group by orka.tool.kind.

Model calls are emitted as client spans named: chat {model} Key attributes include: Attribute Meaning gen_ai.operation.name=chat GenAI operation gen_ai.provider.name Concrete serving provider, for example anthropic, openai, or azure.ai.openai gen_ai.request.model Requested model gen_ai.request.max_tokens / gen_ai.request.temperature Request settings when present gen_ai.output.type Requested output format when present gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / gen_ai.usage.output_tokens Token usage gen_ai.response.model / gen_ai.response.finish_reasons / gen_ai.response.id Response metadata when available error.type Provider status code or Go error type on failed calls Tool calls executed through the built-in registry are emitted as spans named execute_tool {tool.name} with gen_ai.tool.* and orka.tool.* attributes and a duration metric. External HTTP/MCP tools use the same span name and orka.tool.kind=http. OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible API requests emit the same GenAI model-call spans as native Orka chat and AI worker calls.

Built-in ACP runtimes (codex, claude, copilot, opencode) run provider CLIs that Orka does not instrument. The supervisor derives GenAI spans and metrics from what it already observes: the ACP session update stream and the supervisor's provider proxy, which every model call passes through. Telemetry needs the supervisor trace endpoint described above; metrics also need a metrics endpoint (OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT or the generic endpoint). Span Kind Derived from Key attributes invoke_agent {runtime} client One authenticated prompt, from admission to settlement gen_ai.agent.name (runtime), gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.conversation.id (RuntimeSession ID), gen_ai.response.finish_reasons (ACP stop reason), gen_ai.usage.* when the agent reports ACP turn usage, orka.task.uid, orka.acp.prompt.id, error.type chat {model} client One admitted inference request relayed by the provider proxy gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, error.type (upstream HTTP status, cancelled, or _OTHER) execute_tool {tool} internal ACP tool_call / tool_call_update until completed or failed gen_ai.tool.name, gen_ai.tool.call.id (canonical ACP call ID), gen_ai.tool.type, orka.tool.name, orka.acp.tool.kind, error.type (tool_error, incomplete, cancelled) invoke_agent is a child of acp.supervisor.prompt; chat and execute_tool are its children, so model calls and tool calls appear as siblings, as they do for native workers. Spans are written when their outcome is known, with the observed start time. gen_ai.provider.name names the model API the runtime speaks through the proxy: anthropic for Claude and openai for Codex, Copilot and OpenCode. OpenCode pins provider/model but always speaks OpenAI chat completions, so its prefix does not change the label and gen_ai.request.model is the model part. With a gateway such as Vekil in front, that is the wire API, not the gateway's upstream. Tool names come only from the adapter's structured tool identity when it is a plain identifier (letters, digits, _ . : / -, up to 128 characters); otherwise the span uses the closed ACP tool kind (read, edit, execute, ...) or other. Tool titles are free text and never become names. A tool call still open when its prompt settles is recorded with error.type=incomplete, or cancelled for cancelled prompts. Per-call token counts are not available: provider responses stream through the proxy unparsed. Token usage is recorded once per prompt on invoke_agent and in gen_ai.client.token.usage with gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_agent, and only when the ACP agent includes usage in its session/prompt response. A malformed usage report is ignored and never fails a prompt. ACP runtime metrics: Metric Unit Datapoints gen_ai.client.operation.duration s One per chat model call (gen_ai.operation.name=chat) gen_ai.client.token.usage {token} Input and output tokens per prompt, when reported (gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_agent) gen_ai.execute_tool.duration s One per ACP tool call gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration s One per prompt Metric attributes are limited to operation, agent/runtime name, provider, model, token type, tool name/type and error.type. Task, prompt and session identities stay on spans. Supervisor metrics use the supervisor's fixed service.name resource (orka-acp-supervisor), like its spans, plus a service.instance.id: a random UUID drawn each time a supervisor starts. It keeps supervisors that report the same runtime and model as separate series, names no Task, user or Pod, and changes on every supervisor restart, so aggregate across it for fleet-wide totals. Content capture stays off for ACP runtimes. The supervisor never records prompts, completions, tool titles, tool arguments, tool results, or provider error bodies in span attributes, events or metrics, and ignores OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT.

Agent Substrate v1 Actors have no direct network egress: the egress gateway refuses any destination the runtime's allowlist does not name. By default core's allowlist names only the provider proxy and controller API origins, so a supervisor configured to export OTLP cannot reach the collector. Opt in explicitly: orka-controller --enable-telemetry --runtime-telemetry-collector-egress # or ORKA_RUNTIME_TELEMETRY_COLLECTOR_EGRESS=true When both are set, core adds the origin of each OTLP endpoint it projects into the supervisor (the trace endpoint, and the metrics endpoint when it differs) to the allowlist of every new Substrate runtime workload request: http:// endpoints become HTTP rules, which admit cleartext HTTP/1.1 and h2c, so both OTLP/HTTP and insecure OTLP/gRPC work. https:// endpoints become TLSPassthrough rules, so the supervisor verifies the collector's own certificate. The rule names exactly the endpoint host and port (default 80/443). Validation fails closed. The controller refuses to start, and admission reports the pool Degraded, when an endpoint is not an absolute http(s) URL, names an IP address, a single-label or wildcard host, or conflicts with a core origin on the same host and port. Native runtimes cannot resolve a short <service>.<namespace>.svc Service name, so admission also reports the pool Degraded for one. Use a fully qualified in-cluster name such as http://otel-collector.otel.svc.cluster.local:4317, substituting your cluster domain if it is not cluster.local. Scheme-less gRPC targets (collector:4317) are rejected because their transport cannot be determined. The flag does not change Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for Pod-backed runtimes, and it is fixed per workload request: a running workload keeps its admitted allowlist until its next request. The collector sees connections from the Substrate egress gateway, not the Actor, so collector-side k8sattributes enrichment labels supervisor telemetry with the gateway Pod; rely on the supervisor's service.name and the Orka span attributes instead. Every process in the Actor, including provider CLIs, can reach the allowlisted collector, so treat its OTLP ports as reachable by agent code. MCP Tool Actors keep their explicit spec.mcp.substrateActor.egress and are not changed by this flag.
documents.s: Collector egress for Agent Substrate runtimes

documents.t: With --enable-telemetry, Orka's Agent Substrate clients propagate W3C trace context (traceparent/tracestate, never baggage) and record client spans for calls made inside an existing trace. Calls outside a trace pass through unchanged, so background reconciles do not start one trace per Substrate call. Router (HTTPS): each traced request through atenet-router records a substrate.router {method} client span (time to response headers) and carries its context to the routed runtime or MCP Actor. This covers ACP harness v2 calls to Substrate-routed supervisors (under the Task's acp.* spans) and MCP Tool calls proxied by orka-api (under the worker's execute_tool span). Control API (gRPC): substrate.ateapi.v1.Control calls record an otelgrpc client span and carry the active trace, which ateapi extracts for its lifecycle spans and the atelet/ateworker spans beneath them. In core these calls come from the MCP Tool, SubstrateActorPool and template-validation reconcilers, which do not start traces today, so they produce spans only when invoked from a traced context. ACP execution workspace lifecycle operations (Actor resume, suspend, delete and checkpoint) are performed by the separately deployed orka-workspace provider, not by core. Core's instrumentation does not cover those calls; correlate them by time, Actor and template as described below. Substrate samples with parent-based samplers, so a sampled Orka trace is sampled end to end; its default ratios (10% control plane, 1% router) only apply to requests Orka does not trace. Client spans contain no request paths, queries, headers, gRPC metadata, bearer tokens or message bodies; a failed gRPC call's span status carries Substrate's status message. Disabled telemetry adds no instrumentation.

Substrate exports these instruments over OTLP from its own components (see the upstream Agent Substrate observability guide and metric registry for all labels). They explain latency and failures that surface in Orka as slow or Degraded RuntimePools, slow cold resumes, or failed MCP Tool calls: Substrate metric What it tells an Orka operator ate.actor.lifecycle.operation.duration (ateapi) Duration and failure (error.type) of Actor create/resume/suspend/delete. Resume with error.type=ResourceExhausted means no worker capacity, the usual cause of a workspace that cannot start or resume. Already-running resumes are excluded. ate.scheduler.assignment.duration (ateapi) Worker assignment outcome (assigned, no_capacity, error) per pool and sandbox class. ate.actor.restore.duration / ate.actor.checkpoint.duration (atelet) Per-phase cold-resume and checkpoint latency, by snapshot kind/fidelity and template. Orka's data-only suspension uses volume-fidelity snapshots. atelet.snapshot.upload.duration, atelet.snapshot.undurable.age.max, atelet.snapshot.upload.overdue.actors (atelet) Whether suspended workspace data has reached durable storage; a growing undurable age puts later cold resumes at risk. ate.workerpool.desired_workers / ate.workerpool.ready_workers / ate.workerpool.workers (atecontroller, ateapi) Capacity of the private single-replica WorkerPools the provider creates per allocation. atenet.router.route.duration (atenet-router) Router outcome and whether a request woke a suspended Actor (ate.router.resume); covers Orka's routed supervisor and MCP Tool calls. ate.actor.crashes (ateapi) Actors that crashed, for example a supervisor that exited. rpc.server.call.duration (all gRPC servers) Per-method availability and latency of the control API Orka calls. Substrate's SLO guide suggests alerting on resume capacity (the ResourceExhausted share of ate.actor.lifecycle.operation.duration resumes, with multi-window burn-rate alerts), on ateapi RPC availability (5xx-equivalent gRPC codes from rpc.server.call.duration), and on WorkerPools whose ate.workerpool.workers stays below ate.workerpool.desired_workers. Its example Prometheus rules (docs/examples/gmp-alerting-rules.yaml) implement these as AteResumeActorCapacityBurnPage/Ticket, AteApiRpcErrorBudgetBurnPage/Ticket and SubstrateWorkerPoolCapacityNotDelivered. For Orka, pair them with the RuntimePool metrics on the controller's Prometheus endpoint: rising ResourceExhausted resumes alongside Orka queued Tasks or a closed RuntimePool admission state indicates Substrate capacity, not Orka, is the bottleneck.
documents.s: Substrate metrics relevant to Orka operators

documents.t: Find the Task trace by orka.task.id (controller) or orka.task.uid (supervisor and GenAI spans). Under acp.prompt (or a worker's execute_tool for MCP Tools), open the substrate.router client span. Substrate's router spans beneath it show routing time and any resume of a suspended Actor before the supervisor's acp.supervisor.* spans continue the trace. Substrate component logs and Actor lifecycle records carry top-level trace_id/span_id, so the same trace ID finds router-driven resume log lines in your log backend. Substrate metrics carry template and pool labels, not Task identity. Use the time window and the workspace's Actor, template and pool (from the ExecutionWorkspace and provider status) to slice ate.actor.lifecycle.operation.duration, ate.actor.restore.duration and atenet.router.route.duration, including provider-driven resume, suspend and checkpoint operations that are not in the Task trace. Substrate components export to their own configured collector (ate-otel-config); point both installations at the same backend to see one trace. Spans are only joined when both sides sample the trace.

Orka records these OTLP histograms when model/tool calls run: Metric Unit Notes gen_ai.client.operation.duration s One datapoint per model call gen_ai.client.token.usage {token} Separate datapoints for gen_ai.token.type=input and output gen_ai.client.operation.time_to_first_chunk s Streaming calls gen_ai.execute_tool.duration s Built-in registry and external HTTP/MCP tool calls Metric dimensions are intentionally low-cardinality: operation, provider, model, token type, tool name/type, and error type when applicable. High-cardinality fields such as task IDs and result sizes stay on spans, not metric labels.

A development collector can export traces to Jaeger or Tempo. Example collector pipeline: receivers: otlp: protocols: grpc: endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317 exporters: otlp/tempo: endpoint: tempo.observability.svc:4317 tls: insecure: true service: pipelines: traces: receivers: [otlp] exporters: [otlp/tempo] For local Jaeger all-in-one, expose its OTLP gRPC endpoint and set: kubectl -n orka-system set env deployment/orka-controller \ OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://jaeger-collector.observability.svc:4317

Prompt/completion content capture is fail-closed and defaults to none. The current rollout emits metadata, token counts, model/provider identity, tool names, result sizes, and durations, but not raw prompt or completion text. Telemetry must not include: raw prompts or completion content, raw tool arguments or tool result bodies, API keys, auth headers, TxTokens, context tokens, JWTs, cookies, or credentials, raw transcripts or broad local filesystem paths, error message text. A failed span records only an error class, such as a provider status code, a Go error type or a fixed Orka outcome name, in its status description and error.type attribute. Where a failed span also has an exception event, the event carries the same class and no message or stack trace. Orka's tracer providers do not record panics on spans, because the SDK would store the panic value as the exception message. A stop reason that is neither known to Orka nor a documented provider value is reported as unknown_stop_reason. A failed tool result whose errorType is outside Orka's tool error types is reported as tool_error; a Go error returned by a tool is reported by its error class. Future opt-in content capture must pass through Orka redaction and size caps before any span attribute or event is emitted.

Orka serves /openai/v1/chat/completions, stateless /openai/v1/responses, and /openai/v1/models, so clients like Codex, OpenCode and more can point at Orka instead of at a model vendor. Your cluster holds the API keys; the client holds a ServiceAccount token. For teams using separate namespaces, the optional shared compatibility router selects the installation from the validated ServiceAccount token. Clients use one base URL and omit the namespace parameter. Direct installation endpoints keep their existing namespace rules. This is not a transparent proxy by default Orka rewrites your request before sending it upstream: it discards the tools your client sent, injects its own, and prepends its own system prompt. Read Coordinator mode before wiring up a client that relies on its own tools. One header turns it off. Endpoints moved These used to live at /v1/. They are now at /openai/v1/. See Anthropic compatibility for the Anthropic-native equivalent. Video demo Watch Two teams, one AI endpoint.

Method Path Description POST /openai/v1/chat/completions Chat completions (streaming & non-streaming) POST /openai/v1/responses Stateless Responses (streaming & non-streaming) GET /openai/v1/models List available models from configured providers All endpoints require authentication. Send a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token in Authorization: Bearer <token>. OIDC tokens use the same header when OIDC is configured. When transaction-token authentication is configured, send TxTokens in Txn-Token: <token> by default. To accept TxTokens as Bearer tokens, the operator must explicitly include Authorization:Bearer in --context-token-headers, for example --context-token-headers=Txn-Token,Authorization:Bearer. See Authentication.

POST /openai/v1/responses requires store:false on every request. Orka forwards it to upstream OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions requests, including API-mode probes and coordinator tool rounds. Response IDs are transient labels; Orka does not save Responses objects or conversation history. curl https://orka.example.com/openai/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ORKA_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Orka-Tools: disabled" \ -d '{"model":"openai/gpt-4.1","store":false,"input":"Hello!","stream":true}' Provider refusal items are not supported in this first version. They return HTTP 422 with error code unsupported_provider_outcome, or a streaming error event with that code followed by response.failed. The nested response error retains the schema-defined server_error code and an explicit unsupported-refusal message; upstream refusal details are not forwarded. The first version supports: String input, text message arrays, instructions, and system/developer messages. function tools and function_call / function_call_output history. In client tool mode, append the returned output items and a result with the same call_id to your next request's input. Include the preceding history on every request. Responses upstreams receive text and function items in their supplied order. Native Responses output retains message boundaries and text/function order, including SSE calls that finish out of order. Missing stream indices are recovered from known item IDs; ambiguous or contradictory ordering metadata fails explicitly. Entirely unindexed text-only streams remain supported. Coordinator continuation keeps those items together as one turn for context truncation. Chat Completions fallback represents consecutive assistant items as one turn, combining their text and function calls in that API's format. text.format with text, json_object, or json_schema (including schema name and strictness). Structured output requires an OpenAI-compatible upstream; Anthropic structured output returns an explicit error in this version. temperature, positive max_output_tokens, tool_choice:"auto", and the default allowance for multiple function calls. Responses SSE events: creation/progress, output items, text and function argument deltas, item completion, and response completion. Token-budget truncation returns response.incomplete, including an empty output when no text was produced; provider failures emit error and response.failed. For SSE, detected disconnects and the configured duration limit cancel provider and tool work. A client that stops reading is disconnected after the duration limit plus a one-second grace period for terminal events. Non-streaming JSON requests have the same duration limit, but disconnects are not detected while the handler is waiting for provider or tool work; that work may continue until completion or the duration limit. Anthropic-backed Responses streams buffer each model turn until its terminal outcome is known, so refusal text is never forwarded as ordinary text deltas. Creation/progress events and keep-alives still stream while the model runs. A lost response does not prove that coordinator tools did not run. Requests are not deduplicated, including when a client sends Idempotency-Key. Retrying after a disconnect, timeout, or controller crash can repeat tool side effects. Check the resulting state before retrying a coordinator request, or use X-Orka-Tools: disabled and deduplicate tool execution in the client. Coordinator mode is the default here too. Orka replaces client tools and executes its own tools on the server. Streaming emits text progress between coordinator rounds; function arguments are emitted as complete deltas once the upstream provider has assembled a call. Internal coordinator calls are not returned as client-executable function items. Use X-Orka-Tools: disabled for client tools. Unsupported fields and inputs produce HTTP 400 errors. These include missing or true store, previous_response_id (even null), conversation (even null), background execution, saved item references, reasoning items/options, non-empty include, OpenAI-hosted tools, images/audio, non-auto tool_choice, and parallel_tool_calls:false. Retrieval, deletion, and saved-conversation APIs are not implemented. A base URL change alone does not configure a compatible client.

The executable interoperability fixture pins agent-framework-core==1.18.0, agent-framework-openai==1.14.3, and openai==3.14.0. Its OpenAIChatClient uses Responses. Set store=False; set the disabled header for client-managed tools. This pinned client also automatically requests encrypted reasoning, so use its public SDK extra_body option to send include:[]: import os from agent_framework import Agent from agent_framework.openai import OpenAIChatClient client = OpenAIChatClient( model="openai/gpt-4.1", base_url="https://orka.example.com/openai/v1", api_key=os.environ["ORKA_TOKEN"], default_headers={"X-Orka-Tools": "disabled"}, ) agent = Agent( client=client, default_options={"store": False, "extra_body": {"include": []}}, ) session = agent.create_session() # The client owns and resends history. first = await agent.run("Hello!", session=session) followup = await agent.run("Summarize our exchange.", session=session) Omit the disabled header for coordinator mode. Run the deterministic test from a checkout to exercise the real client against Orka's production server routes and JWT authentication, including an actual tool and follow-up in both modes, with and without streaming: python3 -m venv bin/responses-client bin/responses-client/bin/pip install -r scripts/fixtures/agent-framework-responses/requirements.txt make ensure-ui-embed ORKA_RESPONSES_INTEROP_PYTHON="$PWD/bin/responses-client/bin/python" \ go test ./internal/api -run 'TestAgentFrameworkResponsesInterop|TestResponsesPinnedSDKSchema' -count=1 -timeout=120s -v This CPU fixture uses local HTTP servers and ephemeral OIDC credentials. Model output and Kubernetes object storage are fixtures; it does not test live model inference or a deployed controller. These Python checks are opt-in and are skipped by ordinary Go test runs unless the environment variable above is set. The executable client lives in scripts/fixtures/agent-framework-responses/client.py. It verifies client tool execution, coordinator tool execution, and client-owned follow-up history; it does not establish behavior of a particular hosted model.

The model field supports two formats: provider/model — e.g., anthropic/claude-opus-5. The part before / matches a Provider CRD name, and the part after is the model name sent to that provider. model — e.g., claude-opus-5. Uses the default provider (from --chat-provider flag or a Provider CRD named default).

Provider CRD configured in the cluster: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Provider metadata: name: anthropic namespace: orka-system spec: type: anthropic secretRef: name: anthropic-secret key: api-key defaultModel: claude-opus-5 Secret with the API key: apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: anthropic-secret namespace: orka-system type: Opaque stringData: api-key: sk-ant-...

If you use Azure OpenAI, configure a Provider with type: azure-openai: apiVersion: core.orka.ai/v1alpha1 kind: Provider metadata: name: azure-openai namespace: orka-system spec: type: azure-openai secretRef: name: azure-openai-secret key: api-key baseURL: https://<resource>.openai.azure.com defaultModel: gpt-4o-deployment azure: deploymentName: gpt-4o-deployment apiVersion: "2024-02-15-preview" ServiceAccount token and RBAC for authentication and coordinator tools: Follow the API-client setup to configure orka-client and its Task permissions. Coordinator Task creation requires tasks/create. Agent creation currently does not check a ServiceAccount caller's agents/create permission; see the API authorization limitation. Then create a token: export ORKA_TOKEN="$(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)"

Configure Continue to use Orka as an OpenAI-compatible provider. Add to your Continue configuration: { "models": [ { "title": "Claude Opus 5 (via Orka)", "provider": "openai", "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-5", "apiBase": "https://orka.example.com/openai/v1", "apiKey": "YOUR_ORKA_TOKEN" } ] }
Set your Orka API token: export ORKA_TOKEN=$(kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client)

curl -X POST https://orka.example.com/openai/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ORKA_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-5", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 1024 }'
curl https://orka.example.com/openai/v1/models \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ORKA_TOKEN"

Feature Supported Chat completions Yes Streaming (SSE) Yes Tool/function calling Server-side only by default — see Coordinator mode System messages Yes, but Orka's own prompt is prepended in coordinator mode Multi-part content Yes (text parts extracted) max_tokens / max_completion_tokens Yes temperature Yes stop sequences Yes stream_options.include_usage Yes Image inputs Not yet (text extracted from multi-part) Embeddings Not supported Audio / Vision Not supported

Both compatibility endpoints — this one and Anthropic — default to coordinator mode. The idea is that your editor's chat window becomes a way to drive the cluster: ask for a change, and the model creates Agents and Tasks, waits for them, and opens a pull request. It is not a pass-through proxy. Concretely, Orka does five things to every request before it reaches the model: # What happens Consequence for you 1 Your tools array is discarded. Not merged — replaced. Your client's own tools never run. 2 19 built-in Orka tools are injected. The model can act on your cluster with the tools listed below. 3 The tool list is filtered against your context token's allowed tools, if you use transaction tokens. Denied tools disappear rather than failing at call time. 4 A large Orka system prompt is prepended to yours. Your system prompt still applies, but it is no longer first. 5 Tool history is stripped from your messages. role: tool messages are dropped; assistant messages keep their text but lose their tool calls; consecutive same-role messages are merged. Sending back a conversation that contains client-side tool use loses that structure. Orka then runs the tool loop itself and returns the final answer. The 19 injected tools: Group Tools Built-in web_search, web_fetch, code_exec, file_read, file_write Create work create_agent, create_agent_task, create_ai_task, create_container_task, create_pr_monitor Track work check_task_progress, fetch_task_output, wait_for_task, cancel_task, list_agents, list_tasks, list_connections Pull requests create_pull_request, check_pull_request_ci Orka advertises only the tools listed above that are registered for server-side execution. Custom Kubernetes Tool resources are not advertised or executed by either compatibility endpoint. A custom Tool with a built-in name cannot replace or duplicate its definition.

X-Orka-Tools: disabled This header disables the coordinator rewrite and Orka's tool loop. Your client's tool definitions pass through unchanged, and your client manages its own tool execution. Requests still pass through Orka's OpenAI request conversion; for example, top_p, frequency_penalty, and presence_penalty are not forwarded to the provider. Provider resolution and credential handling are unchanged. Use disabled when you want Orka only for centralized credentials and model routing. Leave it on when you want the model to be able to do things in the cluster.

┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ │ Continue │────▶│ Orka API server │────▶│ Anthropic API │ │ (or any │◀────│ /openai/v1/chat/completions │◀────│ OpenAI API │ │ OAI client) │ │ │ │ Azure OpenAI │ └─────────────┘ │ 1. Resolve Provider CRD │ └───────────────┘ │ 2. Read API key from Secret │ │ 3. Coordinator rewrite │ │ (unless X-Orka-Tools: │ │ disabled) │ │ 4. Server-side tool loop │ └─────────────────────────────┘

max_tokens caps the model's entire output for a turn, and for reasoning models that budget is shared with hidden reasoning tokens. Two shapes come back when the budget runs out: Partial text — the response was cut off mid-answer. Orka returns the partial text with finish_reason: "length", matching upstream behavior; raise the budget and retry. Nothing usable — the model spent the whole budget before emitting any text (common when a reasoning model gets a small max_tokens), or the cutoff truncated a tool call, whose arguments would be unsafe to execute. Orka fails the request with an error describing an incomplete completion outcome instead of returning an empty or corrupt message. If you see the incomplete-outcome error, it is not a proxy fault: give the request a substantially larger max_tokens (reasoning models often need thousands of tokens of headroom), or use a non-reasoning model for short completions.

An AgentHost runs one long-lived agent host for one user: a daemon that serves the Agent Host Protocol (AHP) to clients such as the GitHub Copilot desktop app. Sessions, tools, approvals and worktrees stay inside the host; the client is a UI. Orka admits the host, runs it from an operator's AgentHostTemplate, restarts it, suspends and wakes it, and cleans it up. The design is ADR 0035. Each host is one Pod, a PersistentVolumeClaim for its state, a NetworkPolicy and Secrets in a dedicated host namespace. Orka does not see the host's turns; it governs who may run a host, what it runs, what it may reach and the policy pinned in its template. One trusted user per host The sample host, copilotd, serves exactly one GitHub user per process. The host's agent holds the user's GitHub token, and every process in the Pod runs as one uid, so code the agent runs can read it. Egress to public TCP 443 is open. Run hosts only for code the user trusts; "public repositories only" is not a sandbox boundary.

With Helm, set: controller: image: digest: sha256:<controller image digest> agentHosts: enabled: true namespace: orka-agent-hosts The chart creates the host namespace with the restricted Pod Security profile, the controller's Role in it, the controller flags and the AgentHost admission webhook. The orka-host-agent sidecar comes from the controller image, so pin it by digest, or set controller.agentHosts.agentImage to another digest-pinned image that carries it. Agent hosts need controller.mode: harness-v2, and the host namespace must differ from the release namespace and controller.acpRuntime.namespace. Before you disable agent hosts, uninstall, or roll back to a release without them, delete every AgentHost and wait until it is gone. Without agent hosts the controller stops reconciling them, so their Pods keep running and their deletion never finishes; an upgrade that disables agent hosts is refused while AgentHosts remain. Helm keeps the host namespace, with the hosts' volumes and the controller's Role in it, so a controller with agent hosts on can still finish cleaning up, including hosts left in an earlier namespace after controller.agentHosts.namespace changes. Delete the namespace yourself once no AgentHost needs it. With the Kustomize install: Create the host namespace and the controller's Role in it. The Kustomize install binds the controller's manager role per namespace: kubectl apply -k config/agent-hosts Start the controller with: --enable-agent-hosts --agent-host-namespace=orka-agent-hosts --agent-host-agent-image=<controller image>@sha256:<digest> The agent image is normally the controller image itself; it carries the orka-host-agent sidecar. --agent-host-controller-pod-labels selects the controller Pods allowed to read host status through each host's NetworkPolicy; its default, orka.ai/network-role=controller, matches the shipped controller Pods. With either install, create an AgentHostTemplate (see config/samples/core_v1alpha1_agenthosttemplate.yaml) and grant use on it to the people who may run hosts. Write the Role as a manifest: kubectl create role refuses use because the API does not list that verb. AgentHosts, their templates and their token Secrets live in the namespace Orka watches (--watch-namespace), because the controller reconciles AgentHosts only there. Everyone's hosts therefore share that namespace, and whoever may update an AgentHost controls it: they can suspend or delete it, and deleting it deletes its volume. They can also point it at a token Secret they can read, which restarts it on its volume as them. So give everyone one shared Role to create hosts, and each person a Role that names only their own host and token Secret: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: agent-host-creator rules: - apiGroups: ["core.orka.ai"] resources: ["agenthosttemplates"] resourceNames: ["copilotd"] verbs: ["use"] - apiGroups: ["core.orka.ai"] resources: ["agenthosts"] verbs: ["create"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: agent-host-alice rules: - apiGroups: ["core.orka.ai"] resources: ["agenthosts"] resourceNames: ["alice"] verbs: ["get", "update", "patch", "delete"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["secrets"] resourceNames: ["alice-github-token"] verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"] create cannot be limited by name, so agree on host names before hosts are created, and let an operator create each person's token Secret, or grant create on Secrets only where that is acceptable in the watch namespace. The shared Role grants no list or watch, which would show everyone's hosts; kubectl get agenthost alice and kubectl apply need only get on the named host. Creating an AgentHost requires use on its template, and naming a token Secret requires get on that Secret, both checked against the caller by an admission policy.

The sample template runs copilotd in relay mode: it registers the host as an environment on the user's GitHub account and accepts clients through GitHub's relay. The cluster needs no inbound path. In the namespace Orka watches: kubectl create secret generic alice-github-token --from-literal=token=<GitHub token> kubectl apply -f config/samples/core_v1alpha1_agenthost.yaml kubectl get agenthost alice When the host is Ready, the environment orka-alice appears in the client's Environments list. The token's owner is the only GitHub user the host serves. Orka copies the token into the host namespace and keeps the copy current, so rotating the Secret reaches the running host without a restart. Pointing the host at another Secret or key replaces its Pod on the same volume, because the daemon reads its identity from the token when it starts.

A template with access: Standalone skips the relay. access changes only what Orka publishes, not the daemon's arguments, so the template must also start the daemon in its standalone mode: for copilotd, --standalone instead of --relay and the Mission Control token options. The client port-forwards to the host's loopback listener and presents the host's connection token, which Orka writes to the Secret named in status.connectionSecretRef: ns=$(kubectl get secret alice-connection -o jsonpath='{.data.namespace}' | base64 -d) pod=$(kubectl get secret alice-connection -o jsonpath='{.data.pod}' | base64 -d) port=$(kubectl get secret alice-connection -o jsonpath='{.data.port}' | base64 -d) kubectl -n "$ns" port-forward "pod/$pod" "8788:$port" Add the host as ws://127.0.0.1:8788/?tkn=<token>. The per-user Role above does not cover these commands. Add the connection Secret, here alice-connection, to its Secret rule, and grant get on the host's Pod and create on its pods/portforward in the host namespace. The Pod keeps its name for the host's life, so grant them once the host exists, using the pod value above: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: agent-host-alice-standalone namespace: orka-agent-hosts rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] resourceNames: ["<pod>"] verbs: ["get"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods/portforward"] resourceNames: ["<pod>"] verbs: ["create"] Bind it to the same person, in the host namespace.

With connectors, people get a host by linking GitHub: no Secret, no YAML and no Kubernetes access. Create a GitHub App with expiring user tokens and the callback URL <callbackBaseUrl>/api/v1/connections/callback, then install with: controller: connectors: enabled: true callbackBaseUrl: https://orka.example.com agentHosts: enabled: true github: enabled: true clientID: Iv23... clientSecret: existingSecret: github-app # or value: <the client secret> The chart renders the github ConnectorProvider and the copilotd template it names; controller.agentHosts.template sets the template's images, storage and resources. The template's spec is immutable: to change it on an existing install, delete the AgentHostTemplate, then upgrade, and hosts move to the new one on their volumes. Without the chart, add spec.agentHost.templateRef to a GitHub provider yourself. People's Connections outlive an uninstall, and a provider is deleted only once no Connection references it. So Helm keeps the provider, the template and a client Secret the chart created when you uninstall or turn github off, and reinstalling the same release adopts them. To remove them, do it while the controller runs, since it finishes their deletion: delete the Connections that reference the provider, wait until they are gone, then delete the three. After an uninstall, reinstall first. To reach Orka with no domain, set ingress.enabled: true, ingress.className: tailscale and ingress.tls: [{hosts: [orka]}] with the Tailscale Kubernetes operator installed: the API and dashboard are then served at https://orka.<tailnet>.ts.net on your tailnet. Each person then runs orka connect github, or links GitHub on the dashboard's Connectors page. orka connect waits for the host and prints the environment to pick in the Copilot app. Afterwards: orka host status # the host, its phase, and why it is not ready orka host wake # start it after it idled out orka host delete --yes # delete it and its volume; while linked, a fresh one follows The provider needs no tools. A dedicated GitHub App with only the permissions the host needs is recommended: a host's token carries all of the app's permissions, and a tool call's refresh would replace the host's token. When a person links the provider, Orka creates an AgentHost named gh-<login> in that namespace, which appears as the environment orka-gh-<login>. The login is lowercased, and a managed user's underscore becomes --: alice_acme gets gh-alice--acme. Orka writes the link's access token into the host and refreshes it 15 minutes before it expires. copilotd picks up the replaced file without a restart. The refresh token never leaves Orka. A token that never expires is refused with GitHubTokenNeverExpires, since code in the host could keep using a copy of it. The host belongs to the first GitHub account it was given. A later token for another account fails it with GitHubIdentityChanged and keeps the volume. Disconnecting stops the host, deletes its token copy and keeps the AgentHost and its volume. Linking the same account again restarts the host on its volume. Settled failures such as a disconnect, a decline, a refused provider, a grant that no longer covers the link, GitHubIdentityChanged, or GitHubTokenNeverExpires stop the host. While a controller catches up with an edit, or a read fails, the host keeps running on the token it has and gets no new one. A suspended host keeps no token copy. Waking it writes a fresh one, after checking the account. Only the controller may create a host fed by a Connection, and only from the template its provider names. A host keeps that template when the provider later names another one. A link annotated orka.ai/agent-host: declined gets no host, and declining stops a host it already has, keeping its volume. The provider must be on github.com: Orka reads the token's account from api.github.com. The template must use access: Relay. A Standalone host's connection Secret sits in the namespace every person's host shares, so these hosts fail with InvalidTemplate instead. Deleting the AgentHost deletes its volume. While the link stays, Orka creates a fresh host for it. At most one provider per namespace may set agentHost. If several do, none provisions. The same happens when the name gh-<login> is taken by another AgentHost. Each case is reported as an event. Linking such a provider again is required after agentHost is added or changed: it is part of the consent the person gave.

Orka adds to the template's container named host, and promises nothing else: Variable Meaning ORKA_HOST_ID The AgentHost UID, stable for the host's life. ORKA_HOST_NAME The AgentHost name, for display. ORKA_CONNECTION_TOKEN_FILE A per-host random token in a memory-backed volume mounted only into host. Read it once and delete it. ORKA_GITHUB_TOKEN_FILE The user's GitHub token, read-only, when the template's githubToken allows it. ORKA_STATUS_DIR A directory shared with the Orka host agent for the idle status file. ORKA_HOST_AGENT A read-only copy of the Orka host agent, for use as the container's init process. The host must serve AHP on 127.0.0.1:<listenPort>, gated by the connection token, and keep everything that must survive a restart under /workspace. The container's entrypoint is its PID 1, which adopts every orphaned process, such as git's detached maintenance. Agent daemons do not reap processes they never started, so start the daemon with exec "$ORKA_HOST_AGENT" init -- <command>: it reaps them, forwards signals to the daemon, and exits with its status. When the template sets idleStatusFile, the host writes JSON with at least idle and idleSince there, and rewrites it at least every five minutes. Orka judges freshness by its updatedAt, or by the file's modification time when it has none, and treats the status as stale after ten minutes, or when that time or idleSince is more than ten minutes ahead. copilotd's --idle-status-file format fits. The orka-host-agent sidecar answers the host's probes. The Pod is Ready only after an AHP initialize and ping succeed against the loopback listener; the check never sends authenticate, so it cannot claim a single-user host. Afterwards it checks that the host keeps its idle status file fresh, or, for hosts without one, that the listener accepts connections. It never keeps the host from being idle.

A host Pod that terminates, or whose listener stays down, is replaced with a new one on the same volume. A turn that was running is lost; sessions resume from the volume. spec.suspended: true stops the Pod and keeps the volume and Secrets. Setting it back to false starts the host again. A template's spec cannot change. To change a template, delete it and create it again under the same name: each host on it gets a new Pod from the new template, on its existing volume. A running turn is lost, and storage changes apply only to new hosts. When the host agent image changes, such as after an upgrade of the controller, each running host gets a new Pod with it on its volume once the host reports idle, and at the latest 24 hours later. Until then the host has the condition HostAgentUpdatePending. A host replaced at the deadline loses a running turn. A template's idleSuspend.after suspends hosts that report idle for that long. A client cannot wake a suspended relay host; set spec.wakeRequestedAt to the current time to start it: kubectl patch agenthost alice --type merge \ -p "{\"spec\":{\"wakeRequestedAt\":\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\"}}" Hosts stay on unless a template enables idle suspension. copilotd counts a session as busy while its runtime refuses to list dynamic-workflow runs, so a host with such a session never reports idle. Its --idle-ignore-unobservable-factories flag lets those sessions reach idle; set it only where dynamic workflows are not in use, because a pending or running workflow can be lost to suspension.

Ready reason Meaning Provisioning The Pod is starting. The message names a container waiting on an image or volume. Restarting The host's Pod failed; Orka replaces it after a backoff that grows from 10 seconds to 5 minutes. TemplateNotFound The template does not exist in the AgentHost's namespace. InvalidTemplate The template breaks a rule in the message. GitHubTokenRequired / GitHubTokenUnavailable The template needs a token and the referenced Secret or key is missing. ObjectCollision An object with a host's name exists in the host namespace but was not created for it. Orka never adopts or deletes it. ObjectRejected The API server refused one of the host's objects, for example a Pod naming an unknown RuntimeClass, huge pages whose request and limit differ, or a Pod a quota or admission policy denies. The message carries the server's reason; Orka retries on its next resync. StateVolumeLost The host's volume was deleted. Delete and recreate the AgentHost. HostAgentUnavailable The controller has no --agent-host-agent-image. HostNamespaceChanged The controller's --agent-host-namespace changed after the host was created. Delete and recreate it. ConnectionUnavailable The host's Connection is gone, unlinked or needs a new consent: linking again restarts the host. Or its provider no longer serves agent hosts: an operator restores the provider's agentHost, then the person links again. GitHubIdentityChanged The Connection now links a different GitHub account than the one the host's volume belongs to. Link the original account, or delete the AgentHost. GitHubTokenNeverExpires The host's Connection holds a GitHub token that never expires, which code in the host could read and keep using. Turn on user-token expiration in the GitHub App, then link again. A host that fails for a missing template or token has its Pod stopped and keeps its volume. When the token's Secret or Connection is gone, Orka also deletes its copy. Deleting an AgentHost removes every object Orka created for it, and only those.

If a host is Ready but the Copilot app reports Mission Control connect failed (HTTP 403), GitHub refused the connection before it reached the host. GitHub refuses every connection to a host while one of its sessions is in a repository you cannot push to, such as an archived one, so sessions in other repositories are blocked too. Restarting the host does not help: it registers again as the same environment. Restore push access to that repository, for example by unarchiving it, then connect and delete the session in the app. You can archive the repository again afterwards. If push access cannot come back, orka host delete --yes replaces the host with one that registers as a new environment, without the old host's sessions and clones.
AgentRuntime integrations preserve one invariant: runtimes may request work, but Orka owns authorization, durable effects, and delivery.

Zone Trust Notes Orka control plane trusted for policy, approvals, idempotency, audit owns Tool execution and credentials AgentRuntime adapter least-privileged orka.harness.v2 adapter must not store downstream Tool, provider, Git, or forge secrets Remote execution backend untrusted/semi-trusted workload runtime may be prompt-injected or compromised Downstream tools protected systems reached only through Orka Tool execution

Keep credentials out of AgentRuntime.spec.deployment.endpoint. Bind runtime bearer Secrets with orka.ai/agent-runtime-auth=true, optional orka.ai/agent-runtime-name, and required orka.ai/agent-runtime-endpoint. Use namespace-local facades unless and until a tenant runtime catalog is intentionally designed. Materialize the exact brokered policy in AgentRuntime.spec.capabilities.mcpPolicy, and make Task.spec.agentRuntime.allowedTools equal its allowlist. Brokered mode does not imply access to all Tools. Classify remote-exposed Tools with spec.brokeredToolClass. Use write-class Tools for consequential actions so approval and exact-argument digest checks run before execution. Require the per-session loopback MCP proxy to present the active Task, attempt, prompt, lease, RuntimeSession, RuntimePool, runtime-instance, and controller fences on every call. Reserve a durable ExternalEffect identity before consequential execution; replay only a committed matching response. Treat WaitingForApproval=True as an intentional parked state, not a failure. Investigate tool_execution_outcome_unknown before retrying a write; Orka failed closed to avoid duplicate side effects.

Prefer HTTPS, mTLS, private networking, and the v2 bearer plus operation-capability scheme for external adapters. Rotate runtime bearer Secrets and ensure the AgentRuntime observes the new Secret resourceVersion before use. Keep built-in provider credentials behind the central provider proxy; do not add Agent.spec.secretRef to Codex, Claude, Copilot, or OpenCode Agents. Use config/acp-production for direct Kustomize deployments so Vekil accepts ingress only from the authenticated provider proxy. Keep source-read, target-read, target-write, and forge credentials in separate Task workspace references. They are delivered only through the controller credential broker to the clean-room Publisher. Ensure the Publisher uses the controller artifact authorization broker and does not mount the artifact capability signing key. Ensure downstream tools honor Idempotency-Key for write requests. Keep large artifacts in artifact storage and return safe references rather than huge summaries. Redact auth headers, tokens, TxTokens, and raw transcripts from adapter logs.

This page is for running gateways in production: their service levels and bounds, readiness, interim replies, secret rotation, dead letters, backup and restore, upgrades, and cleanup. To set up a gateway and choose an adapter, start with Gateways. Gateways are enabled by default. They use the controller SQLite database for normalized ingress events, Session transcript provenance, and outbound delivery state.

The documented local reference target is p95 durable ingress acknowledgement below 500 ms for a 1,000-event burst with 100 active Sessions. This is an admission SLO, not an end-to-end model response SLO. Defaults: Setting Default Pending events per Session 100 Retained operational event records per Gateway 1,000 Retained rejected audit records per Gateway 250 Event/delivery expiry 24h Delivery timeout 15s Delivery attempts 10 Distinct accepted interim messages per Task 10 (--gateway-interim-messages-per-task) Interim message text 16 KiB UTF-8 Ingress and terminal text 64 KiB Terminal retention 720h (30 days) Claim lease 1m Default persistent volume request 1Gi Controller flags use the --gateway-* prefix. Helm values are under controller.gateway. Gateway dispatch, delivery, and retention maintenance run only on the elected controller leader; SQLite claims preserve crash recovery while leader election makes namespace task-capacity checks replica-safe. Gateway ingress is enabled by default, so the Helm chart also enables the SQLite PVC by default. Helm rejects controller.gateway.enabled=true with store.persistence.enabled=false unless controller.gateway.allowEphemeralStore=true is explicitly set for disposable development; acknowledged events on an ephemeral store are not durable across Pod replacement. For offline GitOps rendering, apply the bundled Task/Gateway CRDs separately and set controller.gateway.crdsReadyOverride: true; live Helm installs normally discover the CRDs with lookup.

A Gateway is Ready only when: its GatewayClass is accepted; exactly one safe HTTPS endpoint or TLS-authenticated selector-backed same-namespace Service resolves; separate inbound/outbound Secrets exist, opt in, and bind to the Gateway; the outbound Secret binds to the exact resolved HTTPS endpoint; authenticated health and capability probes succeed; observed capabilities satisfy the GatewayClass requirements. Agent runtime warmth does not affect Gateway readiness. Accepted events remain durable while downstream execution is temporarily unavailable.

A serviceRef resolves to https://<service>.<namespace>.svc:<port>. The adapter certificate must include <service>.<namespace>.svc as a DNS subject alternative name; an IP address or a different external hostname does not satisfy controller hostname verification. For a private CA, mount the CA certificate into the controller and either install it in the container's system trust store or set SSL_CERT_DIR to the mounted CA directory. Do not disable certificate verification. Roll the controller after changing its trust configuration, and wait for the rollout before expecting the Gateway to become Ready. For a Helm release named orka in orka-system (a kubectl apply install names the Deployment orka-controller-manager instead — see Troubleshooting): kubectl -n orka-system rollout restart deployment/orka-controller kubectl -n orka-system rollout status deployment/orka-controller

GatewayBinding.spec.agentRef supports both native AI Agents and runtime-backed Agents. At Task creation, an Agent without spec.runtime produces a type: ai Task using the Agent's model/provider configuration and the AI worker. An Agent with spec.runtime continues to produce a type: agent Task. taskDefaults.agentRuntimeMaxTurns is runtime-only and makes a binding to a native AI Agent not ready; dispatch also rejects it if an Agent edit races readiness reconciliation. Admission pins the Agent UID, not its generation or execution kind. Agent edits before Task creation can therefore change the selected execution kind. Once the Task exists, crash recovery adopts that Task with its immutable kind instead of selecting again from the edited Agent. Frozen external-runtime tool policy remains authoritative and cannot be discarded by switching to native AI. Both paths consume the canonical Session transcript through the admitted user message, without copying external text into the Task CR or adding the current prompt twice. Native AI startup fails closed when a required transcript has no non-empty final user turn. Gateway terminal projection—not generic Task finalization—appends the canonical assistant message, creates the delivery, and releases the Session lock.

An adapter may advertise optional interimDelivery: true under orka.gateway.v1. Only then can a Running gateway Task enqueue a bounded kind: message delivery. Absent/false capability means final/error-only operation; no message is enqueued or sent. This adds a kind, not delivery statuses: existing final/error meaning and delivered/retryableError/nonRetryableError receipts are unchanged. Interim text is kept in delivery records, not in the Task CR, final result, or canonical Session transcript. It does not complete the event, annotate the Task as delivered, or unlock the Session. Use the gateway delivery view for progress; normal terminal projection still owns completion and history. The controller limit is --gateway-interim-messages-per-task=10. Supply a positive value to change it; the setting is not a per-worker routing option. Every distinct accepted message counts for that Task's lifetime, including failed/expired messages. An exact request replay returns the retained receipt without another enqueue or quota charge. Text is limited to 16 KiB before sanitization, without silent truncation; terminal text remains bounded at 64 KiB.

The production native worker and ACP broker provide gateway-only reply_in_conversation: {"content":"A bounded intermediate update"} content is the only model argument. Its schema requires a string with minLength: 1, maxLength: 16384, and no additional properties. Execute also rejects invalid Unicode, unknown/duplicate fields, empty or sanitized-empty text, and content over 16384 UTF-8 bytes. There is no destination, request ID, count override, or approval argument. Success returns only deliveryID, current durable status, and created inside the tool success envelope. A receipt means durable acceptance, not completed delivery, and the agent continues working normally. The controller enables the tool only after proving exact admitted event/Task UID origin. Names, environment flags, prompt text, and provenance metadata cannot grant it. Ordinary AI/ACP Tasks, delegated children, container Tasks, and compatibility-proxy callers do not gain the tool. Explicit tool denials, closed allowlists, and transaction scopes remain authoritative. Built-in ACP providers preserve their native default tools. An external runtime must explicitly opt in through its registered, conformed profile with exact policy agreement; existing profiles without reply remain final-only. Already-frozen sessions are not upgraded. For native AI, omitted Agent.spec.tools and Task.spec.ai.tools leave automatic reply eligibility unchanged; an explicit tools: [] in either field denies reply even with a proven gateway origin. Nonempty lists must permit reply, and an Agent reply_in_conversation entry with enabled: false remains a denial. Typed Kubernetes JSON writes preserve explicit empty lists. Older writes may already have collapsed an empty list into omission: persisted omission cannot reveal that original intent and is not reinterpreted during upgrade. Where denial was intended, reapply the explicit policy using an updated writer before enabling gateway replies; older writers can still erase empty lists. The host—not the model—supplies a stable operation identity. The tool checks a controller-backed, replay-aware budget before enqueue; final atomic admission still enforces the configured lifetime cap against concurrent calls. Retained receipts can replay at exhaustion without another charge. Distinct logical calls with identical text are distinct messages. Retries must preserve operation identity; regeneration after a restart does not guarantee exactly-once delivery. Known unsupported/capacity/conflict rejections are safe model-visible errors. An uncertain send must not be treated as definite rejection or retried by inventing a new call; ACP retains its consequential OutcomeUnknown fence as well as gateway receipts.

Native workers authenticate durable origin through GET /internal/v1/tasks/{namespace}/{taskName}/gateway-messages/origin, which returns only the exact Task UID. They read GET .../gateway-messages/budget?requestID=... for accepted, limit, and requestExists, then use POST .../gateway-messages with content and a host-derived request ID. All routes retain authentic current Pod/Job/Task UID authorization and revocation checks. The production client uses the projected token file, not an environment token override. New admission returns HTTP 202; replay returns HTTP 200. These are execution-host APIs, not operator/admin send endpoints. Origin is separate from adapter availability: a proven gateway execution retains the tool through readiness/capability withdrawal, but new budget/admission requests still fail the current gate. Missing interim capability returns interim_delivery_unsupported (HTTP 409) without enqueueing. An unproven origin never enables the tool. The client retries origin 503 responses within a bounded startup window; a persistent transient origin-service failure omits this optional tool while normal work continues. Invalid identity is still denied. There is no late tool upgrade in that execution. ACP does not use those native HTTP routes or create a Job. Its sender uses the signed broker call's active prompt/session guard and the authorized task data access, independently for budget and enqueue. Frozen policy, exact Task identity, prompt authority, and durable gateway origin all remain required. Live preparation occurs outside the SQLite writer, with durable admission and mutation fences inside it. No approval or terminal-lifecycle behavior is added.

Gateway-created Tasks remain ordinary Orka Task objects for controller execution, but their CRs contain no external message text; the prompt is loaded from the bounded, task-owned Session transcript. Public Task list/get/log/result/event/trace/fork surfaces require both the ordinary Task permission and gateway-read authorization for the owning Gateway. Destructive Task actions and approval decisions additionally require gateway-operate authorization. The default Helm and Kustomize installs also create a fail-closed ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that permits direct Kubernetes create/update/delete of gateway-owned Tasks only from the owning Orka controller or trusted worker ServiceAccounts. Namespace-isolated Helm releases scope the policy by the immutable Gateway namespace encoded in requestedBy.issuer, so multiple releases do not deny one another and coordinated workers can create inherited child Tasks. Canonical gateway Sessions are hidden from generic Session, Session-event, transcript-search, and chat-loading surfaces; gateway event/delivery APIs are the supported operator view.

Create or update Secret data without changing the configured key. Kubernetes Secret watch events trigger reconciliation; status records only the observed resourceVersion. Token values belong only in the Secret Never put them in Gateway metadata, status, logs, Tasks, or support bundles. Status records the Secret's resourceVersion and nothing else, and support bundles are routinely shared. When an endpoint changes, update the outbound Secret's gateway.orka.ai/adapter-endpoint annotation to the exact new resolved HTTPS endpoint. The Gateway remains not ready until the binding matches and the authenticated probe succeeds.

Inspect event and delivery state in the dashboard or with: orka gateway events list --state DeadLettered,Expired orka gateway deliveries list --state DeadLettered,Failed,Expired orka gateway deliveries retry '<delivery-id>' Manual retry preserves the stable delivery/idempotency ID, resets the bounded attempt window, extends expiry by 24 hours, and increments manualRetryCount. Expired ingress events are not automatically replayed because their original sender/context authorization may no longer be valid. Within an event, live interim predecessors drain in order before later messages and final/error. Permanent failure, exhausted attempts, or expiry abandons a message so terminal delivery can proceed. Capability withdrawal is rechecked before sending and prevents a queued interim post. An earlier message cannot be manually revived once any later delivery has started, including Sending, uncertain, or subsequently expired/abandoned attempts. Do not regenerate IDs to work around this fence. Terminal manual retry is unchanged. Replaying an old delivered message ID after terminal must return its original provider correlation without sending again.

Gateway state lives in two places, and a backup of one alone is not a backup. Where What is in it Controller SQLite database (on the PVC) Gateway Sessions, normalized events, delivery rows, event-to-Task correlation Kubernetes Gateway CRDs, referenced Secrets, Task CRs Back up both, and keep credentials out of the SQLite archive A disaster-recovery backup needs the SQLite volume and the corresponding cluster objects. Credentials belong in the cluster Secret backup only. SQLite runs in WAL mode, which means a committed record may still be sitting in orka.db-wal rather than in orka.db. Copying orka.db alone from a running controller silently loses committed work There is no error. The copy simply comes back missing whatever was still in the WAL. Use one of these consistency-safe approaches: take an atomic CSI VolumeSnapshot of the whole persistent volume, including the database, WAL, and shared-memory files; quiescing writes first is still preferred; use SQLite's online backup API against the live database; or pause adapter ingress, stop every controller replica that can write the store, checkpoint/truncate the WAL from a maintenance process, and then copy the main database file. For a release or disaster-recovery backup: Record the Orka image/chart version, Gateway CRD manifests, controller gateway flags, and adapter versions/capabilities. Pause external ingress and wait for in-flight API requests to finish. Record queued, sending, retry-scheduled, and dead-letter counts. Create a consistent SQLite/PVC snapshot and a cluster backup containing GatewayClasses, Gateways, GatewayBindings, Tasks, referenced Agents, and referenced Secrets.
