The provider advertises checkpoint.data and restore.cold alongside ACP runtime and suspension. A public ExecutionWorkspaceCheckpoint carries an opaque data reference bound to provider, source class/profile, namespace, checkpoint UID, and content digest. It does not expose native Tags or control credentials. Export must finish before deleting the source workspace. Import requires live use authorization for the checkpoint and exact compatible target infrastructure. A fresh target workspace restores data into a new Actor; it never resumes source process memory or credentials. Immutable checkpoint and template references keep required provider-owned storage alive until their consumers are gone. The provider does not advertise pooled ACP capacity, generic exec/files, TLS Actor endpoints, MCP Service workloads, or full-memory restore.

MCP Tools retain spec.mcp.substrateActor and optional SubstrateActorPool placement. Enable only that path with --substrate-mcp-tools-enabled. The core --substrate-api-* and --substrate-router-url settings apply to this MCP integration, not the external ACP provider. controller: substrate: mcpToolsEnabled: true podCertificate: enabled: true podCertificate projects the controller's Substrate pod identity and service trust bundle. The router admits only allowlisted pod certificates, so MCP Tools need it (or another podidentity-signed client certificate); a bearer token alone authenticates control calls but cannot reach Actors. Add the controller's SPIFFE ID to --ingress-allowed-spiffe-ids. The controller is the only Orka client of the router. AI workers and other callers invoke a Substrate MCP Tool through the authenticated orka-api proxy published in Tool.status.endpoint (/api/v1/tools/<name>/mcp?namespace=<ns>). The proxy requires get on that Tool, derives the Actor only from controller-owned status, injects the Tool's configured credentials, and never forwards the caller's Orka credentials. OIDC callers and outboundAccessPolicyRef are not supported for these Tools. Before the proxy injects a Tool's http.authSecretRef credential, it checks that the caller may use it. A Kubernetes caller, including the AI worker's ServiceAccount, needs get on that Secret in the Tool's namespace; a transaction-token caller needs the credential-read scope. Other callers receive 403. The restricted worker profile needs a grant. A Tool stands for the one MCP callable that carries its name, so permission to use a Tool is permission to call only that. The proxy accepts a single JSON-RPC message per request: initialize, notifications/initialized, or a tools/call whose params.name is the Tool's name. It answers 403 for any other method or callable and 400 for a batch or a malformed message, and it forwards the message it checked rather than the caller's bytes. The caller never sees the values the proxy injects. If the Actor echoes the Tool credential, a sensitive configured header value or the forwarded transaction token, the proxy replaces it with [REDACTED] in the response body and headers, also when the value is written with JSON string escapes. MCP Actors get no egress unless spec.mcp.substrateActor.egress allows it, using http, https (gateway-intercepted), or tls (passthrough) rules with a lowercase FQDN or leftmost *. wildcard and ports. The controller applies the policy before every resume and reports EgressPolicyReady. Intercepted https egress requires the operator's ActorTemplate to trust the egress-mitm.ate.dev bundle. An http or https rule on an exact host may add a credential (header, default Authorization; optional prefix; secretRef in the Tool's namespace). The gateway replaces that header, which the Actor sends with any placeholder value, with the Secret value, so the Actor never holds it. It needs --substrate-egress-credential-provider=k8s.io, a credential-provider grant from the Actor's Atespace to the Tool namespace, and a caller allowed to get the Secret; the REST API rejects such Tools. MCP templates must set a wakeupProbe on the routable port and disable golden snapshots when Tools request boot: true. SubstrateActorPool.spec.templateRef is immutable and belongs to native MCP Tool placement. It does not select a Task's ACP workspace. The controller stops an Actor rather than leave it running under a policy it has not verified for the Tool's current spec. If the policy cannot be applied, or an edit is rejected before that step (for example an invalid egress rule or a missing auth Secret), the Tool reports EgressPolicyReady=False and the controller stops the Actor it owns, retrying until it has. It suspends the Actor when the template keeps data, and the next successful reconcile resumes it. A template that snapshots VOLUMES and mounts no durable directory cannot be suspended by Substrate, so its Actor is deleted and created again later. Substrate also lets an Actor outlive its template. When the template cannot be read, the controller cannot suspend the Actor (Substrate refuses without it), so it replaces the Actor's egress policy with one that denies all egress and keeps retrying the stop. While the gateway may still apply the previous rules from its cache (see below), a running Actor is deleted instead, which discards any data on its durable volumes; a suspended one is left as it is. A stored policy is not enforced at once. The Substrate egress gateway caches each Actor's policy by Actor name for --egress-policy-cache-ttl (10s by default) and does not invalidate the entry when the policy changes or the Actor is replaced. The controller therefore waits --substrate-egress-policy-propagation (14s by default: the cache TTL plus the 4s a policy fetch may take) before it lets an Actor run under a policy the gateway may not apply yet. During the wait the Tool reports EgressPolicyReady=False with reason EgressPolicyPropagating and is unavailable. Operators will notice two effects: An egress edit restarts the Actor. When an edit replaces the stored policy, a running Actor is stopped first (suspended, or deleted and created again if its template cannot be suspended) and resumed after the wait. Expect about 15 seconds of downtime for that Tool and, for a template without a durable directory, the loss of whatever the Actor held in memory. Edits that leave egress unchanged do not restart it. A new Actor's first boot waits. An Actor's name is derived from its Tool or pool slot, and a policy deleted and created again looks like a new one, so a new policy can share its Actor name with rules the gateway still holds. The controller cannot tell, so an Actor runs no sooner than one wait after its policy was created or last changed. That includes a pool's Actors created ahead of use: their policy is created when a Tool first claims them. Set the flag to your gateway's cache TTL plus 4s. Set it to 0 only if the gateway runs with --egress-policy-cache-ttl=0; the controller then neither waits nor restarts Actors.

Workers used to read a Substrate MCP Tool's http.authSecretRef themselves, from a Secret mounted into the worker or from the Kubernetes API. The proxy now reads it, and only for a caller allowed to get that Secret. A copy mounted into the worker is no longer used for these Tools. The default AI worker role can read Secrets, so nothing changes there. With workers.ai.rbacProfile: restricted the worker has no Secret access, and a Substrate MCP Tool with authSecretRef fails with 403 not authorized to use the tool credential after the upgrade. Grant the worker ServiceAccount get on that one Secret, in the namespace that holds the Tool. Do not grant Secret access more broadly: the grant also lets the worker read that Secret directly. apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: mcp-tool-credential namespace: orka-system rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["secrets"] resourceNames: ["my-mcp-tool-token"] # the Tool's http.authSecretRef.name verbs: ["get"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: mcp-tool-credential namespace: orka-system roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: mcp-tool-credential subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: orka-ai-worker # <release fullname>-ai-worker namespace: orka-system Tools without authSecretRef need no grant.
documents.s: Grant restricted AI workers the Tool credential

documents.t: Agent Substrate 1.x minor releases upgrade in place by following the upstream upgrade guide, with two Orka-specific rules in its worker step: Patch only operator-owned WorkerPools, and pin each new workerImage by digest. Do not patch the provider's private <actor>-workers pools, which carry the substrate.workspace.orka.ai allocation labels. The provider refuses to resume on a changed private pool, and suspended workspaces pick up the new operator image on their next resume. Before upgrading ate-api-server, move running workspaces off old workers by deleting their private worker Pods (or draining their nodes). Each one drains and suspends as described in Worker eviction, then resumes on the new image. Wait until no private pool runs the old image. Agent Substrate cannot upgrade a pre-1.0 installation in place. Before moving to v1.0.0, retire every workspace, checkpoint, and MCP Actor created under v0.1.0, then install Substrate v1.0.0 fresh and upgrade the provider and core. Records from v0.1.0 fail closed with LegacySubstrateV0State rather than being adopted. The --substrate-actor-dns-suffix and --substrate-session-identity-* settings were removed and fail startup if set; core now issues each Actor's workspace credential itself through the sealed bootstrap. Native Substrate workspaces reach the controller API and the provider proxy through the egress gateway, by the host names in --controller-url and --acp-provider-proxy-base-url. An Actor cannot resolve a short <service>.<namespace>.svc name, so Core refuses one when it admits a native workspace: the RuntimePool reports Degraded with a message naming the flag and the fully qualified name to use. Charts and kustomize manifests from this release set <service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster domain> (chart value clusterDomain, default cluster.local). If you set either flag yourself to a short name, change it to the fully qualified one before using Substrate-native workspaces. Pod-backed workspaces and other workers keep resolving short names. The same rule applies to the hosts in a Substrate MCP Tool's spec.mcp.substrateActor.egress. Installations that run AI workers with workers.ai.rbacProfile: restricted and use Substrate MCP Tools with http.authSecretRef must grant the worker that Secret before upgrading. Substrate MCP Tools behave differently around egress from this release on. A Tool becomes available about 14 seconds later than before when its Actor or its Actor's egress policy is new, and editing a Tool's egress allowlist restarts its Actor, with about 15 seconds of downtime. Both come from waiting for the Substrate egress gateway to apply a changed policy; see Native MCP Tools in core for the --substrate-egress-policy-propagation flag that sets the wait. Drain all old in-tree ACP allocations and retained records through the original owner before applying the pruned RuntimePool CRD or starting new core. The startup gate rejects legacy workspace labels in every state, including Failed and Deleted, across all namespaces. It never adopts native allocations or strips finalizers. See Upgrading. The external Substrate proof installs the pinned v1.0.0 release with ate-setup on a dedicated gVisor kind cluster. It verifies worker sizing, assignments, and the egress allowlist before native Resume, writes a filesystem marker, captures VOLUMES data, observes exact worker/Actor cleanup, and restores that marker in a fresh process after source deletion. It proves native provider lifecycle and checkpoint behavior. Its standalone lane uses fixture Core admission. The native Core Task proof last passed with deployed Core and provider controllers on Substrate v0.1.0 and must be rerun on v1.0.0. It verifies real fail-closed Task admission, sealed bootstrap, authenticated Serving, RuntimeSession execution, and a persisted prompt result. Exact Actor, worker, private pool, Core pool, and credential retirement are required. The agent is deterministic and makes no external model requests. Neither native lane proves packet enforcement; full-memory restore remains gated.

Orka has four kinds of tests: Go unit tests, controller integration tests against a real API server (envtest), end-to-end tests against a throwaway Kind cluster, and frontend tests in the browser-like Vitest environment. This page describes what each covers and how to run it.

# Run test pipeline (manifests, generate, fmt, vet, then Go tests) make test # Run Go tests with coverage report make test go tool cover -func=cover.out | grep total # Run release automation and workspace cleanup tests without a cluster go test ./cmd/build/release ./scripts/tests # Run frontend tests make ui-test # or: cd ui && bun run test make ui-test-coverage # or: cd ui && bun run test:coverage # Run E2E tests (requires isolated Kind cluster) make test-e2e # Run only the deterministic Gateway live E2E KIND_CLUSTER=orka-gateway-e2e \ E2E_GATEWAY=true \ E2E_EPHEMERAL_CLUSTER=true \ E2E_GINKGO_FOCUS="Gateway live E2E" \ make test-e2e # External workspace proof runs from the separate orka-workspace checkout. # See Development's external workspace local proof section. # Lint make lint make lint-fix make ui-lint The E2E runner uses separate Go and Ginkgo deadlines. Local defaults are E2E_GO_TEST_TIMEOUT=50m, E2E_GINKGO_TIMEOUT=45m, and E2E_GINKGO_GRACE_PERIOD=2m. Each CI lane sets its Ginkgo deadline 5m below its Go deadline, and Gateway live E2E uses 75m and 70m. When overriding these values, leave room inside the Go deadline for both an interrupted spec and suite cleanup to finish their grace periods.

The Native Codex handoff job in .github/workflows/test.yml compiles the supervisor test from the current checkout and runs it inside the pinned production Codex 0.160.0 / codex-acp 2.1.1 image. Docker networking is disabled; inference uses a local scripted Responses server and disposable test credentials. The container uses only the production supervisor's CHOWN, KILL, SETGID, and SETUID capabilities. The gate restores the original thread UUID through session/resume, continues across fresh homes with rotated credentials, checks current destination policy, and verifies read and write intents, a publishable workspace delta, native capture, return history, unchanged source bytes, and runtime cleanup. It explicitly enables ORKA_NATIVE_CODEX_TEST=1 and requires the named test to pass, so a skipped test cannot satisfy the job. This verifies the native integration, not live-model recall.

Script test suites need bash >= 4. The suites under scripts/tests/ rely on set -e stopping on failed (( )) arithmetic, which macOS's stock bash 3.2 does not honor — failures would pass silently. The suites refuse to run under bash < 4; on macOS install a modern bash (brew install bash) and invoke the suites with it. A green Gateway E2E can be an empty one. Without E2E_GATEWAY=true the gateway specs skip themselves and Ginkgo prints Ran 0 of N Specs with a SUCCESS exit. If you see that line, nothing was validated — re-run with the environment shown above. (CI fails this shape explicitly.) Running go test directly on controller packages needs envtest assets. make test wires KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS automatically; for a bare go test on packages that start an envtest API server, export it first: KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS="$(bin/setup-envtest use -p path)".

The RepositoryMonitor workflows have an integrated, secret-free suite that runs against fake GitHub servers. It covers durable command intake, replay and coalescing, guard-label blocking, issue implementation to pull request, stop/resume late-task safety, and pull request review, repair, and readiness. These tests do not claim live model execution. make repository-monitor-fake-e2e # the fake-GitHub E2E scenarios make repository-monitor-validate # plus generated CLI docs, example manifests, website docs, and workflow syntax The Repository Monitor Smoke GitHub Actions workflow runs the same fake-GitHub script on relevant pull requests. Live model execution, publication, and GitHub rule enforcement need separate validation against an explicitly selected repository.

Tests use Ginkgo + Gomega (BDD style) for controller/integration tests and standard Go testing for unit tests. Package Test Files Coverage Areas cmd/build/release/ workflow_test.go, prepare_test.go, publish_test.go, version_test.go Release version edits, trusted tooling, branch races, artifact identity, approval evidence, chart publication, and retries. Uses local Git repositories and Helm; GitHub and registry responses are fixtures. scripts/tests/ workspace_lifecycle_test.go Workspace cancellation, session archival, suspension, and deletion ordering using Bash and jq fixtures. internal/api/ handlers_test.go, internal_handlers_test.go, auth_test.go, middleware_test.go, pagination_test.go, server_test.go, openai_compat_test.go REST API handlers, internal API handlers, memory/session APIs, authentication, middleware, pagination, OpenAI compatibility internal/controller/ task_controller_test.go, agent_controller_test.go, tool_controller_test.go, session_manager_test.go, job_builder_test.go, repositoryscan_controller_test.go, webhook_test.go Reconciliation logic, session management, job building, coordination bounded context manifests, prompt helpers internal/security/slices/ mapper_test.go Deterministic review-slice mapper coverage for Go, Node/TypeScript, Python, workflows, scripts, config, path skipping, and stable output internal/store/sqlite/ security_store_test.go Repository security records, findings, review slices, dropped finding diagnostics, patch proposals internal/store/sqlite/ Prometheus metrics recording internal/tools/ registry_test.go, memory tool tests, coordination tool tests, PR tool tests, agent-management tool tests, integration_test.go Built-in tool implementations, memory tools, coordination tools, PR tools, agent management tools internal/worker/ tool_executor_test.go Custom Tool CRD executor workers/ai/ main_test.go AI worker functions rejection, idempotent rescan, and HITL no-auto-patch gating test/e2e/tools_test.go Built-in tools (including web_fetch, file_write) and custom Tool CRD test/e2e/scheduled_task_test.go Cron scheduling, model providers, requires credentials, and bootstraps an ephemeral Kind cluster, Vekil, and the production ACP topology before invoking the canonical validator .github/workflows/release-qualification.yml / scripts/agent-runtime-kind-e2e.sh Environment-approved chart and runtime acceptance, real local Git publication tests, GitHub API fixture tests, and cleanup; no stored Git publication credentials The Gateway Live E2E workflow (.github/workflows/gateway-e2e.yml) runs on manual dispatch and on pull requests or pushes that touch Gateway-relevant source, configuration, E2E, image, or dependency paths. It creates a dedicated Kind cluster, generates disposable TLS and bearer credentials, deploys the TLS reference adapter and deterministic echo AgentRuntime, and verifies invalid bearer rejection, accepted and duplicate ingress, runtime-backed Task completion, final delivery, idempotency, and correlation metadata. The workflow is model-free and secret-free; it does not use repository or provider credentials.

The Kind-based lanes are the slowest checks, so they skip changes that cannot affect them. E2E Tests and Live GitHub OIDC E2E run for any change except ui/, website/, docs/, examples/, Markdown, .agents/, .claude/, LICENSE, .gitignore, and .github/ (a change to the lane's own workflow or to .github/actions/ still runs it). Gateway Live E2E and the other path-listed lanes run only for the paths in their workflow. A UI change is covered by UI Lint, UI Tests, and the Website workflow, whose dashboard build runs tsc -b; example and docs changes are covered by Docs Check and Go Tests. Go Tests and Lint still run on UI changes because they are also the release gates, and one Go test reads ui/src/routes. A new push to a pull request cancels that pull request's in-progress Tests, Lint, and E2E Tests runs. Pushes to main and release runs are never cancelled. The Gateway Live E2E GitHub Actions workflow deploys the TLS reference adapter, a deterministic external AgentRuntime, and a test-only native worker image in Kind. It preserves private-CA trust, readiness, ingress deduplication, and external-v2 final-only/no-Job coverage. Native coverage creates real gateway Tasks and controller Jobs/Pods, authenticates origin, and executes the production ReplyInConversationTool with the reusable native client. It verifies budget-backed admission/replay, observes a delivered interim receipt while the Task is still Running, and only then releases final completion. A rolled adapter with --interim-delivery=false must produce the tool's typed unsupported rejection with no enqueue and still deliver final. Local start/release fences are driven through Kubernetes exec; no production authorization exception is added. CI requires all three specs, retaining the zero-spec guard. It does not run the conformance CLI and does not replace conformance testing against each adapter build before rollout. That deterministic fixture does not prove model-driven worker registration or live ACP tool execution. Native worker unit/integration tests separately cover actual registration, advertisement, dispatch, and continued model work. ACP integration tests exercise the production tool through a signed broker capability, active prompt/session guard, and real SQLite, with no native Job; Kubernetes and broker credential resolution use test fixtures, not a live RuntimePool/provider. Local unit/integration results and tagged E2E compilation are not evidence that the live suite ran. Live native delivery requires the workflow's three specs to execute successfully; the external-v2 spec remains final-only. The Repository Monitor Smoke workflow runs in GitHub Actions on pull requests and pushes that touch the workflow, API, controller, CRD/config, worker, or Go dependency paths. It creates the UI embed stub and runs focused go test selections for the monitor store, API handlers, GitHub pull request event handling, targeted single-PR inventory runs, controller queue/review flow, blocked status counts, read-only review job construction, result stdout forwarding, create_pr_monitor repository URL and credential validation, GitHub tool repo_url scope enforcement, and PR review marker signing/detection tooling. The workflow is secret-free: exact PR event queueing is tested with synthetic signed webhook payloads and fake GitHub clients rather than live repository credentials. The normal Go Tests workflow runs make test for non-doc code changes and covers worker-level PR review diff context generation. Repository security E2E coverage should include initial deterministic slice creation, incremental scan behavior, invalid v2 evidence being dropped and visible through API, validation task persistence, successful verified patch proposals, and patch proposals with missing or mismatched artifacts staying not ready.
documents.s: Which CI lanes run for a pull request

documents.t: The adversarial-eval label is part of the agent-runtime lane. These evals script a model acting on an untrusted repository file or brokered tool note and check the resulting system boundaries. They do not measure model judgment or resistance to prompt injection. The existing fast, in-process evals remain unchanged. The legitimate prompt asks to read a fixture file or tool note. The malicious action is scripted only after its nonce returns as a real tool result. Passing a prevention case requires both the returned refusal and independent evidence that no forbidden Task, token exchange, workspace change, push, or PR occurred. Permitted controls exercise the same tools and consume the fixture credentials; absence of a credential that was never used is not containment evidence. Public broker/CLI refusals intentionally redact private executor errors. Each delegation denial is paired with a permitted same-tool control and independent Task, token-exchange, and access receipts; generic failure alone is not proof of a specific authorization boundary. A test-only proxy in front of aimock retains complete request bodies, including bodies above aimock's own 64 KiB journal cap. It stores no headers or response bodies and never logs captured content. Capture is bounded to 4 MiB per request, 64 MiB in total, and 4096 entries; exhaustion rejects requests rather than silently discarding evidence. Snapshot exports stream one entry at a time with a single concurrent exporter, rather than buffering a potentially expanded whole-store JSON response. Eval helpers require a stable capture instance, retained request identities, completed responses, and matching fixture receipts. Missing or incomplete observation cannot pass. Auxiliary requests are scanned as well as the case's marked inference requests. All credentials are synthetic and local to the test cluster. The provider canary covers Orka's upstream proxy bearer, not vendor credentials held by a real Vekil deployment. Child-local loopback capabilities are distinct from that bearer. Transaction tests use cryptographically valid, ephemeral mock authority and inspect actual child-token exchange results; malformed tokens are not a scope-containment control. Canary detector tests deliberately plant exposure and verify that failure messages omit the values. Built-in ACP Tasks reject transaction-token delegation before inference. The shared TxToken cases therefore use the conformed external harness-v2 E2E fixture, which runs a bounded aimock loop against the real controller's public MCP broker using accepted running-Task fences. An exact fixture-only ingress grant connects it to isolated aimock; the production proxy-only ingress policy is unchanged. The injected note is a real brokered tool result, not native repository content. Parent and permitted child tokens must be valid, and the child consumes its token in a brokered control. The fixture keeps these Tasks running until normal cancellation cleanup; a completed model loop is not presented as native Task success. Publication checks use real Claude Tasks without a transaction context. Its flat MCP protocol fits the pinned mock; this case does not cover Codex namespaced MCP calls. No test claims that built-in runtimes support TxTokens or that external fixtures exercise native CLI workspace isolation. Run the focused label through the usual isolated E2E bootstrap: E2E_GINKGO_LABEL_FILTER=adversarial-eval E2E_ACP_IDLE_POOL_TTL=15m make test-e2e Every runtime must satisfy native refusal plus ReadValidated and no publication. Claude, Copilot, and OpenCode refuse the write tool itself. Codex reads and writes through one shell tool, so its refusal comes from the filesystem: under read intent the supervisor owns the workspace and the session root, and the Codex shell's write fails with Permission denied. The capture, signing-fixture, detector, and fixture-contract tests also run without a cluster: make ensure-ui-embed go test ./test/fixtures/aimockcapture/... ./test/fixtures/aimockauthority/... go test -tags=e2e ./test/e2e -run 'Test(AimockEval|RuntimeEval|AuthorizationEval)'

scripts/agent-runtime-e2e.sh --context <context> is the canonical ACP deployed-cluster validator. Its default mode is a smoke test of runtime behavior against real models. RELEASE_GATE=1 checks the shipped artifacts instead: one workspace read with its API result per runtime, unsafe workspace rejection, and image digests. The Kind wrapper also requires uncached publication tests. A smoke result cannot qualify a release. Live GitHub publication is available only through an explicit local opt-in. scripts/agent-runtime-kind-e2e.sh is the CI/local bootstrap entrypoint. It creates an ephemeral Kind cluster, deploys Vekil and the production ACP topology with digest-pinned local images, and then calls the canonical script. .github/workflows/agent-runtime-e2e.yml runs by manual dispatch only. It requires the repository's COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN secret so Vekil can exercise Codex, OpenCode, Claude, and Copilot against real model providers without mounting provider credentials into RuntimePools. The workflow rejects dispatches from other branches before using the secret. It runs as ordinary CI without a deployment environment. When migrating from live-acp-runtime-smoke, ensure the provider secret is available at repository scope. After the renamed workflow succeeds, retire the old environment and preserve its deployment history. .github/workflows/release-qualification.yml uses workflow_dispatch and is serialized. The release workflow dispatches it automatically. Restrict the release-qualification environment to main and exact permitted release branches, require a trusted reviewer, and disable administrator bypass. It accepts a full source SHA that must equal both the dispatched workflow commit and selected branch head. GitHub observations use the job's temporary GITHUB_TOKEN with contents: read. Agent execution runs against aimock (ACP_E2E_MODEL_BACKEND=aimock), so no model-provider secret, stored Git publication token, or fork setting is needed. Publication tests use real temporary Git repositories and local GitHub API test servers. They do not prove the complete cluster-to-GitHub publication path or live organization permissions. Release qualification documents trusted dispatch, required test evidence, report verification, and cleanup. Qualification needs the report for the exact candidate; smoke success is insufficient. Neither Agent Runtime E2E nor Release Qualification runs for pull_request, so PR-controlled code never receives provider credentials. Both check out with persisted credentials disabled and expose secrets only to the final local script step. The release gate adds actions: read to contents: read to verify the environment branch rules and download candidate artifacts using the native token. Neither workflow requests id-token: write; GitHub OIDC validation remains isolated in live-github-oidc-e2e.yml. The release gate additionally requires digest-pinned controller, Publisher, Codex, OpenCode, Claude, and Copilot images; a Ready central provider proxy; the config/acp-production Vekil ingress boundary; durable controller/Publisher PVCs; a distinct publication fork; and authenticated gh access for independent remote and PR verification/cleanup. The validator runs Codex, then OpenCode, Claude, and Copilot, deleting each provider's pools before starting the next. Every provider phase verifies exact Pod UID, image ID, runtime instance/profile, and RuntimeSession identity. Smoke mode also checks continuation, OpenCode's read-intent tool policy, and, for Codex, concurrency, cancellation and timeout settlement, controller restart, and pool replacement. Release mode runs only the reads and, with the local opt-in, the live publication canary. E2E_OPENAI_API_KEY and E2E_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY remain inputs for older native type: ai test cases. They are not mounted into built-in ACP RuntimePools. When either key is unset, the suite deploys aimock in the test namespace and backs that provider with scripted fixtures from test/e2e/testdata/aimock, so those specs run in the E2E lanes without credentials. Set E2E_DISABLE_MOCK_LLM=1 to skip them instead. Fixture conventions are in test/e2e/testdata/aimock/README.md. The Anthropic-compatible API, coordination memory tool, and agent runtime matrix specs also run on aimock by default; with E2E_LIVE_COPILOT_PROXY_BASE_URL set they use the live proxy instead. The suite enables Task provenance trust after verifying the orka-admission provenance webhook that make deploy installs, so coordination messaging and cancel_task run in the default lane. The Agent runtime lifecycle job in test-e2e.yml runs the agent-runtime label on its own Kind cluster, and the default job excludes it. Those specs restart the controller and park, replace, and scale RuntimePools, and they need the production idle pool TTL, so the job sets E2E_ACP_IDLE_POOL_TTL=15m (the default lane uses 5s). Run them locally with make test-e2e E2E_GINKGO_LABEL_FILTER=agent-runtime E2E_ACP_IDLE_POOL_TTL=15m. The default lane also runs one clean-room publication end to end without github.com: a scripted Codex RuntimePool talks to a second aimock deployed as vekil-system/vekil behind the production provider proxy, and the publisher clones from, pushes to, and opens a pull request on an in-cluster fake forge (test/fixtures/fakeforge: real Git smart HTTP plus the GitHub REST endpoints the publisher calls). COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN also remains the credential for live-copilot-proxy-e2e.yml, which covers the external proxy as native Provider test infrastructure. Agent Runtime E2E provides the provider-execution evidence for the built-in RuntimePool profiles. Structural e2e tests for native worker Jobs run without external model keys. Live Agent Sandbox E2E and Agent Substrate E2E do run workspace-backed ACP Tasks end to end against a local model fixture, but they are not the full release gate: external-provider execution stays with Agent Runtime E2E, and release acceptance with Release Qualification. Every Substrate run includes DataOnly suspension, cold continuation, and checkpoint file recovery against the unmodified upstream provider. Security Scan E2E is secret-free and model-free, but requires Docker plus the local Go, Kind, kubectl, curl, and jq toolchain. Gateway Live E2E is model-free and secret-free. Its focused invocation sets E2E_GATEWAY=true and E2E_EPHEMERAL_CLUSTER=true; the last flag skips per-resource suite cleanup because the caller deletes the entire Kind cluster. GitHub Actions id-token: write permission: required by the live GitHub OIDC workflow. For local/manual runs of scripts/live-github-oidc-e2e.sh, set ORKA_GITHUB_OIDC_TOKEN to a valid JWT instead. Provider-specific transaction-token E2E lives in the external integration repositories. E2E_LIVE_COPILOT_PROXY_BASE_URL (or E2E_COPILOT_PROXY_BASE_URL / COPILOT_PROXY_BASE_URL): enables the focused live copilot-proxy spec against a running proxy E2E_LIVE_COPILOT_PROXY_SERVICE_NAMESPACE, E2E_LIVE_COPILOT_PROXY_SERVICE_NAME, E2E_LIVE_COPILOT_PROXY_SERVICE_PORT: direct-access proxy coordinates used by the legacy Provider, Chat, and Anthropic compatibility specs. E2E_LIVE_ACP_PROVIDER_PROXY_SERVICE_NAMESPACE, E2E_LIVE_ACP_PROVIDER_PROXY_SERVICE_NAME, E2E_LIVE_ACP_PROVIDER_PROXY_SERVICE_PORT: model-discovery coordinates for the ACP RuntimePool matrix. The full live script pins these to vekil-system, vekil, and 1337 so built-in RuntimePools traverse the production provider-proxy DNS and NetworkPolicy boundary. Live provider/chat tests prefer gpt-5-mini and claude-haiku-4.5 when available. The runtime smoke and release qualification scripts default to gpt-5.4-mini for Codex and OpenCode, claude-haiku-4.5 for Claude, and gpt-5.3-codex for Copilot. Override these with ACP_E2E_CODEX_MODEL, ACP_E2E_OPENCODE_MODEL, ACP_E2E_CLAUDE_MODEL, or ACP_E2E_COPILOT_MODEL. Configured models must pass the Vekil catalog and streaming probes. Run the trusted smoke bootstrap locally with the token exported in the shell rather than placed on a command line: read -rsp 'Copilot provider token: ' COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN && echo export COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN export ACP_E2E_OPENCODE_MODEL=openai/gpt-5.4-mini export ACP_E2E_OPENCODE_CONTEXT_WINDOW=32768 export ACP_E2E_OPENCODE_MAX_TOKENS=4096 ACP_E2E_KIND_TAG=local bash scripts/agent-runtime-kind-e2e.sh For a local qualification diagnostic, use read-only GitHub CLI access and the same model-provider configuration as the smoke run. GitHub's automatic job token is available only inside Actions. To use that token without configuring local GitHub access, dispatch Release Qualification. The local wrapper runs the required Git and PR fixture tests before creating the cluster: export RELEASE_GATE=1 export ACP_E2E_WRITE_CREATE_PR=0 export ACP_E2E_REPO=https://github.com/orka-agents/orka.git export ACP_E2E_REF="$(git rev-parse HEAD)" export ACP_E2E_BASE_BRANCH=main bash scripts/agent-runtime-kind-e2e.sh The fixture tests, image build, and runtime phases use the same candidate. The wrapper requires a clean checkout at that commit, and the candidate must equal the selected branch head. Local reports are saved under bin/acp-release-*/acceptance.json, or ACP_E2E_REPORT_FILE when set. --keep-cluster leaves cleanup pending and cannot qualify a release; use the trusted workflow and report verifier above for release records. The existing local live GitHub diagnostic remains available with ACP_E2E_WRITE_CREATE_PR=1 and separately authorized canary credentials. Its four-role and distinct-fork requirements are listed in the validator's --help. The hosted release workflow cannot enable it and explicitly reports live GitHub publication as not_tested. Do not enable shell xtrace for either invocation. The scripts create Kubernetes Secrets without printing their values and redact provider/GitHub token patterns from failure diagnostics. External workspace provider and core handoff tests live in the shared repository. The fake provider lane checks two-replica leader election, API field ownership, unauthorized writers, exact public Pod identity, and authorized retirement. Its core lane runs the production supervisor and a real RuntimeSession/Task with a deterministic ACP agent, verifies authenticated boot and prompt fences, and observes credential revocation and exact Pod termination. Standalone Sandbox and Substrate lanes verify native allocation, cold resume, filesystem data, and exact cleanup. Substrate also exports and imports verified data checkpoints after source deletion. They do not claim real core credential bootstrap or full-memory restore. NetworkPolicy object checks on default kind do not prove packet enforcement. An additional native Core Task lane passed real fail-closed admission, sealed bootstrap, authenticated Serving, RuntimeSession and prompt execution, persisted result, and exact native/Core compute and credential retirement. The upgrade lane tests stock binary rejection of legacy pools and every retained workspace state before and after schema pruning. See external workspace local proof for the two-repository workflow. The RepositoryMonitor validation bundle covers the canonical signed orka:implement entrypoint, durable intake, pause controls, and replay against GitHub fixtures. The live GitHub OIDC workflow (.github/workflows/live-github-oidc-e2e.yml) runs scripts/live-github-oidc-e2e.sh in GitHub Actions with id-token: write. It builds the controller from the PR, deploys it to a fresh Kind cluster, configures the GitHub OIDC issuer and workflow audience, fetches a real Actions OIDC token, and validates: unauthenticated API requests return 401 OIDC-authenticated Task creation returns 201 the created Task contains verified spec.requestedBy provenance top-level requestedBy and nested spec.requestedBy client tampering are rejected with 400 the OIDC token does not appear in controller logs Native Substrate MCP Tool and actor-pool behavior remains in core. External ACP allocation, lifecycle, and checkpoint conformance belongs to the shared provider repository. Each native proof records the pinned backend, provider source, resource identities, and observed termination; it does not add native lifecycle UID/version preconditions that the upstream protocol lacks.

Frontend tests use Vitest + Testing Library + MSW. cd ui && bun run test # what CI runs cd ui && bun run test:coverage # adds the coverage report and threshold check The UI coverage thresholds are a local target, not a merge gate ui/vite.config.ts declares thresholds of 95% statements, 80% branches, 90% functions, and 95% lines. Those only apply to bun run test:coverage. The ui-test job in .github/workflows/test.yml runs plain bun run test, so a pull request that drops coverage still passes CI. Run the coverage command yourself before assuming a number.

Normal binary e2e tests build and invoke bin/orka directly with isolated config/home directories. They intentionally avoid real secrets in command arguments and assert stdout/stderr do not leak configured tokens or sentinel secret values. CLI area Binary e2e status Notes auth Covered validate, whoami; invalid-token negative path. models Covered OpenAI and Anthropic compatibility list output. config Covered Isolated HOME, set-server, fake set-token, masked view. status Covered Health/readiness/task/agent summary. task Covered Manifest create, flag create (including read/write workspace policy), structured status, list/filter, get, wait, result, logs, children, plan, artifacts, download, delete. workspace Covered Canonical workspace intent, credential-role presence, and delivery status. runtime-pool Focused unit coverage CRUD routing plus lifecycle/admission/capacity table output. agent-runtime Focused unit coverage CRUD routing plus v2-only identity/profile table output. provider Covered CRUD and secret redaction expectations. agent Covered CRUD. tool Covered CRUD. skill Covered init, validate, import, list, get, content, update, delete. secret Covered Metadata-only list. audit Covered Trace no-match path. session Covered List/get/delete against a controlled fixture. memory Covered Create/list/get/disable/enable/update/delete and proposal-list smoke. security Partially covered Repository scan create/get/list/delete, threat model update/get, scan/finding/slice/dropped-finding list; repository scan update is not covered. monitor Partially covered Repository monitor create/get/list/delete plus runs/items/events list; monitor update is not covered. usage Compiled-binary fixture coverage Summary table, work JSON, other-usage YAML, configured authentication, and nonzero exit for a missing work request. substrate Covered Pool create/get/list/update/delete. run Negative covered; positive live-gated Unreachable-server error path is safe for normal e2e; positive chat/SSE flow needs provider fixtures. dashboard Negative covered The default install serves no dashboard, so the e2e covers the refusal before any token URL is printed; the browser-open token URL remains unsuitable for normal e2e logs. completion Covered Binary smoke generates bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell completion output. security scan run Deferred/live-gated Creates downstream scan Tasks and requires live agent/GitHub/provider setup. monitor run Deferred/live-gated Creates downstream monitor work and can require GitHub/provider setup. security finding actions Deferred/live-gated Need stable finding fixtures or live scan data. Use this matrix as a coverage guide when adding CLI commands: non-live command groups should have at least one compiled-binary e2e smoke path, and CRUD-style groups should cover create/get/list/update/delete where the API supports it.

Some commands intentionally create downstream work or require external services. Keep these behind explicit operator intent in automation and e2e tests. orka run​ orka run streams chat responses over the Orka chat API. A positive smoke needs server-side chat enabled plus a configured provider/model or agent: ORKA_API=http://127.0.0.1:8080 ORKA_TOKEN="$(kubectl create token orka-client -n orka-system)" orka --server "$ORKA_API" --token "$ORKA_TOKEN" \ run --session cli-live-smoke "Reply with one short sentence." For normal non-live validation, prefer a negative smoke against an unreachable or deliberately unconfigured server and assert a clean error without printing tokens. orka security scan run​ Manual security scan runs can create scan Tasks and may require GitHub credentials, analysis agents, provider credentials, and repository network access: orka security scan run my-repository-scan orka security scan list my-repository-scan -o json Gate this path with explicit environment variables in CI, for example ORKA_CLI_E2E_LIVE_ACTIONS=1, and skip by default when credentials or fixtures are missing. orka monitor run​ Manual repository monitor runs can enqueue repository review/repair work and may require GitHub credentials plus reviewer/repair agents: orka monitor run my-monitor --target-kind pull_request --target-number 123 orka monitor runs my-monitor -o json orka monitor items my-monitor -o json Use live-gated tests or manual verification for this path until stable GitHub/provider fixtures are available.

tests := []struct { name string input string want string wantErr bool }{ {"valid", "input", "output", false}, {"invalid", "bad", "", true}, } for _, tt := range tests { t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) { // test logic }) }
scheme := runtime.NewScheme() corev1alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme) corev1.AddToScheme(scheme) client := fake.NewClientBuilder().WithScheme(scheme).WithObjects(objs...).Build()
server := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK) w.Write([]byte(`{"result": "ok"}`)) })) defer server.Close()
app := fiber.New() app.Get("/test", handler) req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/test", nil) resp, _ := app.Test(req)
// Mock zustand persist middleware vi.mock('zustand/middleware', () => ({ persist: (fn: unknown) => fn })) // Use test utils with QueryClient wrapper import { render } from '@/test/test-utils'

When testing features via the chat endpoint, use natural prompts — the kind a human would actually type. Never reference internal concepts like agent names, tool names, or implementation details. Describe what you want done, not how the system should do it. The chat should infer the right agents, tools, delegation patterns, and cancellation logic on its own. Good examples: "Research the benefits of Kubernetes and write a technical guide based on the findings." "What's the best container orchestration tool? Get me an answer as fast as possible." "Draft an outline for a blog post about containers and turn it into a full post." "Compare microservices vs monoliths from three angles, then synthesize into a recommendation." Bad examples: "Create a coordinator agent and a researcher agent, then delegate two tasks..." "Use the send_message tool to send a message to task msg-receiver..." "Have three researchers race to answer..." (users don't think in terms of "researchers") "Use the first answer and cancel the others." (the system should infer this automatically)
Common failures, what causes them, and what to do. If you are looking for day-to-day operational procedures instead, see the runbook.

Two, depending on how you installed. Every kubectl command in these docs assumes one of them, so check before you copy one: Install method Deployment name kubectl apply -f .../deploy/orka.yaml orka-controller-manager helm install orka ... orka-controller The Helm name is <release-name>-controller, so it changes if you name the release something other than orka. When in doubt: kubectl -n orka-system get deploy
documents.s: What is my controller Deployment called?

documents.t: The chart validates its inputs before producing any manifests, so a bad install fails at helm install rather than at 3 a.m. The message names the value it wants. The common ones: Message mentions What it wants agentExecutionSnapshot.existingSecret Immutable once installed. Keep the name the live controller mounts. See below. watchNamespace Must be set, and must equal the release namespace. providerProxy When enabled, provide your gateway endpoint and egress rules. It can stay disabled during installation. See Provider proxy. upstreamBaseURL Your gateway's HTTP(S) URL, without credentials, a query, or a fragment. image Use a valid tag or SHA256 digest. Runtime overrides need a full registry/repository reference. replicas / leaderElect Must be 1 and true. The controller is a single writer. caBundle or caInjectionAnnotations You set webhooks.tls.existingSecret, so the chart needs the CA that signed it. Leave both empty to let the controller issue its own certificate. mode Only harness-v2 is supported.

controller.agentExecutionSnapshot encrypts stored agent execution records. A fresh install generates the key into a Secret named <release>-agent-execution-snapshot and reuses it on every upgrade, so you normally never touch it. To bring your own, create a Secret containing either 32 raw bytes or their base64 encoding before installing, and pass its name as existingSecret: kubectl -n orka-system create secret generic orka-agent-snapshot-key \ --from-literal=key="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" Do not rotate this casually The Secret name, the item key, and the key material must stay the same for the life of the release. Changing any of them makes every retained snapshot permanently unreadable. The chart guards only two of those three. On upgrade it compares the Secret name and item key against the live Deployment and fails if either changed. That includes switching between a generated Secret and your own. It cannot see the key material, so replacing the bytes under the same name and key passes the guard silently — and the controller then restarts unable to read any snapshot it wrote before. The generated Secret is kept on helm uninstall and reused by a reinstall under the same release name for the same reason. Treat the material as immutable yourself, and never use helm upgrade --force.

The controller-generated snapshot key is gone, but the SQLite dataset it belongs to already completed key bootstrap or was adopted from an older layout during an upgrade. The dataset records that history itself, so this applies even if every ordinary record has since been deleted. The controller refuses to mint a new key that could not read existing records. Restore the Secret from backup. If the data is expendable, delete the data volume and restart the controller to start over. See Dataset identity and key bootstrap.
documents.s: the SQLite dataset requires an existing key but snapshot key Secret ... has no "key" item

documents.t: At startup the controller forces a full SQLite checkpoint so dataset metadata is durable before it loads the key. The checkpoint could not finish because another process holds the database open, for example a sqlite3 shell or a backup job reading the data volume. Stop that process and restart the controller. Nothing is lost: committed metadata is kept, and startup resumes from it.
documents.s: synchronize SQLite dataset metadata: checkpoint incomplete

documents.t: The dataset metadata row inside the database is malformed. If the row is missing, the message is SQLite dataset identity must contain exactly one record instead. Either usually means the database was edited outside Orka. The controller never regenerates this row, because it decides whether a new snapshot key may be minted. Restore the data volume and its key from backup rather than editing the row by hand.

The database's schema version marker is one this controller does not support. Usually a newer Orka release wrote the database and the controller image was then downgraded. Migration is forward-only, so run the release that wrote the database. Rolling back further needs a coordinated restore of the database, its original key, configuration, and Kubernetes state; see Automatic pre-upgrade backup. The controller leaves the database unchanged.

Check the logs first. The Deployment name depends on how you installed, so discover it rather than guessing: # The two installs label the controller differently, so try both. # Helm sets app.kubernetes.io/component=controller; the release manifest # sets control-plane=controller-manager and no component label at all. CONTROLLER="$(kubectl -n orka-system get deploy \ -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller \ -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}' 2>/dev/null)" CONTROLLER="${CONTROLLER:-$(kubectl -n orka-system get deploy \ -l control-plane=controller-manager \ -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')}" kubectl -n orka-system logs "deploy/$CONTROLLER" --previous That is orka-controller for a Helm release named orka, and orka-controller-manager for the release manifest, as the table above shows. unable to resolve ACP runtime images At startup the controller resolves the coding-agent runtime image tags to digests by asking the registry, ghcr.io for the default images, over HTTPS. If the controller Pod cannot reach it, through a proxy or an egress policy, the controller stays up but every coding-agent runtime is unavailable until it restarts: AI and container Tasks work, agent Tasks fail with an unavailable runtime. Either allow that access, or pin the runtime images to digests so no lookup is needed, or set the images to empty strings to run without coding agents, then restart the controller: helm upgrade orka orka/orka --namespace orka-system --reuse-values \ --set-string controller.acpRuntime.codexImage= \ --set-string controller.acpRuntime.claudeImage= \ --set-string controller.acpRuntime.copilotImage= \ --set-string controller.acpRuntime.opencodeImage= See Image overrides. --watch-namespace is required; controller modes cannot use a cluster-wide watch Orka watches exactly one namespace. Set controller.watchNamespace to the release namespace. controller-mode namespace claim failed or namespace "...": unsupported execution mode "..." The namespace already carries an orka.ai/controller-mode label other than harness-v2. The controller claims an unlabeled namespace on its own, but it never takes over a namespace claimed for another mode, and the label cannot be changed once set. Install into a new namespace. If you run the controller with --claim-namespace-mode=false, label the namespace yourself before starting it: kubectl label namespace orka-system orka.ai/controller-mode=harness-v2 Do not relabel a namespace another installation owns. unable to read controller-mode namespace The namespace does not exist yet, or the controller's ServiceAccount cannot read it.

In order of likelihood: Wrong namespace. Orka only sees its watch namespace. A Task in default is never reconciled and produces no error — it just sits there. kubectl get task '<name>' -A # where did it actually land? kubectl -n orka-system get tasks # where Orka is looking The Agent or Provider is missing, or is in a different namespace. Check kubectl -n orka-system describe task <name> for the reason. Concurrency limit reached. If maxTasksPerNamespace is set, new Tasks queue. kubectl -n orka-system get tasks shows how many are Running. No pool capacity for a type: agent Task. kubectl -n orka-system get runtimepools — a pool that is not Serving and Accepting will not take new sessions.

The runtime image was not configured. If you did not set controller.acpRuntime.codexImage (or claude/copilot/opencode), that runtime is unavailable and Tasks asking for it fail rather than falling back to another. This is intentional. The provider proxy is not reachable or not ready. Built-in coding agents need the optional provider proxy enabled and connected to your gateway. Check that gateway's readiness and network access, then check Orka's proxy: kubectl -n orka-system get deploy -l app.kubernetes.io/component=provider-auth-proxy See Provider proxy. Codex with allowBash: false. The Codex CLI has no reliable shell-disable mode, so Orka fails fast instead of pretending the restriction is enforced. Set defaultAllowBash: true. OpenCode without contextWindow and maxTokens. Both are required and must be set on the Agent.
documents.s: A type: agent Task fails immediately

documents.t: The Pod filesystem is read-only outside /tmp, /home/worker, and /workspace, and bash -lc breaks official language images. Both are covered in Container tasks.
documents.s: go: command not found or read-only filesystem errors

documents.t: A pool drains before it is replaced: in-flight sessions finish, new ones are refused. If it is stuck, something is still holding a session. Check kubectl -n orka-system describe runtimepool <name> for the sessions it is waiting on. Deleting the Pods directly does not help — the controller will wait for the drain regardless.
documents.s: A pool will not replace or scale down

documents.t: Namespace mismatch. The API serves exactly one namespace. Asking for another returns namespace not allowed, with the requested and allowed namespaces in the controller log. The token has no namespace. With enforceNamespaceIsolation on (the default), authenticated callers must carry a namespace. A token from a ServiceAccount in the wrong namespace, or a user token with no namespace at all, is rejected. The caller lacks the requested permission. Kubernetes TokenReview callers need RBAC permission for each protected API operation, checked through SubjectAccessReview. This includes Agent creation, chat, approval decisions, and stored records such as sessions and memories. Nested chat tools need their own resource permissions. A successful authentication check does not grant access to those actions. OIDC and transaction tokens retain their separate policies; see API authorization. The Helm chart creates a client ServiceAccount and namespace-scoped Role. Raw-manifest and Kustomize installs do not create a client ServiceAccount. Current-source bundles include orka-api-viewer-role and orka-api-editor-role; for a client that can create Tasks and use chat, bind the editor role: kubectl -n orka-system create serviceaccount orka-client kubectl -n orka-system create rolebinding orka-client \ --clusterrole=orka-api-editor-role --serviceaccount=orka-system:orka-client Use orka-api-viewer-role for read-only access. The editor also permits Agent, Tool, and Provider changes, memory review/apply, and security actions. Use a narrower Role from the permission inventory when that exceeds the client's needs. Both helper roles keep Secrets and workspace-class use separate; nested tools that run Kubernetes workloads need explicit workload grants as well. If a bundle does not include these helper roles, apply config/rbac/api_viewer_role.yaml and config/rbac/api_editor_role.yaml from a checkout containing the authorization update. Files applied directly use the unprefixed names api-viewer-role and api-editor-role; use those names in the RoleBinding instead. GatewayClass reads require a separate cluster-scoped grant. If the client needs them, bind the installed GatewayClass viewer role: kubectl create clusterrolebinding orka-client-gatewayclass-viewer \ --clusterrole=orka-gatewayclass-viewer-role --serviceaccount=orka-system:orka-client Sessions, chats, memories, and other stored records use virtual RBAC resources without CRDs. Their grants are included in the API helper roles.
Add -n orka-system. The ServiceAccount lives in the watch namespace. If it is still not found, create it and its RBAC roles; raw-manifest and Kustomize installs do not create it.
ORKA_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS controls the allowed origins and defaults to *. If you have narrowed it, add your origin. See Configuration.
documents.s: Browser requests fail with a CORS error

documents.t: Helm does not create or update CRDs during helm upgrade — a Helm behavior, not an Orka one. Apply the CRDs from the target chart yourself first. See Upgrading.
documents.s: Custom resources disappear or the controller reports unknown fields

documents.t: Several values are immutable for the life of a release: controller.mode, controller.watchNamespace, the snapshot key Secret and item key, the release fullname, and the ACP runtime namespace. Changing any of them means a new release, not an upgrade.
Gateway state lives in the controller's SQLite store, and its failure modes are specific enough to have their own page — including the two ways to corrupt a backup. See Gateways.

kubectl -n orka-system logs "deploy/$CONTROLLER" -f # $CONTROLLER from above kubectl -n orka-system describe task '<name>' kubectl -n orka-system get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp orka task events '<name>' orka task trace '<name>' Durable per-Task history is in execution events, which survive Pod restarts and are the right thing to read when the logs have rotated away. Set controller.logLevel=debug for more detail. If you think you have found a bug, open an issue.

Orka includes a web dashboard built into the controller. There is nothing extra to deploy, but it is off by default: the API and the orka CLI work without it, and a signed-in browser keeps its token in localStorage on the same origin as every API, so leave it off where nobody needs a browser UI.

With Helm, set controller.dashboard.enabled: helm upgrade orka orka/orka --namespace orka-system --reuse-values \ --set controller.dashboard.enabled=true Without Helm, start the controller with --dashboard-enabled, or set its ORKA_DASHBOARD_ENABLED environment variable: kubectl -n orka-system set env deployment/orka-controller-manager ORKA_DASHBOARD_ENABLED=true While it is off, paths outside the APIs answer with a JSON 404, orka dashboard stops with an error, and connector consent finishes with orka connection complete (see Connectors). Try it without a cluster The dashboard demo runs in your browser on sample data, with a guided tour of the main pages. Nothing in it reaches a cluster or a model.

Forward the API port if it is not already forwarded, and have a client token ready (see Connect to the API): kubectl -n orka-system port-forward svc/orka 8080:8080 kubectl -n orka-system create token orka-client Open http://localhost:8080. The login page asks for a token; paste the one you just created. From there you can create Tasks, chat with the orchestrator, watch Tasks run live, and browse sessions and artifacts. If you use the CLI, orka dashboard opens the dashboard already signed in.

Page Route What it shows Dashboard / A Needs you card with the top attention items, Task, session, agent, and tool counts, and recent Tasks Usage /usage Model usage and tokens per merged pull request by team. See Usage and PR outcomes Chat /chat The chat orchestrator, with streamed tool calls. See Interactive chat Monitors /monitors Repository monitors: runs, pull request and issue queues, workflow timeline, blocked reasons, implementation jobs, and GitHub mutation audit. See Repository monitors Security /security Repository scans, threat models, findings, validation, patch proposals, and remediation pull requests. See Security scanning Tasks /tasks Create, monitor, and manage Tasks, with log streaming Task detail /tasks/:taskId Overview (current activity, progress, delivery, tokens, derived checks, child tasks), Activity (trace and raw events), Approvals, Result and artifacts, Logs, Spec (the Task resource), and Plan for autonomous runs Board /kanban Tasks as a Kanban board. ?view=phase (the default) groups by status; ?view=attention groups into Needs you, Agent working, and Done Approvals /approvals Every approval in the namespace that can still be decided, including parked sign-offs, soonest deadline first Gateways /gateways Gateway readiness, bindings, per-Session queues, event timelines, and delivery attempts. See Gateways Sessions /sessions Sessions with message counts and token use; each one's transcript and timeline across its Tasks Runtimes /runtimes RuntimePool capacity and admission, and external AgentRuntime registrations Agents /agents Agents with their model and tools, and a form to create one Tools /tools Built-in and custom tools, with their parameter schemas Connectors /settings/connectors Link your own accounts, such as GitHub, for agents to act as you. See Connectors Login /login Sign in with a token

The dashboard card, the attention board and the approvals inbox read the namespace's attention view (GET /api/v1/attention) and approvals inbox (GET /api/v1/approvals?status=pending). See Find pending approvals across Tasks for what each item holds and who can see it. Needs you lists, in order: approvals that can still be decided (soonest deadline first), Tasks with an unknown outcome, failed Tasks from the last 24 hours, Tasks whose Pod cannot start, and blocked repository monitor actions when your token may list monitors. Agent working holds Pending, Scheduled, Running, and Finalizing Tasks, Tasks waiting for runtime or workspace capacity, and Tasks parked on child Tasks or a timer. Done holds every other Task. A Task parked on a sign-off has ended its turn, so its phase is Succeeded, but it shows Waiting for approval everywhere until the sign-off is decided. On the board, a Task whose own state shows it waiting for approval (a waiting-for-approval condition or status message, or an armed parked sign-off) is never put in Agent working or Done. When the ranking has no item for it, because you cannot read its approvals or the ranking is behind, Needs you shows a Waiting for approval card built from the Task alone. It links to the Task and shows no approval detail. Items show only a short summary. The inbox shows Review to approve only when the server reports that you may approve; it opens the Task's Approvals tab, so you inspect the exact operation before approving there. Decline appears only when you may decline and posts the decision for the exact Task the inbox listed. If someone else decided first, the row says Already decided. When neither hint is settled, the row links to the Task instead. The inbox loads further pages with Load more. The board reads up to 2,000 attention items before it groups Tasks; past that it says Agent working and Done may include Tasks that need you. When a scan bound was hit, each view says the list may be incomplete. Agent working and Done wait for the attention ranking. If it cannot be loaded, they say the Tasks are not sorted instead of placing them in Done. When the controller has no execution event storage, approvals cannot be read: the views say so and an empty list says approvals were not checked. When your token may list Tasks but cannot read some of those waiting for approval, for example a context token without orka:tasks:get, the views say some approvals could not be checked, and an empty list says so too. When your token cannot list repository monitors, a quiet note says blocked monitor actions are not shown. A permission error, or an inbox that becomes unavailable, replaces any list already on screen, so you never act on stale rows. Other refresh failures keep the last list with a note that it could not be refreshed; on the board, Agent working and Done stay unsorted until the ranking loads again.

Task and session detail pages surface the evented execution backbone (see the Execution Events reference for the underlying APIs): Activity tab, Trace view (the default) — an explainable, grouped view from GET /tasks/:id/trace: lifecycle summary, model requests, tool calls, child tasks (linkable), workspace, artifacts, approvals, fork provenance, and errors/warnings, with a raw-timeline fallback when no structured groups exist. Activity tab, Raw events view — the semantic execution event stream for a task, loaded from GET /tasks/:id/events and followed live over GET /tasks/:id/stream. Events are deduplicated by sequence, grouped by category, and filterable by category, severity, and free-text search. Redacted/truncated payloads are marked and the raw (already-redacted) payload is available behind a disclosure toggle and a copy-JSON action. Live follow stops on the terminal stream_complete frame. Approvals tab — pending high-risk approvals from GET /tasks/:id/approvals with approve/decline actions (optional reason) posted to POST /tasks/:id/approvals/:approvalID/decision. Buttons disable while a decision is in flight; conflicts (decided elsewhere/expired) surface inline. Fork from a checkpoint — each raw event row offers "Fork from here", which opens a dialog seeded with that event's sequence and posts to POST /tasks/:id/fork. Forked tasks show a provenance card derived from their orka.ai/fork-source-task and orka.ai/fork-source-seq annotations. Session timeline — session detail aggregates events across the session's tasks from GET /sessions/:id/events / GET /sessions/:id/stream, with each row linking to its originating task. These surfaces hide gracefully (with a clear message) when execution event storage is not enabled on the server (501 Not Implemented).

The UI uses ServiceAccount bearer tokens stored in localStorage: CLI: orka dashboard creates a 24-hour ServiceAccount token with kubectl create token (or uses --token) and opens the browser with #token=<token> Manual login: Paste a ServiceAccount token on the login page Token creation: kubectl create token orka-client -n orka-system All API requests include Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Dark/light theme: Toggle with localStorage persistence Namespace selector: Filter all views by Kubernetes namespace Security workflow: Manage repository scans, edit threat models, triage findings, validate/reproduce issues, generate patch proposals, and open remediation PRs Skeleton loaders: Loading states for all list/detail pages Error handling: Global error boundary, toast notifications, 401 redirect Responsive design: Mobile-responsive sidebar, tables, and cards Auto-refresh: TanStack Query refetchInterval for live status updates Live event streams: SSE-backed task/session execution timelines that reconnect from the last sequence and recover history after refresh Cursor pagination: Kubernetes-style continue token pagination
The dashboard's source, its development server, and its tests live in ui/; see its README.

Orka supports in-place SQLite upgrades from the exact layouts listed below. This is a narrow database compatibility guarantee, not support for every older release or deployment topology. This procedure covers harness v2 installations only. Follow Install Orka for new installations.

The release checks install the chart after creating CRDs and internal Secrets separately. They restart the controller using the same data and encryption key, confirm that tasks still work, and check that Helm rejects an unsupported controller.mode. Results are in the release's acceptance.json. These checks do not test Helm's automatic CRD and Secret creation. Broader coverage for upgrades between versions and restoring a lost installation from backups is tracked in #499 and #505.

This release is the compatibility/warning phase of #680. All native type: ai Tasks still receive recall_memory, remember, propose_memory, and search_transcript, regardless of their selected tools or coordination configuration. This includes Tasks with orka.ai/disable-coordination-tool-injection: "true" and Agents whose memory-tool references have enabled: false. This release does not yet provide per-Agent memory-tool denial. The worker emits a structured warning when the model calls a memory tool that will lose automatic access in the next release. Unused tools do not warn. Tools explicitly selected by the Agent or Task do not warn, nor do automatically injected tools for an Agent with coordination.enabled: true and no disable-injection annotation. Child-task identity alone is not coordination opt-in. Update the controller and AI worker together so the worker receives the controller's deprecation metadata. The next release will enforce opt-in. Before upgrading to that release: List the memory tools the Agent needs in spec.tools, with enabled omitted or true, or list them in the Task's spec.ai.tools. Explicit selections will remain available even with the disable-injection annotation. Alternatively, use an Agent with coordination.enabled: true and no disable-injection annotation. This also adds other coordination tools; prefer explicit memory selections when those capabilities are not needed. Keep transaction-token tctx.allowedTools grants for all four memory tools throughout this warning release. Narrow grants only after the enforcing release's effective tool list no longer contains the omitted tools. For example, preserve only the memory tools an Agent needs by adding these selections before the enforcing release (the warning release still exposes all four): spec: tools: - name: recall_memory - name: remember remember and propose_memory still create review proposals rather than applying durable memories. Startup loading of reviewed memories into the prompt is separate and unchanged; tool opt-in does not disable that context. ACP/coding-agent runtime tool policy is unchanged.

spec.webhookURL notices are now signed, durable, and bounded. Review receivers before upgrading: Every request carries an Ed25519-signed X-Orka-Signature and a stable X-Orka-Delivery-ID. Unverified receivers keep working, but should start verifying against /.well-known/orka/task-webhook-jwks.json. See Task webhooks. The signing key lives in a new namespace that holds only that Secret and binds only the controller: <release namespace>-task-webhook-signing for Helm (value controller.taskWebhooks.signingNamespace), orka-task-webhook-signing for kustomize (flag --task-webhook-signing-namespace). The chart and the kustomize install create the namespace and a controller Role in it; the controller creates the Secret and mints the key on first use. Installs that grant RBAC some other way must grant the controller get and update on that Secret and create on Secrets there. The controller refuses to start if the signing namespace is its own, the watch, ACP runtime or agent-host namespace. See Who can read the signing key. Builds of main from before this change kept the key in the controller namespace, where Tasks could mount it. They mint a new key in the new namespace, so receivers see a new kid and refetch the JWKS. Delete the old Secret (<fullname>-task-webhook-signing or orka-task-webhook-signing in the controller namespace) after upgrading. A new ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, <fullname>-ai-worker-identity-protection (orka-ai-worker-identity-protection for kustomize), limits what the AI worker ServiceAccount may create. Before, the default AI worker role could create a ServiceAccount-token Secret or a Job that named the controller's ServiceAccount and act as the controller, or delete and recreate a platform ServiceAccount to inherit its RoleBindings. Now it may write only Opaque Secrets, create or delete only code_exec's own orka-code-exec-* ServiceAccounts, and create only code_exec-shaped Jobs: named orka-code-exec-*, running as the ServiceAccount of the same name with automountServiceAccountToken: false, with only code_exec Pod labels (so the Pod joins no other component's Service or NetworkPolicy allowance), no subdomain, only emptyDir and Secret volumes, no host namespaces or ports, no init or ephemeral containers, and non-root, unprivileged containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, all capabilities dropped and none added, and a RuntimeDefault or Localhost seccomp profile. Orka's own worker already works this way. Anything else that writes Secrets, Jobs or ServiceAccounts as the AI worker ServiceAccount is now rejected. If you run such code and cannot move it to its own ServiceAccount, set workers.ai.identityProtection: false (Helm) or drop orka-ai-worker-identity-protection and its binding from your kustomize build. Under the default AI worker RBAC profile, that lets the AI worker act as the controller again, including reading the webhook signing key. Orka's ServiceAccounts now carry orka.ai/platform-identity: "true", in both installs and on worker accounts the controller creates. An OutboundAccessPolicy whose serviceAccountRef names one, or names the controller or a worker ServiceAccount the controller is configured with (labeled or not, for example an externally managed controller account), now reports ReferenceDenied, and the controller revokes any TokenRequest grant it held. The AI worker's own ServiceAccount is the one exception: a token for itself gives it nothing new. Point other such policies at a dedicated ServiceAccount. Check the release namespace for ServiceAccount-token Secrets (kubectl -n <namespace> get secrets --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token). The default AI worker profile can read them; delete any you do not need, and treat a token for a privileged account as exposed. With signing enabled but no usable key (the Secret cannot be read or holds a malformed key), nothing is sent and no attempt is consumed: the delivery stays Pending until a key is available. With signing disabled (--task-webhook-signing-secret=""), notices are not sent and their deliveries are marked Failed; enabling signing later does not retry them. Destinations are checked at connect time. A DNS failure, any non-public resolved address, a redirect, or a proxy is no longer tolerated, so a host name that resolves to a private address stops receiving notices. Use a Service in the Task's namespace for in-cluster receivers. Failed deliveries are retried at most 8 times with exponential backoff, not every 30 seconds forever. Literal private IPs and other policy violations fail at once. The JSON body gains deliveryId, eventType, occurredAt, and taskUID. Existing fields are unchanged.
documents.s: Task webhooks are signed and fail closed

documents.t: This affects installs from the raw installer (deploy/orka.yaml); the Helm chart does not ship this role. orka-workspace-executionworkspaceclass-admin-role used to grant * on ExecutionWorkspaceClasses. It now lists its verbs: create, delete, deletecollection, get, list, patch, update, watch, and use. Anyone bound to it can still manage classes and select them for Tasks. The role no longer grants operator-access, the verb required to opt a class into orka task exec and orka task cp. Grant that verb separately to whoever should enable operator access; see Operator workspace access.
documents.s: The class admin role no longer grants every verb

documents.t: Orka creates its SQLite database on first startup. Restarts reuse that database and keep its records. Keep the data volume and encryption key together. The controller compares the complete schema, including every table and index definition, before upgrading. These immutable main-branch revisions identify supported source layouts; they are unreleased baselines, not release-version compatibility promises. Other commits with the exact same layout are equivalent. Object counts alone do not establish compatibility.
